epub_10.title: Five Great Campus Novels
epub_10.text:
Five Great Campus Novels
What We’re Reading
Five Great Campus Novels
By Merve Emre
September 02, 2026
“Half the campus
was designed by Bottom the Weaver, half by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe,” Randall Jarrell writes in his 1954 satire, “
Pictures from an Institution
.” In the novel, the university is home to two types: the asses and the industrialists. The former are dreamy, romantic; the latter, hard-nosed, pragmatic. Each of the campus novels below makes comedy out of these types, and warns us, as Jarrell did, “This institution’s drunk.”
The Amanda Cross Mysteries
, by Carolyn Heilbrun (1964-2002)
Heilbrun was the first tenured woman in Columbia’s English Department. In her detective series, under the pen name Amanda Cross, an English professor solves murders whose motives include bad psychoanalysis, student riots, and biographers who know too much for their own good. My favorite, “
Poetic Justice
,” was described as a “homicidal valentine” to Heilbrun’s mentor, Lionel Trilling.
“
Possession
,” by A. S. Byatt (1990)
A swoony double romance. The first love affair is between a Victorian poet and poetess who wrote coded letters and poems to each other in the nineteenth century. The second is between two scholars in the nineteen-eighties who set out to answer the only question worth asking: Did the poets
do it
? A little-known fact: great chunks of the poems are sentences in blank verse from Henry James’s “
The Golden Bowl
.”
“
Moo
,” by Jane Smiley (1995)
A pastoral satire about a Midwestern land-grant university, for readers who find John Williams’s “
Stoner
” too nostalgic and sentimental. The campus novel with the funniest building name (“Old Meats”), and the only one I have read that features the workers of the university: cafeteria servers, horse trainers.
“
The Last Samurai
,” by Helen DeWitt (2000)
A zany modern epic about a suicidal mother and her genius son, who trade perusing the dust-choked libraries of Oxford for riding the Tube, and the pathetic utilitarianism of the élite university for a useless love of ancient languages, atonal music, and games of chance. Also: a helpful book for teaching young children the Greek alphabet.
“
I Am Charlotte Simmons
,” by Tom Wolfe (2004)
Wolfe’s most hated novel, but my guilty pleasure since freshman year of college. At the fictional Dupont University, the beautiful, naïve, and self-superior Appalachian protagonist learns that what counts in the twenty-first century is not what you know, it’s who you know. Its alternative title could have been “Hillbilly Elegy.”
Our editors and critics choose the most captivating, notable, brilliant, surprising, absorbing, weird, thought-provoking, and talked-about books.
Find your next great read »
On Our Radar
Everybody’s talking about:
Marlon James’s “
The Disappearers
” is “the novel of the decade, if not the century,” a
Times
headline declared this week. We asked Katy Waldman, who has
a review of the book in this week’s magazine
, to weigh in: “I loved this novel, and I love Dwight Garner’s passion! At a certain point, if a book thrills you enough, you kind of owe it to the work to dig into how it achieves its effects. For me, James’s maximalism and his emotional delicacy work in counterpoint, and he’s fearless—he really presses us to wonder for six hundred pages whether embracing your gayness in nineteen-eighties Jamaica is worth the suffering. It is worth it, and the affirmation is beautifully hard-won.”
Coming soon:
“
Children of the Wolf
,” by Abby Geni, is about a woman who, decades after her childhood of being raised like a Viking in rural Iowa, notices that the men in her Michigan town are mysteriously disappearing. It’s out September 15th.
Sarah Blakley-Cartwright’s “
Heavy Cream
,” centering on a sixteen-year-old girl abandoned by her mother in New York City, will be released on September 29th.
Also out on the 29th is Robert Kolker’s nonfiction follow-up to “
Hidden Valley Road
”: “
The Vanishing Family
,” about the members of a nine-sibling family afflicted with a genetic mutation that causes a dramatic form of dementia.
In small-screen news, Kit Harington is starring in an adaptation of Charles Dickens’s “
A Tale of Two Cities
,” out on MGM+ on September 6th. You have just enough time for a read (or a reread).
Our critic Becca Rothfeld is loving:
“One of life’s greatest pleasures is selecting an author and reading her obsessively for months at a time,” Rothfeld notes. “I’ve been inhabiting the world of Edith Wharton since February, and, as far as I’m concerned, she can do no wrong. All her most famous books are exactly as good as everyone says they are, and several of her less famous books are better than most people care to tell you. Perhaps best of all is her 1917 novella, ‘
Summer
,’ which is so luscious and earthy that it reads almost like D. H. Lawrence. What could be better than a book that can be read in one long gasp and which blends Wharton’s biting social commentary with sublime flights about the body and the seasons? Not much!”
P.S. The Mary Oliver
documentary is
now streaming
.

epub_12.title: The America That 9/11 Made
epub_12.text:
The America That 9/11 Made
Comment
The America That 9/11 Made
A quarter century after the attacks, the grief, wars, and political furies of their aftermath still shape American life.
By Jill Lepore
September 06, 2026
I was jammed into an elevator in Minneapolis this summer, heading for the fiftieth floor, up like a shot, when someone tapped my shoulder. I wiggled in place, craned my neck around. “Hey, I know you,” a woman behind me said, smiling. “I took a class with you. I was in your lecture when the planes hit the towers.” We stepped off together—floor fifty turned out to be a wall of windows—and looked out at the city spread vertiginously below us, remembering that moment, twenty-five years ago, in a Boston University lecture hall. The class, The Emerging United States, started at 8
A.M
., so early that the student athletes brought breakfast and the room smelled like Egg McMuffins. That morning, we’d been in the eighteen-twenties, and I’d been blathering about Andrew Jackson and the penny press when cellphones across the hall started bleating like lost lambs.
Goddammit
, I’d thought.
No phones in class.
Then someone gasped, and someone shrieked, and someone called out that he’d received a text from his sister in New York, and the towers, oh my God, oh my God, the towers, thousands of people, Jesus no, oh my God. That couldn’t be true. Could it? Plenty of students didn’t have phones then (I didn’t), and texting was spotty. The phones kept ringing,
baa baa.
The Pentagon? The students were polite, hesitant. “Please, please answer your phones,” I said. “Pick up, call back, call.” The rest of us waited. A student talking to her father said that the planes had come from Logan and he wanted to know, Was she O.K., was Boston under attack? We knew nothing. What was safest: stay or go? Go, I decided. I ended class. Go straight to your dorms, and be safe, be safe. Then I got on my bicycle, turned on a radio bolted to the handlebars, listened to the unfathomable news, looked up at the clearest, bluest sky—no planes, no planes, no planes—and pedalled across the river to a day-care center to pick up my very little boys because mammals gather their young.
Every September 11th, people assemble near Ground Zero for the tolling of a bell, the whispering of prayers, the offering of flowers, the waving of flags. For twenty-four years, the bell has tolled six times: at 8:46
A.M.
, when a plane crashed into the north tower; 9:03
A.M.
, when a plane hit the south tower; 9:37
A.M.
, when a plane hit the Pentagon; 9:59
A.M.
, when the south tower fell; 10:03
A.M.
, when Flight 93 crashed into a field in western Pennsylvania; and 10:28
A.M.
, when the north tower fell. Between bells, mourners read aloud the names of the nearly three thousand people who died that day. There will be a seventh bell-tolling this year, for the thousands who have since died by suicide, or from cancer and other illnesses caused by the ravages of terrorism.
The day’s events are measured in minutes, a ticking clock; the grief in years, a beating heart. “When it began, September 11, 2001, seemed like just another ordinary day,” Mike Kelly writes in “After Ground Zero: Everyday Americans and the Unhealed Scars of 9/11.” Just before 7
a.m.
, a teen-ager heads to high school; his father goes into the city for a meeting. A young mother dresses her children; her husband begins his commute to Cantor Fitzgerald. A firefighter starts his shift in Queens. A priest dons his robes. A Morgan Stanley assistant vice-president boards a train. By noon, thousands have died, including a two-year-old girl flying to Disneyland, an eighty-five-year-old man travelling to his son’s wedding, and more than four hundred of the first responders who raced to the Twin Towers. Kelly focusses on what followed—“the emotional ruins and brokenness left behind in the lives of ordinary people”—as when, a month later, Kristen Breitweiser was informed that her husband’s left arm had been found, or when, three years later, she was notified that one of his shoulders had been identified, and that, given improved DNA testing, more news would likely follow. How long would this go on? “Would there be a call about Ron’s leg?” she wondered. “His torso? His head?”
Breitweiser has been a prominent voice among family members and survivors who have pressed for a fuller account of 9/11. Their efforts led to the 9/11 Commission Report, published in 2004, which, though riveting and detailed, held no one in the U.S. government responsible for intelligence lapses that failed to stop the hijackings. For many families, the opening of the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, in 2014, brought no solace. Steve Kandell—whose twenty-eight-year-old sister, Shari, was among the more than a thousand people whose remains were never identified—was an early visitor. Later, he wrote about inspecting artifacts and images in the three-hundred-and-fifty-million-dollar, hundred-and-ten-thousand-square-foot museum, from “the husk of an ambulance” to “handwritten pleas for help” and “dusty, ownerless Topsiders encased in glass”:
Everyone should have a museum dedicated to the worst day of their life and be forced to attend it with a bunch of tourists from Denmark. Annotated divorce papers blown up and mounted, interactive exhibits detailing how your mom’s last round of chemo didn’t take, souvenir T-shirts emblazoned with your best friend’s last words before the car crash. And you should have to see for yourself how little your pain matters to a family of five who need to get some food before the kids melt down. Or maybe worse, watch it be co-opted by people who want, for whatever reason, to feel that connection so acutely.
The rubble had been cleared, a report written, a museum built. Artifacts are still being collected: the Smithsonian National Museum of American History is exhibiting severed seat belts from Flight 93, singed I.D. badges from the Pentagon, battered briefcases from the Twin Towers. But there are other kinds of rubble, the dust and debris of anguish and fury.
On the fifteenth anniversary of 9/11, Kristen Breitweiser told Mike Kelly, “I’ve waited fifteen years. My husband was murdered with three thousand people and not one person has been held accountable. How is that possible?”
But
has
no one been held accountable? Millions have suffered, and hundreds of thousands have died. George W. Bush declared a global war on terror on September 20, 2001; the U.S. went to war in Afghanistan on October 7th. That war, the longest in American history, lasted twenty years. The Iraq War began in 2003. U.S. Special Operations Forces killed Osama bin Laden in 2011. The global war on terror has never been declared over. Brown University’s Costs of War project estimates that post-9/11 American military operations in Iraq, Afghanistan, Syria, Yemen, and Pakistan killed nearly a million people between 2001 and 2023, including more than four hundred thousand civilians. Non-civilian deaths include more than seven thousand U.S. service members, more than eight thousand military contractors, more than twelve thousand allied troops, and more than twenty-eight thousand U.S. service members and veterans who have died by suicide.
Janet Reitman weaves together character sketches to reckon with the aftermath of 9/11 in “The Inheritance: An American Tragedy in Five Acts.” After Marlo Cadeddu, an East Dallas lawyer who had once worked on the forty-sixth floor of the north tower, learned of the attack, Reitman writes, “she started to cry and kept on crying for what felt like five years.” She couldn’t stop thinking about how “one of the planes had flown directly into an elevator shaft, severed the cables, and sent cars filled with people plummeting seventy, eighty stories.”
The hijackers were dead. The search for their collaborators and other terrorists in what was now called the homeland proceeded under terms established by the Patriot Act. Many Muslim Americans hid or fled; between 2002 and 2003, thirteen thousand faced deportation proceedings. People around Cadeddu began disappearing: “The Lebanese stock boy at Kroger. The assistant professor of Middle Eastern history. The Palestinian grocer. The Pakistani computer scientist who spent every single night and weekend with his family. Sometimes they’d vanish for a few hours, or a day; other times they’d be gone for good.” Cadeddu became a leading defense attorney for Muslim Americans caught in dragnet sweeps that the F.B.I. was conducting across the country. Her clients included Mufid Abdulqader, whose half brother led Hamas; the F.B.I. arrested Abdulqader in 2004 and charged him with raising millions for terrorists. (Sentenced to twenty years, he was released in 2024.)
Terry Albury joined the F.B.I. as a counterterrorism expert in Minneapolis in 2001. He told Reitman that his training included viewing 9/11 footage over and over: “The planes hitting the towers, the smoke pouring out of the buildings, the people jumping to their deaths, the buildings collapsing into a toxic cloud. Death, destruction, devastation.” It was, he said, “like watching a snuff film.” He knocked on doors and grilled people based on what he considered scant evidence. In 2016, Albury began leaking documents to
The Intercept
. He was discovered, arrested, charged under the Espionage Act, and sentenced to four years in prison.
Nathan Damigo, a marine, completed two tours in Iraq, returned with P.T.S.D., attempted suicide twice, then committed violent crimes. He needed someone to blame—for the friends he watched die, his pain, everything. In prison, he began reading David Duke:
“Doesn’t it bother you that white people are being replaced by foreigners in our own country?” he asked his brother.
“Actually, man, not really.”
Out of prison, Damigo founded a white-supremacist group. In 2016, after attending the Republican National Convention, in Cleveland, he went to San Francisco and called through a bullhorn, “If you are here illegally, it’s time to go home. America is not your home.” The next year, at the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, neo-Nazis carrying tiki torches chanted a slogan of his coinage: “You will not replace us!” Dust and debris, anguish and fury.
In Minneapolis this summer, looking from the fiftieth-floor windows, I thought of how masked federal immigration agents had killed Renée Good and Alex Pretti in this beautiful city, and how the head of the Department of Homeland Security accused them of “domestic terrorism,” digging through the rubble, in vain, for Americans to blame.
A quarter century—a generation—has passed since the towers fell. My little boys are grown men. The students from that lecture hall have children of their own. They live in a different, and even angrier, America.
For years, as a first-day icebreaker, I asked students: What’s the first event of worldwide historical significance that entered your consciousness when you were young? One year, every student said 9/11, and a sophomore said, “My father died in the towers.” The room fell silent. There was no coming back from that answer. I stopped asking the question. ♦

epub_13.title: Can You Feel the Dub Tonight?
epub_13.text:
Can You Feel the Dub Tonight?
The Pictures
Can You Feel the Dub Tonight?
For years, a Peruvian voice actor has tried to get Disney to sign off on his Quechuan translation of “The Lion King.” The new documentary “Runa Simi” follows his path unwinding.
By Daniel Alarcón
September 07, 2026
Unlike the tourists pushing strollers and browsing bedazzled “Frozen” T-shirts at the midtown Disney Store on a recent morning, the activist and voice actor Fernando Valencia and the filmmaker Augusto Zegarra were on a pilgrimage, riding up a preposterously long escalator to the second floor with a sense of expectation and anxiety. “It’s like entering the Death Star,” Zegarra said, referencing “Star Wars,” a piece of very lucrative intellectual property that Disney did not create but that it does now own. “You feel like the cashier might introduce you to Mickey himself, and we could make our pitch.”
Valencia, handsome and slight, with a black ponytail and an embroidered fedora, was a bit more nuanced. “My relationship with Disney has changed every day since I was a little boy,” he said. “But I can’t help but see it as that impossible giant.”
The pitch they’d make, to Mickey Mouse or to anyone else in the Disney organization who might listen, is fairly simple: Valencia and Zegarra were in town to screen “Runa Simi”—a new documentary about Valencia’s years-long quest to dub Disney’s movie “The Lion King” into Quechua, an Indigenous language spoken by more than three million people in Peru’s highlands. Zegarra, burly, with a friendly smile partially obscured by a mustache, is the documentary’s director. And although showing the documentary in New York was exciting, what Valencia and Zegarra really wanted was to release it in Peru. The film—or, rather, the films, both the Quechua-dubbed “Lion King” and the documentary—is a love letter to a language, and to the culture woven into and defined by that language. (All told, there are some ten million Quechua speakers across the Andes, from northern Chile to southern Colombia, making it the most widely spoken Indigenous language of the Americas.)
The documentary chronicles Valencia’s stubborn attempts to get permission from the Disney corporation for his “Lion King” project. He e-mails, he calls, he D.M.s, but he never hears back from the company. “Runa Simi” uses very little copyrighted material, but Peru has more rigid rules regarding fair use than does the U.S. So far, Zegarra told me, no commercial distributor has been willing to risk showing “Runa Simi” in Peruvian theatres without written permission from Disney. It’s all very meta: a documentary about the unauthorized translation of a film, both caught in a legal limbo. When “Runa Simi” screened at the Lima Film Festival last year, it won the Audience Award. Zegarra has made the most celebrated Peruvian documentary in decades. Still, only a handful of Peruvians have been able to see it. (Disney declined to comment.)
The two collaborators last visited New York in June, 2025, for the Tribeca Festival, when Zegarra won the award for Best New Documentary Director. After attending a screening of “Runa Simi,” an audience member was so moved that he gave Valencia tickets to see “The Lion King” on Broadway with his teen-age son, Dylan, who voices Simba in the Quechua version. (There are no lions in the Andes—or kings, for that matter—so the title is one of the relatively few phrases that remain untranslated.) When the curtain went up, Valencia spent the first several minutes overcome by emotion, glassy-eyed and weeping. “Every language has a spiritual meaning,” he said. “And the characters had different personalities for me because I’d translated them.” Watching the musical, he felt as if he knew the lines by heart. “In my head, I was hearing it in Quechua.”
Released in 1994, the original “Lion King” was the highest-grossing film of the year, and the highest-grossing animated film in history until “Finding Nemo” broke that record, in 2003. But, more than three decades later, “The Lion King” doesn’t take up much real estate in the Disney Store: besides plush toys of Simba and Nala, there’s hardly any trace of it. So, why did Valencia tackle “The Lion King”? He saw it in 1995, when he was six years old, on a small black-and-white television at home in Cuzco. “It was the first movie I saw all the way to the end,” he said.
This was more than Zegarra had managed. He, too, was six years old when he saw the film, at a theatre in Lima; he cried so much that he was dragged out halfway through. “My version of ‘The Lion King’ ends with Mufasa dying,” he said.
Valencia believes that the way to preserve a language is to get kids to speak it. “Entertainment is a right,” he said. “Quechua saved my life. It gave me purpose.” Just then, the strains of a familiar song wafted across the store, and Valencia and Zegarra followed it, past a Lightning McQueen replica, to a tiny area where a half-dozen child-size chairs were arranged before a screen. The song was “Hakuna Matata,” sung by Timon, Pumbaa, and a young Simba. The scene happened to be the first clip that Valencia had translated and dubbed a decade ago, when his quixotic project had begun. “The Lion King” has been dubbed into more than forty languages, most of which keep the song’s Swahili title. For the unauthorized Quechua version, Valencia took the liberty of changing it: “Hakuna Matata” became “Hakuchu Munayta,” which means, roughly, “Let’s walk together in beauty.” As the chorus played, and as the cartoon characters bounced along the screen, he sang along, in Quechua. ♦

epub_14.title: The Anti-A.I.-Ad Ad Campaign
epub_14.text:
The Anti-A.I.-Ad Ad Campaign
Make-Believe Dept.
The Anti-A.I.-Ad Ad Campaign
The comedians Harris Alterman and Dave Ross have been putting up posters for fake tech products across the city, including a wearable grandpa, underwear that thinks, and A.I. cutlery.
By Bruce Handy
September 05, 2026
Ambiguity is generally not welcome on the subway. Are those seats empty for a neutral reason or an unpleasant reason? Is the person sitting across from me dangerous or just eccentric? That stain is . . . what, exactly? But one sweltering noontime at the West Fourth Street station, three flights down on the Brooklyn-bound B-D-F-M platform, ambiguity was the point. Two comedians, Harris Alterman and Dave Ross, were taking videos of themselves hanging big print advertisements for nonexistent tech companies on the back and sides of an abandoned newsstand. The ads conveyed just enough Silicon Valley messianism to be believable, and just enough absurdity to be funny. Or maybe it was the other way around? One read “UnderwAIr: Panties that think.” Another depicted a gold coffin engraved with a dollar sign. The copy: “Grieving? Trade on it. WakeMarket.”
It was Alterman and Ross’s second time pulling this stunt. A video of an earlier round of fake subway tech ads had gone viral in June, earning more than five million views on Instagram. (The first batch was even more absurd: “What if forks were spoons? Cutlery.ai” and “We put the Q in QR1777. FiveTable.”) Today, the collaborators were dressed identically in black shorts and white T-shirts that read “
AI.CONGLOMERATE
,” the pretend parent company for their pretend roster of startups. The pair had a lot on their plate: not only shooting the video but also prepping for a happening at the newsstand, which Al Mullen, a friend and a fellow-comedian, was transforming into a kind of art installation (with the M.T.A.’s blessing and a grant from an organization funding small projects to improve the city). Alterman and Ross were going to take it over one Saturday for a fake-A.I.-palooza.
The ads were printed on large vinyl sheets, and Alterman and Ross were hanging them with low-tech loops of duct tape. (Each ad is a one-off that Alterman and Ross remove when they’re done; the jokes live online, not on subway walls.) It wasn’t hard work, but the platform’s kiln-like conditions sapped their stamina, as well as the tape’s stickiness. People waiting for trains seemed not quite sure how to take the ads. A man with dreadlocks contemplated the promise of “the world’s first wearable AI grandfather.” (This was a parody of an actual product, a talking A.I. pendant called Friend that retails for two hundred and forty-nine dollars.) Was an A.I. grandfather something the man might want? “Get the fuck out,” he responded when asked.
Alterman, thirty-four, and Ross, forty-three, were friends from the comedy circuit before they collaborated. They look a bit alike, both with beards and thoughtful demeanors, but Alterman is marginally more hirsute and possesses an unexpectedly high-pitched laugh, whereas Ross wears glasses and is more voluble. Both have worked techy jobs—Alterman as a social-media manager, and Ross as a website designer. The fake ad campaign germinated about a year ago, when Alterman began noticing subway ads for A.I. companies that annoyed him with their promises to make existence easier, even frictionless. The idea seemed to be that “eventually you do nothing,” he said. “Your life lives itself.” Another quirk he noticed: the ads were often impenetrable to non-techies. “They all use the same words,” he said. “It’s the same voice, which I’ve called slop voice.” He and Ross compiled a long list of terms they’d spotted in the wild—“prompt,” “next gen,” “merging,” “deck,” “one click”—and from there “we basically just do Mad Libs, where we put different words in different orders until it makes us laugh.”
“Blank plus blank equals blank—that’s one of our favorites,” Ross said.
“From blank to blank in just one blank,” Alterman added. He claimed that they’d come up with their first batch of ads in an hour.
Ross, who’d executed the designs, called that an exaggeration, but maybe not by much. “It was fast, for sure,” he said. “We’ve been thinking about it for a long time.”
They didn’t have a goal for the project, aside from being funny, but among the millions amused by the initial video were several actual tech companies that approached the comedians about working for them. “One of them floated a very high number, a five-figure number,” Ross said. “And it was a moral quandary even thinking about it, because I very much want a job. My financial situation is scarier than it’s ever been. And this A.I. company wasn’t the worst of them. I don’t think their app itself is bad for humanity necessarily, but that entire world disgusts me.” He and Alterman talked the deal over and consulted friends. “Literally everyone was, like, ‘Dude, take the money,’ ” Ross continued. “But then it ended up not being an offer, so we didn’t have to worry.” Exhale. Faustian bargain averted. “But I would have taken the money,” Ross added.
“I’m glad we didn’t have to decide,” Alterman said. ♦

epub_15.title: “Paranormal Activity” Creeps Onto Broadway
epub_15.text:
“Paranormal Activity” Creeps Onto Broadway
The Boards
“Paranormal Activity” Creeps Onto Broadway
Oren Peli, the creator of the original horror-film series, stops by the new stage production and dishes on the creaky house that spooked—and inspired—him back in 2005.
By Anna Russell
September 07, 2026
There are many pubs in London that claim to be haunted. Victorian ghosts, lingering by the stairs, have a way of drawing visitors. One recent evening, the horror director Oren Peli stopped by one such boozer, in an alleyway off the Strand, looked around amiably, and ordered a Coke. He wore shorts, a baseball cap, a paisley shirt, and blue Hokas, and was undisturbed by rumors of a grisly spectral presence. “I’m not a believer in that kind of stuff, but it makes for a cool story,” he said.
In 2005, Peli was working as a video-game programmer in San Diego, a job that he hated. He was living in a creaky wooden house, with his “kind of jumpy” girlfriend at the time. “In San Diego, it gets very hot during the day and very cold at night, so the wood expands and contracts,” he said. “The houses kind of groan.” His girlfriend claimed to hear voices and footsteps. “I didn’t hear any of that,” Peli said. But one night, at 3
a.m.
, they woke up to a loud bang and a crash, “coming from inside the house, for sure, a hundred per cent.” All the doors and windows were closed. “I was, like, ‘What’s going on here?’ ”
It turned out that a Costco-size container of laundry detergent had fallen onto the washing machine and then rolled behind an open door. Mystery solved. But the episode gave Peli an idea. “I just thought, What if we got a video camera?” he said, and recorded “all night to see if there’s something happening. Will we be able to capture any proof of anything supernatural?” He never did it (“too lazy”), but “I thought, How scary would it be to watch footage of yourself sleeping” and catch “a little evidence, the door opening, just something that lets you know there is some invisible entity in the room?” He imagined that it would make a good movie.
About a year later, Peli used his creaky house as the set for “Paranormal Activity,” a horror film about a couple who record themselves sleeping to try to identify the weird noises they hear at night. The shoot lasted a week and had a crew of three, including Peli and his girlfriend, and a budget of fifteen thousand dollars. After the movie played at Screamfest, in L.A., DreamWorks acquired it, and eventually it got a wide release. It went on to make close to two hundred million dollars and has spawned seven sequels. “Surreal,” Peli said.
The story of the creepy house, and the creeped-out couple, is now running on both Broadway and the West End. There have been some tweaks. In this version, the couple has moved from Chicago to London for a fresh start—bad things happened in Chicago—and the set features a wide town house with dark corners and William Morris wallpaper. Peli was not involved in the stage adaptation, but he had tickets to see it that night with his wife, Staci. “I hope I’m not going to scream,” he said. “That’ll be really embarrassing.”
At the theatre, he and Staci, who now live in New Zealand, reminisced about the San Diego house. Peli and the girlfriend who lived with him had broken up, and Staci visited the house after the film’s release. It “looked exactly the same” as in the film, she said. The first night she slept over, the doorbell rang in the wee hours. (A prankster.) Later, a friend stayed in the guest room and was surprised when the lights suddenly went on. (Peli had forgotten to turn off a timer.) “She stayed up the whole night, just so freaked out,” Staci said.
When Peli was eleven, his parents let him watch “The Exorcist,” which gave him nightmares. As a young adult, he couldn’t even watch “Ghostbusters.” But years in the industry have hardened him; now he watches horror with an analytical eye. “Like, I wonder, How did they do that?” he said. “How many takes did
that
take?” The best horror “is something that doesn’t necessarily shock you with a jump scare, or with gore, but kind of gets into your soul, your deepest fears,” he said. Showering. Camping. Sleeping in your bed. It should “make people worry about something that actually relates to their own life.”
When the lights went down, Peli watched stoically. After one deft scare, the person sitting next to him jumped so hard that she pulled a muscle. “That was well done,” Peli said. Afterward, he checked his phone. He had set up cameras at his New Zealand house to monitor it. “We’re getting alerts. Something’s happening in the garage,” he said. “Let’s see if there’s anyone in the house.” He scrolled through footage of the kitchen, the garage, the front door. Eerily empty. He shrugged: “The house still stands.” ♦

epub_17.title: Have Conservatives Taken Sexy Back?
epub_17.text:
Have Conservatives Taken Sexy Back?
Annals of Style
Have Conservatives Taken Sexy Back?
The culture wars have come for lingerie as the right, once the advocates of promise rings and purity culture, embarks on a crusade to “Make America Hot Again.”
By Jennifer Wilson
September 07, 2026
Martin Luther King, Jr., once observed that one of the “most segregated hours” in American life is Sunday at eleven in the morning, referring to church service. Today, the same might be said about the month of April as it unfolds in Indio, California, where throngs of people descend each year to worship at the altars of live music and brand activations. Two weekends are set aside for Coachella, the music festival known for its eclectic mix of headliners, from Björk to Bad Bunny; for its Summer of Love-inspired dress code (e.g., crocheted booty shorts); and for being the preferred setting for celebrity couples to make it desert official on Instagram. (This year, Katy Perry and her boyfriend, the former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, sporting a backward baseball cap, posted from the arid environs.)
But, on the weekend
after
Coachella, the very same grounds are occupied by Stagecoach, a country-music festival that’s often thought of as the conservative Coachella—or “Trumpchella,” as one Reddit user put it. An event where influencers in cowboy boots and Marlboro Man jackets can take selfies with the Budweiser Clydesdales, it has a reputation as a safe space for uncritical displays of red-blooded American patriotism. Since 2020, though, the festival has been trying to promote a different image by banning displays of the Confederate flag, which some venders used to sell in bikini form. This year, near the main stage, where the rising star Ella Langley was singing her hit “Choosin’ Texas,” I saw a man wearing—in a show of inclusivity, perhaps—a shirt that read “
Show me your boobs if you hate racism
.”
Funnily enough, I was actually at the festival to investigate the political implications of cleavage. The month before, it had been announced that
SYRN
, the newly launched underwear line from the actress Sydney Sweeney, would be the “official lingerie partner” of Stagecoach. (The brand would have a pop-up karaoke bar on site—the
SYRN
Saloon—with daily panties giveaways.) The setting was certainly an interesting choice on the part of the “Euphoria” star, who spent the better part of last year running from the controversy over her ad for American Eagle Outfitters—also a sponsor of this year’s Stagecoach—in which, following a brief explainer on genetic determinism, a voice-over boasted of the blond, blue-eyed actress’s “great
jeans
.” The inspiration had seemingly been “Genes,” a near-identical ad that Brooke Shields did for Calvin Klein in the nineteen-eighties, but, in 2025, jokes about Sweeney’s supposed physical supremacy appeared to be giving free press to a right-wing talking point. By then, conservatives had concocted a theory that the fifties-pinup physique of Sweeney, a registered Republican, was an affront to progressive sensibilities; a year earlier, the
National Post
, a right-leaning news site, had raised the question “Are Sydney Sweeney’s breasts double-D harbingers of the death of woke?” While we were pretending not to be looking, breasts had somehow become Republican-coded.
Sweeney remained mostly silent throughout the fracas; “I’m in the arts. I’m not here to speak on politics,” she told
Cosmopolitan
. But was launching a lingerie brand itself a statement? When Lauren Sanchez showed up alongside her fiancé, Jeff Bezos, to Trump’s second swearing in with a white lace bra peeking out from under her Alexander McQueen pants suit, she inaugurated a surprising new front in America’s culture wars: lingerie. Through the tech venture-capital fund Coatue, Sanchez and Bezos have both provided financial backing for
SYRN
, as has Michael Dell, the billionaire founder of Dell Technologies and a prolific G.O.P. donor. And Trump himself, according to financial-disclosure documents filed with the U.S. Office of Government Ethics, purchased as much as a million dollars’ worth of Victoria’s Secret corporate bonds in December of 2025. Maybe he liked what he saw. In 2024, the company, under its new C.E.O., Hillary Super, had announced the return of its signature fashion show, which had been paused indefinitely in 2019. The year before, Ed Razek, the event’s producer, told
Vogue
that he had no plans to begin casting plus-size or transgender models (whom he called “transsexuals”) because the show was about “fantasy.” After public outcry, the company replaced its Angels—supermodel brand ambassadors—with the VS Collective, an advisory panel featuring the soccer star Megan Rapinoe and the transgender model and activist Valentina Sampaio. It also began selling nursing bras. But when Super came aboard, in 2024, she struck a different tone, telling the
Wall Street Journal
that her predecessor had “made decisions out of fear.” She also shared with
Fortune
that Victoria’s Secret would now be less “performative” when it came to diversity and would no longer necessarily “check every box and make sure every single thing someone could think of is covered.” This June, the company’s stock ticker was changed from VSCO to VSXY. (In a statement, Super told me that “what became clear” from her takeover “is that sexy still matters.”)
Inside the
SYRN
Saloon, which I had entered through batwing doors labelled “SS,” the crowd sang a rowdy rendition of Shania Twain’s “Man! I Feel Like a Woman!” I wondered whether anyone there knew that the song had been inspired by drag queens or that, when Twain made her début in Nashville, in 1993, she was shamed for her bare midriff and bed-tousled hair. When I was growing up, in the early two-thousands, “conservative” meant
conservative
. The right was the party of George W. Bush, abstinence-only sex education, and Christian evangelical teens who recited chastity pledges and wore promise rings under the banner of “True Love Waits.” Now, at Trumpchella, I was sipping a Made You Look margarita while examining
SYRN
’s Hoedown Throwdown: a three-pack of thongs emblazoned with slogans such as “
tight jeans, loose morals
” and “
cowboys ride harder and stay on longer
.”
Outside, I’d passed a man holding a sign that read “
Hot Girls Eat Arby’s
.” Last summer, the sandwich chain, which is owned by Roark Capital Group—named for the protagonist of Ayn Rand’s “The Fountainhead”—hired Sophie Cunningham, a W.N.B.A. player for the Indiana Fever, as a brand ambassador. (Cunningham, who follows the conservative provocateur Candace Owens on TikTok and recently told ESPN that “young girls” in sports “shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” became a right-wing darling for being her fellow white teammate Caitlin Clark’s on-court attack dog.) To announce the partnership, Cunningham posted a picture of herself slyly smiling in an Arby’s tee with the words “
look who has the meats now
.” How did this happen? How did the right get the meats?
“There’s been a mega-shift,” Raquel Debono, the founder of Make America Hot Again, which organizes mixers for young conservatives in New York City, told me. “It’s like the Mar-a-Lago face. Look at Fox News. Everyone’s got Botox, filler, and their tits out. It’s the bimbofication of
MAGA
.” The first election of Donald Trump, weeks after a 2005 “Access Hollywood” tape of him talking about grabbing women “by the pussy” was released, helped inspire the rise of “Barstool conservatism,” a kind of libertine libertarianism named for the comedy website Barstool Sports, whose founder, Dave Portnoy, once blogged that a certain female ESPN journalist’s “#1 requirement” was to “make men hard.” (Portnoy recently authored the memoir “Cancel Me If You Can.”) The “anti-woke” beer brand Ultra Right put out a “
MAGA
Babes” calendar that included women in red-white-and-blue bathing suits and Dana Loesch, the former
Breitbart
editor, hoisting two assault rifles into the air. “The vibe shift is real, and it’s spectacular,” Kat Rosenfield, of
The Free Press,
quipped, in a callback to the “Seinfeld” episode “The Implant,” in which Jerry questions the provenance of his new girlfriend’s breasts. For this faction, #MeToo had been not a reckoning but an opportunity—to cast the left as sex scolds and their own party as the one now singing along to Shania Twain: “I ain’t gonna act politically correct / I only wanna have a good time.”
The
SYRN
Saloon was filling up. Two young men standing near me began chanting, “We want Sydney! We want Sydney!” I asked why they liked the actress, not wanting to make assumptions. One replied, with a knowing grin, “Because she has great
jeans
.” A figure-skating coach from a nearby town shared that she hadn’t understood the fallout over Sweeney’s American Eagle ad. “Her job was to do a commercial, not to please every single person all across the country,” she said, sounding annoyed. Then she placed her hand on my shoulder and said, “I’m sorry.”
Finally, Sweeney—blindingly blond—arrived, wearing
SYRN
’s Date Night Satin Corset in Dew Me blue and Cowgirl Crush lace-ruffle miniskirt. “I have a special guest, everybody!” she yelled into a microphone, before inviting Chase Rice, who performed at the 2022 Turning Point USA festival, onstage to sing his 2012 bro-country anthem, “Cruise.” Next, she brought up the country star Riley Green, who had
also
performed at that festival. Sweeney’s boyfriend, the music manager Scooter Braun (a villain to Taylor Swift fans everywhere for purchasing her master recordings), watched from the side of the stage as the actress and Green began belting Garth Brooks’s “Friends in Low Places.”
I didn’t know what was real and what was provocation anymore. I just knew that I loved that song, though it seemed to mean something different in this context, as did the lacy bras in desert pastels that were hanging from the ceiling. How had everything been turned so upside down? Had conservatives taken sexy back, or was this all just an optical illusion, not unlike the kind created by a padded bra or a pair of Spanx? Or maybe it was as simple as a friend of mine had said: “Everyone is convinced their enemies are having bad sex.”
In 1965, Helen Gurley Brown, the author of “Sex and the Single Girl”—a self-help book for the career-minded woman in no rush to settle down—took over as the editor-in-chief of
Cosmopolitan
. Her very first issue included an article titled “Oh, What a Lovely Pill!,” about a new medication that could prevent unwanted pregnancies. “Good girls go to heaven—bad girls go everywhere,” Brown famously quipped, as her magazine became a user’s manual for the sexual revolution.
In 2019, a former model named Brittany Hugoboom, née Martinez, co-founded
Evie
magazine, envisioning it as “a conservative
Cosmo
” and “feminine, not feminist.” Scrolling through the site’s soft-pink hues and headlines such as “What the It Girls Are Wearing in Italy This Summer,” you could mistake it for a lot of content aimed at women these days, until you stumble on an article like “Being on Birth Control Made Me Feel Like a Failure, So I Chose Happiness Instead.” Much has been made of the manosphere, but
Evie
has set its sights on the red-pilled woman, who has replaced the supposed Kool-Aid of “having it all” feminism with
MAHA
-approved raw milk. (Evie even sells a “raw milkmaid dress,” which resembles a saucy peasant costume from Halloween Adventure.) According to internal company analytics,
Evie
, a mostly digital publication, received two hundred million impressions across its social-media channels in a month earlier this year. Its reader spends her pregnancy—one of many, ideally—pondering “The Most Masculine Boy Names of 2025.” If she does want birth control, she can use 28,
Evie’s
“menstrual wellness” app, which tracks users’ cycles and received funding from the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel. For the woman who “does her own research,” there are pieces such as “Why You Shouldn’t Have Sex with Him If He’s Covid Vaccinated.”
Most
Evie
articles, however, encourage the act. This year’s annual print edition is titled “The Sex Issue” and includes a guide to dirty talk and a “blowjob checklist.” On the cover is a photo of a model dressed in lingerie—bridal, of course. At my suggestion, Hugoboom and I met for lunch at Altesi, an old-school Italian restaurant on the Upper East Side beloved by Ivana Trump, who reportedly purchased six dozen bras every six months. Hugoboom, who greeted me wearing a low-cut, form-fitting leopard-print dress and black high heels, had just seen “The Devil Wears Prada 2” and felt a pang of recognition. “When all the drama with that one article came out,” she said—referring to Miranda Priestly’s green-lighting of a fashion spread featuring a brand reliant on sweatshop labor—“I’m just, like, ‘Oh, I feel like I’ve been there.’ ” I asked which
Evie
article had stirred the most controversy. “The most recent one, which shouldn’t have caused drama, was ‘I’m a Hot Mom, and I’m Tired of Being Mom-shamed for It,’ ” she recalled, before imitating her detractors: “
Moms shouldn’t have to be hot—they have a lot of things going on in their life.
” She rolled her eyes.
Hugoboom, who grew up in California and Texas, told me that she conceived of
Evie
when she was living in Los Angeles and working as a model—what she described as her “Zoolandery” chapter. “A lot of it was sitting in traffic, going to castings in downtown L.A., getting things thrown at you by homeless people,” she explained. She needed a change and realized that, through her personal networks, she had “all of the categories of a magazine lined up.” From modelling, she knew a lot of makeup artists. “O.K., so that’s Beauty,” she recalled thinking. She knew the personal trainers who worked with Victoria’s Secret models—“So that’s, like, Health.” She co-founded
Evie
with her husband, Gabriel Hugoboom; the two met at the University of Dallas when she was eighteen, at a pool party. She remained a virgin until her wedding night, seven years later. “So we know relationships pretty well,” she told me. She also saw an opening in the media landscape. The world of women’s magazines had become “hyperpolarized,” she believed, made up of avowedly feminist outlets like
Jezebel
and Vice’s
Broadly
, but she couldn’t find “the kind of girly-pop type of magazines that I loved when I was younger.” She took a sip of her cappuccino. “I’ve always just loved femininity,” she said. “I think because my mom was a flight attendant.”
In a Substack post announcing “The Sex Issue,” Hugoboom wrote that right-wing critics of “casual sex” had “no clear and exciting vision for an alternative.” The glittering signifiers of the sexually liberated life style—stilettos, mimosas, moaning—had been ascribed by shows like “Sex and the City” to single women in Democratic cities, as conservatives preached restraint. “Who wants that?” she asked. Hugoboom was essentially proposing a takeover: “The best, most fulfilling sex comes when you and your spouse commit to learning the art and science of pleasure.” “The Sex Issue” was in fact quite technical, with a detailed diagram of the clitoris and a comprehensive list of pelvic-floor exercises. Hugoboom explained that
Evie’s
readers needed the basics covered; she had received frantic D.M.s from women who had saved themselves for marriage and were feeling less than rapturous. “It would be, like, ‘I waited twenty-seven years to have sex, and now I’m psychologically damaged,’ ” she said.
Evie
isn’t alone in offering belated sex ed for the religious right. I came across a website called christianfriendlysexpositions.com, which claims to have introduced twenty million couples to “sex poses and sensual tips diagramed and described in a tasteful, God-honoring, marriage-focused manner.” Lingerie is a popular topic in this very specific corner of the internet. The Christian blogger Phylicia Masonheimer has extolled the virtues of lingerie showers. “We gathered around the bride, laid hands on her shoulders and prayed for the power of God to cover her marriage, to bless her union, to encompass her sexuality,” she reported on her blog, “Every Woman a Theologian,” adding, “I am deeply saddened when women are awkward at parties like this.” And there are new lingerie brands that cater to the God-fearing garter-belt enthusiast, such as Ginger & Peach (“All we do is bathed in prayer,” its owner promises) and Mentionables, a Mormon-owned company whose product photos are model-free so that your husband can peruse them without “feeling guilty for checking out other women,” according to its website. There were limits, though, to the right’s new sex positivity. A podcast for Christian couples called “The Naked Marriage” warned against the spouse-replacing perils of using a sex toy: “Like seasoning on a steak, it should enhance the experience, not become the meal itself.”
But it turns out that the right doesn’t need purity culture to reboot the policies that went along with it. In June, the Department of Health and Human Services began withdrawing federal grants from nonprofits that had received money through the Teenage Pregnancy Prevention Program. Going forward, the agency said, funding would be restricted to organizations that prioritized “abstinence-until-marriage-only ‘sexual risk avoidance’ ” education. But H.H.S. defunded some of those programs as well. Organizations using an abstinence-only curriculum called “Love Notes,” developed by the Dibble Institute, in Berkeley—which teaches “relationship skills” to teens—were defunded because of a module on the harms of pornography; H.H.S. flagged the material for promoting pornography. (Some suspected that the agency had relied on A.I. for the audit.)
Hugoboom insisted that she wasn’t a hard-liner. She didn’t see, for instance, how her opposition to the
COVID
vaccine was any different from “L.A. liberal girls” avoiding microplastics. “People in the comments called us alt-right,” she said. “It was so weird.” Inside “The Sex Issue” was a graphic that read “Body Count? One. Orgasms?
Countless
.” Was
Evie
against premarital sex? “We’re not taking a stance,” Hugoboom replied. “We do focus on a healthy sex life when you’re married. What’s the one thing that you can do that you can’t do with your friends?” I laughed, telling her that, in Brooklyn, it wasn’t unheard of for a married friend to ask you out for coffee and then let you know, in case you were interested, that they were opening their relationship. She asked whether that had ever happened to me. I confessed that it had. “That would freak me out,” she said. “I would die.”
After lunch, we visited the Madison Avenue outpost of Agent Provocateur, the British lingerie brand.
Evie
publishes shopping guides for the #MyBodyHisChoice customer, such as “The Valentine’s Lingerie He Hopes You’ll Wear.” We were greeted by the store manager, Samantha, who was wearing the A.P. uniform—a tight pink Vivienne Westwood minidress—as well as stockings with the words “
whip me, bite me, eat me, tease me
” stitched into the back seam. The bridal section had fewer items in white than I was expecting. That made sense to Hugoboom: “I was a virgin on my wedding night, but a lot of brides aren’t.” Samantha and I went silent. I pointed to a mannequin’s torso that was covered in an elaborate network of crystal chains. “This would be more for, like, a play party,” Samantha explained. “Here we go again,” Hugoboom remarked.
Samantha asked whether we would like a fitting. This was tempting. I had never been professionally measured for a bra, but I was worried about being in my underwear with a source. “You should! It’ll be fun,” Hugoboom said. I told Samantha that I thought I was a 36B. She eyed my chest and said no, I was most likely a 34D. I explained that this wasn’t possible—if I were a D cup, I would have lived an entirely different life.
She brought me one of their latest designs—the Clarette, a navy-blue lace balconette push-up bra—in my new size and had me try it on. It was so ostentatiously sultry that I knew I could never tell anyone who had critiqued “the male gaze” in a college essay what I really thought of it. When I emerged from the fitting room, Hugoboom squealed. “You look insane!” she said. I agreed, but I used a different term.
We left the store, sans bra. (It cost two hundred and fifty-five dollars.) Hugoboom seemed sad. “You looked really hot in that bra,” she told me as we said our goodbyes. “I don’t mean that in a lesbian way,” she added.
T hroughout its history, lingerie has gotten tangled up in politics. If the story of women’s liberation is often told as one long unlacing of the corset, an early salvo came from the French barricades. During the Paris Commune of 1871, a socialist tailor named Herminie Cadolle experimented with corset design in the hope of allowing women to move around more freely and, presumably, evade the gendarmes. The Commune lasted just seventy-two days, but the
corselet-gorge
, a chest covering with straps which Cadolle later developed, has been called one of the first modern bras. Later that century, suffragettes on both sides of the Atlantic took up the cause of dress reform; corsets could be replaced by sleeveless vests sold in specialty catalogues as “emancipation waists.” In 1896, the journalist Nellie Bly reported that one attendee at a suffragette meeting in Washington, D.C., was “corsetless, and, I fear, petticoatless!”
By the nineteen-thirties, corsets had gone out of style among women of all political stripes, but, if whale boning couldn’t contain the fairer sex, advertising would. A company called Maidenform—named to distinguish its cupped bra from the boyish bandeau popularized by flappers—launched its “I Dreamed” campaign in 1949. “I dreamed I was a lady editor in my Maidenform girdle,” read an ad showing a woman in a “Bi-line glamour girdle” juggling telephones. Another, from 1953, featured a woman in a fireman’s helmet, a hoop skirt, and the era’s signature bullet bra, saying, “I’m the chief and the siren.” Working was always presented as a fantasy scenario; men home from the war needed their jobs back, after all. The campaign eventually earned a place in the Smithsonian and an episode on “Mad Men” in which Don Draper is tasked with devising a competing bra ad for Playtex. (“I find they both open easily,” the account man Ken Cosgrove offers.)
In 1968, bras got their biggest political stage yet when a group of women’s liberationists protested the Miss America pageant in Atlantic City by dumping bras, pots and pans, and copies of
Playboy
—all of which they called “instruments of female torture”—into a trash can marked “Freedom.” Art Buchwald, the Washington
Post
humorist, wrote a mocking column titled “The Bra Burners.” Though the group didn’t actually light any matches, the image stuck. Critics leapt at the chance to cast feminists as prudes and housewives as vixens. In 1973, Marabel Morgan advised readers of her self-help book for Christian housewives, “The Total Woman”—which went on to sell ten million copies—to greet their husbands at the door dressed as “a pixie or a pirate, a cowgirl or a showgirl.” A rumor spread that she had even suggested wives open the door wearing nothing but Saran Wrap. (The idea was spoofed in the 1991 film “Fried Green Tomatoes”: Kathy Bates’s character, a shy housewife, puts on sandwich wrap to surprise her husband, who responds, “Have you gone insane?”)
In the late eighties and early nineties, it was men’s underwear that became politically weighted, as religious leaders blamed the “gay life style” for the spread of H.I.V. Calvin Klein plastered posters of men in tight white boxer briefs, a gay fetish object, on billboards and bus stops. “The best protection against
AIDS
is to keep your Calvins on,” the rapper Marky Mark teased in a 1992 commercial from the era. Sex was dangerous, conservatives said, so Madonna, an L.G.B.T.Q. ally, fired back with a satin bullet bra designed by Jean Paul Gaultier, which she wore during her 1990 Blond Ambition tour. In England, women calling themselves “ladettes” were similarly rejecting Thatcherism and adopting bawdy behaviors: heavy drinking, swearing, wearing bras out in public. Then, in February of 1994, a billboard appeared in Piccadilly Circus, showing the model Eva Herzigová in a black Wonderbra, which seemed to rival
NASA
in its gravity-defying technology; the ad was captioned, simply, “Hello Boys.” When the Wonderbra came to New York City that May, demand was so high that the first shipment arrived at Macy’s in an armored vehicle. The
Times
wrote, “The New York woman knows what she wants. She wants rent control, good restaurants, a seat on the subway and—apparently—better cleavage.”
But times have changed, or so I heard on an episode of “Hello Girls,” a 2023 podcast about the history of underwear, co-hosted by the fashion journalists Emily Cronin and Kate Finnigan. The two devoted an episode to reëxamining the Wonderbra’s legacy in light of recent events. “Donald Trump happened. MeToo happened. Jeffrey Epstein happened. . . . So how does an advert that shows a thin white woman offering her boobs up for the boys look to us now?” Cronin asks. Then someone introduced as a “Gen Z fashion consultant” responds, quite forcefully, “It’s so disgusting. It’s almost embarrassing to think at some point a woman looked at that and was, like, ‘Oh, gosh, yeah. I need to get that same bra.’ ”
I’m not a fashion journalist. I wasn’t a journalist at all at the start of #MeToo. In 2016, I had recently finished grad school, and the only question I was asking myself when shopping for underwear was where the clearance bin was. But, while reporting this story, I learned that the estimated hundred-billion-dollar lingerie industry had apparently experienced #MeToo as an existential crisis. A 2018 article in
The
Hollywood Reporter
asked “Did #MeToo Kill the Push-Up Bra?” after sales of the style declined by forty-five per cent during the previous year. The article stopped short of a definitive yes, but it suggested that, “with women redefining what’s ‘sexy’ outside the bounds of the male gaze, and feminism driving the fashion conversation,” #MeToo had “likely played a role.”
That a newer item—the bralette—had been flooding the market since 2014 seemed a likelier explanation, but a narrative had formed that women were enlisting their undies in the fight against the patriarchy. Other articles—“Victoria’s Secret? In 2018, Fewer Women Want to Hear It,” “Lingerie looks for a new bottom line after #MeToo”—followed. Sarah Shotton, the creative director of Agent Provocateur, recalled marketing meetings in which people said, “ ‘We can’t talk about sex anymore because of what’s happened.’ I said, ‘If we can’t be sexy, we’re not Agent Provocateur.’ ” (She hired the filmmaker Charlotte Wales to shoot a commercial with female Olympians in A.P. lingerie getting hot and sweaty—from exercise.) “There was just, like, a microscope on everything,” Jennifer Zuccarini, the founder of the lingerie brand Fleur du Mal, said, echoing Shotton’s recollection. Fleur du Mal released a behind-the-scenes photo from 2017 of a male photographer standing over a female model to take a shot. “People were, like, ‘He’s dominating her.’ I’m, like, ‘Oh, my God, he’s just a photographer getting a photo. This is crazy,’ ” Zuccarini said.
There was a feeling among the female founders and executives I spoke to that they were cleaning up a mess made by men. After the Victoria’s Secret fashion show came under fire in 2018, reports emerged of a close friendship between the company’s owner, Les Wexner, and Jeffrey Epstein. Using that relationship, Epstein had posed as a talent scout for the brand, luring young women to his hotel room under the pretext of auditions. Then, in 2020, the
Times
reported that multiple women had accused Ed Razek, who cast the Angels, of sexual harassment (accusations he deemed “categorically untrue, misconstrued or taken out of context”).
Lingerie brands across the industry entered a phase of penitent marketing. Aerie, American Eagle’s underwear line, announced a capsule collection with the Olympic gymnast and sexual-assault survivor Aly Raisman, fifteen per cent of whose proceeds would go to a nonprofit combatting child sexual abuse (though only up to seventy-five thousand dollars). Kim Kardashian launched her shapewear company,
SKIMS
, in 2019, and its first model was Alice Marie Johnson, a formerly incarcerated woman whose case Kardashian had publicized. And Parade, one of the many female-led direct-to-consumer brands that entered the underwear market during #MeToo, included a donation button on its website’s checkout page; the company later told
The Cut
that those customer donations had covered, among other things, “twelve weeks of therapy for Black women.” Even Emily of “Emily in Paris” was stumped, last season, when she had to come up with a campaign for the Italian lingerie brand Intimissimi. “We see a couple kissing passionately. She starts to take off her lingerie, but he stops her,” she tells a room of executives. “The lingerie is so beautiful it takes center stage.” The Italians look on, confused.
Had the right sensed an opening in all this hesitation? Sarah Leonard, the editor-in-chief of
Lux
, a socialist-feminist magazine that has covered sexual harassment and labor abuses in the fashion industry (and which I’ve contributed to), believes that this era of corporate advertising produced a useful caricature of liberal causes, not unlike the fictitious bra burners of yore. “The right conflated the left with dumb, progressive-lite marketing to sell underwear. It was fuel for them, and it did nothing for us,” she told me. Moira Donegan, a writer who, in 2017, created a crowdsourced spreadsheet naming men who’d been accused of sexual misconduct which became known as the Shitty Media Men list, said she found it frustrating that #MeToo is so often remembered this way. “We were asking that sexual harassment not be a precondition to accessing public life,” she told me. “It was not about wanting to see fewer bikinis on billboards.” But in America it can be hard to know your opponent from the version of them that’s been molded into a consumer base. (Coachella and Stagecoach, for example, are owned by the same Republican billionaire, Philip Anschutz, who has donated to anti-abortion groups.)
Women do consider lingerie political, but their concerns aren’t always the ones that companies want to advertise. The gothic-inflected lingerie brand Thistle and Spire, popular with romantasy readers, received blowback after its latest line was revealed to have used A.I.-generated designs, pushing the company to reverse course. At the Rack Shack, a bra store in Bushwick I visited, sex workers get a fifteen-per-cent discount for such items as “smart pasties,” which can be tapped with a phone to tip the wearer. A rep from the gender-inclusive brand tomboyx, which sells boxer briefs lined with blood-absorbing material, told me that a customer once e-mailed to say, “Your underwear saved my life.”
Some consumers maintain an old-school view of lingerie’s core objective. At a pop-up in Nolita for Cou Cou, a “clean girl” underwear line whose products are almost entirely compostable, I met a thirty-three-year-old tourist from Houston named Chloe. Her reasons for shopping at Cou Cou weren’t exactly ideological. “I’m not going to buy La Perla just to hang out at home,” she told me, referring to the luxury lingerie label. “I don’t have a man. Cou Cou is a good in-between.” She went on, “You can wear it out to a club, and, on the off chance you go home with someone, you have this on, not your old Hanes period-stained underwear. I’m not saying this is a true story.”
In July, I travelled to Bologna, Italy, to visit what I had started thinking of as the Vatican of lingerie. This was the atelier of La Perla, which was founded in 1954 by the corset-maker Ada Masotti. She sought to apply the most sophisticated methods and fabrics, usually reserved for dresses or veils, to women’s undergarments:
frastaglio
(hand-sewn embroidery on tulle), silk soutache (ornate braided trims), and Leavers lace (woven on a specialized English loom). Masotti called the last of these “the fabric of desire.” She delivered her items to the wives of Bologna’s élite in red-velvet boxes like those used for jewelry.
Over the decades, La Perla became the uniform of screen sirens. It is thought that Sophia Loren wore one of its bustiers for her famous striptease scene in “Yesterday, Today and Tomorrow” (1963), opposite Marcello Mastroianni. Daniel Craig sported a pair of baby-blue La Perla swim trunks on a beach in the Bahamas in “Casino Royale” (2006). I first heard of the brand as a teen while watching the reality show “Newlyweds: Nick and Jessica” (2003), in which Jessica Simpson calls her husband, Nick Lachey, to confess that she “accidentally” ran up a bill of more than seven hundred dollars at La Perla. “You gotta look at price tags before you pay, babe,” he told her. (The pair separated two years later.)
Hoping to retire one day, I wasn’t at La Perla to shop. I wanted to meet the company’s seamstresses—known as
le perline
, or “the little pearls”—who saved their own jobs after a Bologna court declared the company insolvent in 2024. In 2007, Masotti’s son had sold the company to the San Francisco-based private-equity firm JH Partners. After two subsequent sales, Brexit-related tax issues, and a series of risky investments by its latest owner, the company had gone bankrupt.
Bologna is nicknamed La Rossa, or “the Red One,” in reference to both its terra-cotta rooftops and long history of leftist politics; the Italian Communist Party governed the city from 1945 to 1991. In 2025,
le perline
protested in Piazza Maggiore under a red banner shaped like a bra and petitioned the European Parliament. “We denounce the predatory practices of speculative finance, which sacrifice the real economy for immediate profit,” they wrote in a manifesto. “We are fighting for the survival of a company founded by a pioneer of women’s entrepreneurship.” In a resolution, the Italian government negotiated a sale to the American billionaire Peter Kern, formerly of Expedia, and required the reinstatement of two hundred employees. (Kern’s wife was reportedly a fan of the brand.)
From my hotel, just off Via Antonio Gramsci, I set off for the factory alongside my interpreter, a Welsh woman named Glesni Williams. We arrived at a hunter-green building with huge windows and shaded porticoes. It had been designed by Pier Luigi Cervellati in 1972, to maximize worker comfort. In the lobby was a twenty-foot-wide poster, from 2017, of Kendall Jenner in a fuchsia lace bodysuit. (Earlier that year, she had posed for the company in front of a burning bra and shattered glass.)
We were met by Anne d’Ambrosio, the company’s head of communications, who invited me to preview the fall collection, the brand’s first since reopening; the inspiration was the legacy of La Perla itself. I was introduced to Stefania Lonati, the house archivist, who had been pulling old samples and advertising materials for the designers. I asked if I could see Sophia Loren’s bustier. Lonati looked pained. “We don’t know where it is,” she confessed. As it should be, I thought. Upstairs, I browsed the collection, which included a nightgown embellished with the brand’s signature La Maison lace embroidery, giving the appearance of flowers winding up the décolleté. It was being paired with a shimmery chrome silk. “In the blue, it looks like liquid on you,” D’Ambrosio said. “This is innovation.”
D’Ambrosio led me across the factory floor, where
le perline
were back at their stations. We entered an alcove. There were what looked like enormous bullets lined up on a shelf. (They were used, I learned, to create the molds for bra cups.) A worker named Vincenza placed a triangle of fabric on a machine labelled “
Watch Your Hands
.” Next, we walked over to the embroidery department, where a woman in her sixties named Pina was using a magnifying glass as she sewed tiny pearls onto a lace bra. Pina had been a leader in Unicheunite (“Unique United”), the association
le perline
formed to resist the factory’s closure. “We took to the streets,” she told me, “to prove that this is who we are.” Every La Perla piece is “ ‘unique’ because it’s made by hand,” she explained, “not by machine.”
I had found the impossible—ethical consumption under capitalism. The politics of lingerie must stem from the labor conditions that produced it, right?
SKIMS
may purport to offer “solutions for every body,” but it scored the lowest possible marks in a 2024 accountability report from the watchdog group Remake, for its lack of transparency about its working conditions and environmental impact. As we left, Williams, who also works for Cineteca di Bologna, the film archive and restoration center, mentioned that there was an archiving push across Italy because of an initiative, under Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, of the right-wing Brothers of Italy party, to protect Italian cultural heritage. This may have also played a part in saving La Perla. The right was trying to co-opt sexy here, too, it seemed. Even at the Vatican of lingerie, nothing was sacred.
Back in New York, I found a package waiting for me: a small pink box from Agent Provocateur. I opened it and was face to face with the Clarette again. “You can’t be a D Cup and not have this bra,” the note said. It was signed “Brittany.” I didn’t know what to make of the fact that the only person who had ever gifted me lingerie was the editor of a magazine that had just published an article titled “Dear Men, Please Stop Drinking Beer. It’s Making You Effeminate and Infertile.” In the end, I guess it didn’t bother her that I was unmarried. As I grudgingly put it back in the box to be returned (journalistic ethics), I found it a relief to know that everyone was having trouble living their politics. ♦
An earlier version of this article misspelled Kate Finnigan’s name.
