How Hermès Unharnessed Fashion
Profiles
How Hermès Unharnessed Fashion
Under the stewardship of Nadège Vanhée, the artistic director of women’s wear, a house known for craftsmanship is exploring the risqué.
By Lauren Collins,Jet Swan
September 07, 2026
The light, the light. It was all anybody could talk about—the soft, weightless Los Angeles light, melting between the columns of an open-air pavilion, which was perched on a hilltop above Bel Air, and painted a highly specific shade of pale yellow that made several hundred assembled guests appear as though they were standing in the middle of a banana cream pie. The structure resembled a Greek temple and was as big as a mansion. It had been purpose-built by Hermès, the French luxury-goods company, at unimaginable cost. Tomorrow it would all come down. But, for one June evening, the sun was streaking the horizon, and a fashion show was about to start.
The sound of drumbeats filled the pavilion. The first model emerged onto a sinuous runway in a nubuck coat paired with chiffon pants that fluttered in the breeze, revealing knee-high calfskin boots. The outfit matched the pale yellow of the venue but upheld the Hermès aesthetic of discreet, horsey timelessness. So when the next model came out, also wearing shades of margarine and lemon, it took a moment to register that her look—a skintight, bell-bottomed catsuit covered in blinking sequins—represented a deviation from, if not a challenge to, the Hermès ideal. Hermès does not employ celebrity ambassadors, as most other major luxury brands do, but, perhaps in a nod to the setting, the evening’s front row was a touch starrier than usual. Miley Cyrus, open-mouthed, nudged Kerry Washington as the woman in spangles swept by—this was red-carpet clothing, flashbulb clothing, clothing to be seen in once rather than excavated annually from a closet of perennials. Nadège Vanhée, the artistic director of Hermès women’s wear since 2014, described the event’s conceit to me as “How do I create a conversation between the mystique of a French fashion house talking about horse carriages and the spirit of Los Angeles, which is rewind, erase, restart?”
Thierry Hermès, an Alsatian-born harness-maker, founded Hermès in 1837. (Pronunciation hint: “air mess.”) Over nearly two centuries in trade, the company has dealt in germinal francs, Poincaré francs, de Gaulle francs, and euros, always remaining family-owned. The current C.E.O., Thierry’s great-great-great-grandson Axel Dumas, presides over an empire of sixteen
métiers
, as the divisions are known in the house lexicon, including everything from saddlery, gloves, and belts to timepieces and tableware. Many people know Hermès for its intricately printed silk scarves (Grace Kelly once used one as a sling) and for its savagely coveted Birkin bags (whose rate of appreciation is said to outperform the S. & P. 500). The latter have inspired so many knockoffs that Judge Judy once devoted an episode of her show to a Birkin-counterfeiting scam, marvelling, “
Twenny-nine hundrud dollas
for a pockabook!
”
These days, that would be a bargain, as even the most modest models cost five times as much. Hermès is worth an estimated hundred and ninety billion dollars, making it the second most valuable luxury-goods firm in the world. Last year, it briefly overtook the front-runner, L.V.M.H.—the slick conglomerate behind the likes of Louis Vuitton and Dior—its eternal nemesis and spiritual foil.
In the capricious luxury sector, Hermès has a reputation for steady thinking. Protestants in a traditionally Catholic country, the family—now a tripartite mishmash of Dumases, Guerrands, and Pueches, owing to a surfeit of daughters at the end of the nineteenth century—is known for avoiding debt and investing for the long term. Its bags inspire a fevered economy of influencers, resalers, and aspiring buyers, thanks, in large part, to the company’s choice to keep supply diabolically low. Hermès positions itself above the melee, as a guardian of tasteful continuity. According to one former executive, the family sees money “merely as a means, especially for buying time,” and, according to one relative, “moral elegance” is considered a job requirement at Hermès. In 2016, at a benefit auction, Jeffrey Epstein placed the winning bid on an internship at Hermès; the company withdrew the lot and reimbursed the charity. Dumas later explained that the last thing Hermès needed was to get involved with a “louche financier.”
Hermès is a sporty house, but it is also the wonkiest house. The company employs a paleographer, for deciphering handwriting in old company correspondence, and maintains a collection of leather-bound ledgers containing the specs of every saddle made from 1900 to today. The first sixteen pages of last year’s annual report consisted of a cartoon about a globe-trotting Pegasus. It would be difficult to find another luxury brand that promoted an employee from sewing bags to designing them after he submitted a plea written entirely in Alexandrines. But Hermès did, and it is still producing that designer’s first creation, from 2002: the Picotin, inspired by feedbags. Suckers for a touch of whimsy, the company’s window dressers once garnished a display inspired by the Garde Républicaine, a famous French cavalry division, with a pile of horse manure. Such is the Hermès commitment to authenticity that the poop was sourced directly from the unit.
The company’s twin values of work and quirk can sit uneasily in the distractible, self-serious fashion world, to the point that fashion at Hermès has historically been regarded as something of an oxymoron. Unlike its competitors, Hermès is a pre-haute-couture enterprise, founded before the rigid bureaucracy of French fashion was put into place, in the eighteen-sixties, with the establishment of a governing syndicate. Emilie Hammen, the director of the Palais Galliera fashion museum, explained that, as a result, the company “has never felt a need to prove itself within this framework.” Hermès tends to express itself through craft rather than through novelty. “I’m not doing fashion,” Véronique Nichanian, who designed menswear at Hermès for more than three decades, told
GQ,
in 2021, preferring to call her creations “clothes-objects.” The house is, in many respects, the antithesis of the kind of fashion described in Miranda Priestly’s famous cerulean speech, from “The Devil Wears Prada”: unlike its bags, whose imitators include Walmart’s seventy-eight-dollar Wirkin, Hermès’s clothes have traditionally trickled down nowhere, influencing no one. You will certainly not find an “equestrian gilet dress in satin-gray plongé ostrich” hanging on the racks at Target next year just because Hermès sent one down the runway.
Yet, under the stewardship of Vanhée, fashion is an increasingly important venture for Hermès. Internally, the division has grown by forty-four per cent since 2022, accounting for more than a quarter of the sixteen billion dollars in revenue that the company reported last year, and Hermès’s cultural influence is likewise on the rise. Lauren Sherman, the fashion reporter for
Puck
, wrote admiringly of the L.A. show, “This was the most Vanhée has ever inserted herself into the broader fashion conversation, which you don’t really have to do at Hermès.” A friend of mine who works in the industry was recently raving about a pair of stretchy, high-waisted black pants designed by Vanhée that she said insouciantly bundled together several desirable codes: equestrian, prep, surf, S & M. She continued, “You can wear them with literally anything and look like a sexy luxury bitch.” The writer and filmmaker Miranda July, who attended the show in L.A. wearing a blue turtleneck under a black leather Hermès overalls minidress, told me, “It’s kind of crazy that she’s making clothes for such wealthy people that are so sensuous and kinky. It’s for flesh—for beating skin with blood under it.”
Vanhée doesn’t fit the obvious profile of a provocatrice. The first time I met her, this past spring, she was reading an essay by the French sociologist Nathalie Heinich about “visibility capital” and the economics of being seen. She likes Austrian spas and Jon Fosse novels. The tech executive Charles Porch, a close friend of Vanhée’s, told me, “She’s really nerdy, in the best way possible.” She dislikes digital mood boards, so much that she forbids her designers to use them, and she has zero presence on social media, which she dismissed as “kind of a sad-girl thing.” Her inspirations for another recent show included the fashion photographer Deborah Turbeville and the Greek goddess Hecate.
In Los Angeles, the sexy luxury bitches continued down the runway. The most persuasive dialogue between French pedigree and Californian freedom came in the form of a pair of short jackets, one in calfskin and one in goatskin, featuring motifs, realized in complicated leather marquetry, that equally recalled the Longchamp racecourse and the Wild West. After a series of slouchy suits and bustier dresses in turquoise and scarlet silks, the show exploded to black, culminating in a series of bravado gowns. A two-piece set featured palazzo trousers trailing a nimbus of silk and a stomach-baring bandeau top cinched with a leather belt at the bust. Vanhée has said that she thinks of leather as the conscious and silk as the subconscious, the former structuring and the latter flowing—this look, then, was integration, fusing the banker’s accessory with the sexpot’s attitude.
Vanhée emerged from backstage at the end of the show in red trousers, a red top, a caramel-colored leather bomber, and a pair of yellow-and-black La Sportiva trail-running sneakers that she wears everywhere, maybe to offset all those hides and tulles. Because she is indifferent to self-mythologizing and thinks intently about what she says—and perhaps also because, physically, she corresponds to some people’s idea of a melancholic Pre-Raphaelite maiden—she has often been characterized as “an enigma” or “mysterious,” or even “cold-blooded.” The more straightforward reality is that she is someone with a healthy sense of priorities, who considers it more radical to act as a steward than to play the renegade, even if she prefers to do a little bit of both. “My work isn’t my personal diary,” she told me matter-of-factly. “As a creative, I want to give a certain orientation, but to work at Hermès is also to be of service.” She is, in other words, the anti-auteur—a mature, cerebral mortal to fashion’s babbling gods and kings. Free of undue pressure from her bosses or the public, from above or from below, she may be the last fashion designer unbeholden to the comments section.
The company’s historic seat in Paris’s Eighth Arrondissement, 24 Rue Faubourg Saint-Honoré, is central to the mythology of Hermès. In 2019, the company released the first versions of a bag it calls the Faubourg Birkin, which depicts the building’s arch-windowed façade in different conditions—day, night, rain, midnight. (A rare snow edition, made of alligator skin, recently sold for some four hundred thousand dollars at a private sale.) A few years later, Hermès commissioned the journalist and filmmaker Frédéric Laffont to write a book about the headquarters. After months of hanging around the labyrinthine premises—going up and down “the red staircase,” which is red, and “the green staircase,” which is also red—Laffont came away thinking that Hermès resembled a cult, or a tribe, with its own grammar, rites, and totems. Pascale Mussard, a sixth-generation family member, recalling the all-night Christmas celebrations she attended at the headquarters as a girl, during which each worker’s child would receive gingerbread and an orange, reached for another metaphor: “It was like the village of the Smurfs.”
Charles-Émile Hermès, the founder’s son, moved the company to 24 Faubourg in 1880. Baron Haussmann, making way for the boulevards, had demolished the original headquarters, near La Madeleine, and Charles-Émile wanted the company, which specialized in saddlery at the time, to be closer to the Élysée Palace, with its great stables and tony crowd. By the turn of the twentieth century, the area counted some forty
maisons du cheval
, including riding schools and makers of saddles, harnesses, and carriages. With Charles-Émile’s sons, Émile and Adolphe, at the helm, the company became the area’s star tenant, furnishing saddles to a Continental élite, including Nicholas II, the Tsar of Russia. Émile’s leatherworkers often married Jeanne Lanvin’s seamstresses, who were confecting gowns for society women just across the way.
A photograph from the era shows Émile’s four daughters, in braided buns and white drop-waist dresses, posing with an iron rocking horse that still sits in his former office at 24 Faubourg. In July, Menehould de Bazelaire du Chatelle, who was Hermès’s artistic director of cultural patrimony until her recent retirement, welcomed me into Émile’s lair, which has been lovingly preserved as a private museum. The place teemed with treasure: a samurai’s coral-studded stirrup, a miniature game of dominoes that could be worn as a pendant, a cane whose head popped open to reveal a mustache brush and a pick for gathering wild mushrooms. Bits and bridles filled every corner, giving the place the feel of the world’s poshest Cracker Barrel. A shelf held dozens of obscure cookbooks, which Hermès scarf designers can consult for gastronomy-themed prints. There was a nineteenth-century praxinoscope that recalled the magic lantern from Marcel Proust’s “In Search of Lost Time.”
“Émile and Proust were born in the same year,” de Bazelaire du Chatelle told me. “Proust said he built his book the way a couturier constructs a dress.”
It was touching to hear her speak about the long-dead men as though they were her intimate friends, two neighborhood guys frequenting the same haunts in an eternal Belle Époque. Hermès is a luxury-goods company, but it operates a bit like a farm or a vineyard, rooting itself in a sense of place. “We are peasants of the city, and twice a year we have our own crop,” a family elder once told Axel Dumas. Part of the brand’s appeal is that even its placemats and wristwatches seem imbued with terroir.
The First World War changed everything for everyone, but Hermès faced a double problem: in addition to decimating its workforce and its clientele, the conflict clarified the need to transform the business. In 1914, the French government had sent Émile to the Americas to requisition horses and cavalry equipment. He came back talking about cars, having witnessed Henry Ford’s assembly lines in Detroit. Émile chose not to modernize his company’s way of working—one man, one saddle—but it was clear to him that the automobile owned the future. Soon, some eighty thousand horses had disappeared from a capital newly thrumming with Citroën Type As. Company legend holds that a pair of veterans appeared at 24 Faubourg: one had lost his left hand and the other his right, so they went Dutch on a single pair of gloves.
Émile could have folded the company, but he had an idea. On his requisitioning tour, he’d observed another newfangled creation fastening the cloth top of a Cadillac convertible—the zipper, which he introduced to France in 1922, having obtained the patent to the invention in the country. The next year, Hermès launched the Bolide, thought to be the first handbag to use a zip closure. Émile continued to diversify. In 1937, Hermès débuted a silk scarf, depicting horse-drawn omnibuses inspired by a popular board game. When the Second World War broke out, Hermès was not existentially threatened. With less money to spend on clothes, clients gravitated toward more affordable accessories; silk became difficult to obtain, so the company released rayon scarves. Perhaps the most lasting consequence of the war years occurred when the manufacturer that supplied Hermès with mustard-colored bags and boxes ran out of paper, forcing the company to switch to a bright-orange hue. Hermès embraced the shade as its signature, to the point that, years later, when Eric Clapton custom-ordered a crocodile-skin guitar case, it arrived in an enormous orange box in the shape of a Martin 000-28EC.
The business podcast “Acquired” has described Hermès’s strategy as “the opposite of everything you learned in Econ 101.” The company maintains a scarce supply of its handbags on the ground that it’s impossible to expand production without decreasing quality. Competing luxury brands have wildly increased the prices of their bags in recent years—a Chanel classic flap bag that cost fifty-eight hundred dollars in 2019 cost ten thousand eight hundred dollars by 2024—but Hermès has taken a relatively restrained approach, with hikes at several percentage points less than the rate of inflation. Even when outsourcing could provide opportunities or economies, the company is maniacally focussed on controlling all aspects of the process. It doesn’t sell sunglasses, for example, because it would have to subcontract the manufacturing of the lenses. Parts of the belts and ties are sewn by machine, but artisans, many of them trained in schools established by Hermès, still saddle stitch leather goods by hand and screen-print scarves using up to forty-nine separate screens per scarf from an archive of more than seventy-five thousand proprietary colors. (By superstitious tradition, an Hermès scarf never features a knife or a sword—anything that is not “nice” to the neck.) Vanhée’s pride in her team’s impractical craftsmanship was evident during a rehearsal for the L.A. show, at a studio in Culver City, as we walked by a leatherworker molding the shoulders of a dress with a hammer and a marble plate he’d brought all the way from Paris. Vanhée said, “You only see that chez Hermès, eh?”
Eccentricities aside, Hermès is capable of acting with steely discipline when necessary. In 2010, Bernard Arnault, the chairman of L.V.M.H., called Bertrand Puech, then the chairman of Hermès’s supervisory board. Arnault told Puech that he had managed to accumulate a 14.2-per-cent stake in Hermès and would be announcing this to the media in two hours. Hermès executives and family members hadn’t had a clue. (Arnault, who eventually acquired a twenty-three-per-cent stake, was later fined for failing to make mandatory disclosures.) The C.E.O. at the time, Patrick Thomas—not a family member, it should be noted—indelicately conveyed his sense of shock, telling reporters, “If you want to seduce a beautiful woman, you don’t start by raping her from behind.” Business bros still recount what happened next with the kind of awe usually reserved for events like the siege of Stalingrad: in a remarkable show of unity, more than fifty family members banded together to form a holding company, fighting off the possibility of a takeover by pledging not to sell some 50.2 per cent of the company’s stock for twenty years.
Hermès’s symbolic capital was on display at this summer’s World Cup. The tournament basically doubled as an Hermès fanboy convention, with players such as Ousmane Dembélé, Lamine Yamal, and Erling Haaland showing off their bag collections as they shuttled between matches. According to one estimate, Haaland, Norway’s star striker, helped generate nine million dollars in brand value by carrying rare specimens such as an Haut à Courroies (
HAC
) Endless Road, featuring palladium hardware and a patchwork vista inspired by David Hockney landscapes. The Birkin, above all other models, has become a vessel for popular culture, name-checked by Real Housewives and A$AP Rocky alike. The singer Drake is not married, but, a few years ago, he admitted that he’d started collecting Birkins for his future wife.
The Birkin dates to 1984, when Jean-Louis Dumas, the executive chairman of Hermès at the time, boarded a flight and encountered the famously basket-carrying actress Jane Birkin, who complained that she could really use a bag big enough to hold both scripts and diapers. Dumas mocked up a sketch on the spot, and the Birkin was born—a squarish satchel with top handles and a trim leather belt to hold down the flap, although, according to
Connecticut Luxury
magazine, many owners prefer to leave their bags open, in imitation of Jane herself. Her original Birkin (which sold last year at Sotheby’s for some ten million dollars) was black, but diehards today compete for models like the Himalaya, made in white-and-gray crocodile skin that supposedly mimics snowcapped mountains, and any bag in such colors as Rose Confetti or 5P Bubblegum Pink; the latter is said to have a “near-mythical” status among connoisseurs.
The
Financial Times
has compared the hype that surrounds the bags to the tulipomania that seized seventeenth-century Holland. Both the Birkin and the smaller but nearly as coveted Kelly—created in the nineteen-thirties but popularized by Grace Kelly, who used it to camouflage her pregnancy in the fifties—are known in fan circles as “quota bags.” Hermès decides who gets them and who doesn’t, refusing to sell them online and tightly controlling their availability in boutiques. Because of the bags’ popularity, Hermès has developed an unusual relationship with some of its clients, who ask not only what Hermès can do for them but what they can do for Hermès. At the L.A. show, I met a pair of young women named Brittany Kane and Andrea Henderson, D.M.D. and D.D.S., respectively. (“We love dentistry and we love fashion,” Kane told me.) Henderson explained later that “you don’t go into the Hermès store and ask for a Birkin” off the bat, adding that she’d broached the topic only after paying her respects by buying jewelry and shoes. This works for some people but apparently not for others. In 2024, three customers filed a class-action lawsuit alleging that Hermès uses the promise of handbags to induce people to buy teacups and trinkets and seven-thousand-dollar wastepaper baskets, all the while knowing that many of them “will not in fact get a Birkin bag.” The suit was dismissed. Hermès told me, “Under no circumstances is the sale of a product conditional upon the purchase of another.”
The “Hermès game,” as it’s known, has spawned an entire repellent vocabulary. The ancillary purchases, for example, are euphemized among shoppers as “pre-spend” or “Birkin bait,” and tales circulate of aspirants attempting to curry favor with sales associates, or “S.A.s,” by offering cash and trips on private jets. In order to justify the expenditure, or perhaps the humiliation of having to beg for the privilege of parting with their money in a public store, some participants tend to treat what is realistically a one-way capitalistic transaction as some sort of bilateral spiritual quest. Reddit abounds with threads such as “What was your journey to a Special Order?”(A “special order” allows a client to customize her bag.) One lucky buyer replied, “In my case, I think my SA felt that I had enough neutral bags (two Birkins, an Evelyne, a KTG) that it was time for me to go through a special order to get a bag unique enough for me.” Drafting on Hermès’s cachet, a New York City plastic surgeon recently began providing a package of procedures for new moms known as the Birkin Body—lipo, a tummy tuck, breast surgery, and a butt lift.
All this rapacious consumerism sits somewhat awkwardly alongside Hermès’s image of Old World gentility. You can see why the company would want to move further into fashion and other retail categories, hedging its bets as leather goods, traditionally its most profitable division, risks overexposure. Hermès deals nonchalantly with the discordance. When I asked Vanhée about the bag-unboxing videos that proliferate on Instagram, she quickly dismissed the topic, saying, “Isn’t that old?” The company does, though, sell a scarf called Tulipomanie, covered in frilly blooms of an exquisiteness that seems to rebut the charge of excess hype with a wink.
Hermès has long employed superior designers, including, in recent decades, Martin Margiela, Jean Paul Gaultier, and Christophe Lemaire. Vanhée fits easily into a lineage of potent minimalism (Margiela and Lemaire) and sly subversion (Gaultier), but, unlike her predecessors, who continued to work on their own lines, she has devoted herself entirely to Hermès. Also, it must be said, she is not a man. “What really sets her apart is that there’s a sense of interiority and psychology and even autobiography to many of her collections,” CNN’s senior style reporter, Rachel Tashjian, said. “You can see what she’s thinking about and feeling, or you
wonder
what she’s thinking about and feeling.” The artist and director Alex Prager told me, “When you look at her characters, you can imagine a whole life for them.”
By the time Hermès recruited Vanhée, she had an impeccable résumé: the Royal Academy of Fine Arts Antwerp, the Institut Français de la Mode, Margiela, Phoebe Philo’s Celine. She had just finished a three-year stint as the design director at the Row, Mary-Kate and Ashley Olsen’s brand, known for making unsurpassable basics at outrageous prices. Vanhée recalled, of her time there, “They had confidence, but what I think I gave them was a strong spine, and I encouraged them to be even more who they are, to push the American elegance of the brand further.”
The aura of regimented cool that Vanhée created at the Row caught the attention of Hermès executives. When the call came from Axel Dumas’s office, she was in the middle of a hiking trip in Okinawa. “I was wearing this beautiful brand from the West Coast of America which is called Patagonia,” she joked. “Total look Patagonia. All I had was a little duffelbag.” Dumas summoned her to Paris, but she had nothing appropriate to wear. “Of course, big drama,” Vanhée recalled. “What do I do? I’m a pretty tall girl. It’s Japan.” She ended up with a navy-blue suit from the men’s department at Comme des Garçons. “And then I went with some classic loafers, because I was a wild animal!” she said. When she finally made it to 24 Faubourg, she sat down and started talking about Plato’s cave. Dumas, who has a degree in philosophy, was impressed. Upon hiring her, the only brief he gave was that he be “pleasantly surprised.”
Vanhée was born in 1978 in Seclin, a small town near Lille. Her father was a doctor, a French Catholic who had lived in Morocco before moving to Algeria, where he met her mother, a Muslim nurse from Constantine. As Vanhée’s birth approached, the expecting couple decided that the baby should be born in France, so they went to Seclin, where she had relatives living—“Voilà,” Vanhée told me. Soon, the family was back in Algeria, living in Algiers. “I spent my first two years there,” Vanhée recalled. “And after that we moved back, and there was a certain melancholy, because,
bon
, when you go from those beautiful white views, it takes time to love the North of France.”
Vanhée was a studious child. She thought that she might like to be an archeologist, until, as a teen-ager, she started contributing music reviews of indie bands such as Placebo and Moloko to a zine. Fandom led to flea markets, which led to a curiosity about fashion. She began taking apart the garments she bought and sewing her own. Sure, she dyed her hair black and wore it half-punk, half-goth style, but the classic fashion narrative of the yearning provincial outsider, slavering over
Vogue
spreads and dreaming of urban glamour, holds little resonance for her. Fashion was “a hyper-repressed desire”—something to admire, maybe, but not to join or conquer. “I had as much cultural stimulation there as I do in a big city like Paris,” Vanhée said of Seclin one day at the Hermès atelier, proffering a dark-chocolate-covered speculoos cookie, a favorite northern delicacy.
Designing clothes at Hermès isn’t the easiest job. In addition to fashion’s historically muted role at the brand, there is the simple fact that an Hermès designer must use a lot of leather, to honor the house’s equestrian heritage, but that, if the looks get too leathery, they can easily veer toward barnyard or bordello. The Birkin and the Kelly have been around for decades and look much the same as they ever did, but a fashion designer at Hermès has to think about freshness as much as function and form. “Don’t be too much of a creator, and don’t be too much of a traditionalist,” one house motto goes. Vanhée handled that dilemma confidently in her first collection, for the Fall 2015 season. Even if the looks could be uneven, ranging from a sublime pair of blue-black lambskin dungarees to a frumpy quilted parka with saddlebag-like pockets, the collection was received warmly, with
Vogue
calling it “a respectful journey around the house.” Vanhée told the
Telegraph
that year, “I don’t think a garment needs three sleeves to be experimental.”
In the seasons that followed, Vanhée mostly stuck to making incomparably crafted, gimmick-free, calmly intelligent clothes. They performed well with customers, but detractors suggested that she was uninspired, dismissing her as “Nabeige.” The idea that Vanhée’s work was dull or overly conservative sprang, in part, from her tenure at the Row, which is often credited with launching the “quiet luxury” trend of monochrome wearable pabulum for a public obsessed with projecting good taste. Still, in her early years at Hermès, she was crucified on the rare occasions when she attempted something different. In 2017, she showed boho vests and plaid trousers to criticism that, as the Business of Fashion put it, her “remarkable clarity and sense of intent had gone completely
AWOL
this season.”
Vanhée loathes the phrase “quiet luxury” and seems exasperated by the association. She emphatically rejects the idea that she was ever “playing it safe.” What some people see as “boring as hell,” she said, is “delicacy and structure” done to an extremely high standard. One season, she sent models down the runway in rigorously cut leathers and then made it rain, dumping droplets from the ceiling. Tashjian, the style reporter, told me, of Vanhée’s designs, “I have moments where I feel like I’m eating at one of those fussy restaurants where everything is square, but there’s something punk in that she just does whatever she wants.” She added, of the rain stunt, “It was so aggressive and sensual and then just completely arrogant, these extravagantly expensive clothes in a downpour.”
Sometime around the pandemic, Vanhée’s clothes got perceptibly more outspoken. “Hedonism just upended the classy, even classic, austerity that seemed to be Vanhée-Cybulski’s signature,” the French newspaper
Libération
wrote delightedly, in 2021, reviewing a show that featured crop tops, peekaboo bralettes, and snatches of strategically exposed skin. Vanhée-Cybulski was Vanhée’s married name. Gossips contend that the transformation in her designs coincided with her divorce from Peter Cybulski, an English art gallerist with whom she has a young daughter. “That’s sexist, and it’s not true,” Vanhée told me. In fact, she insists, she’s been exploring notions of feminine desire for years. (“I still believe the Hermès woman is seen as a vestal,” she told
W,
in 2019, vowing to spice up that image.) Max Pearmain, a stylist who often works with Vanhée, told me that, almost every season, she “homes in on an erogenous zone and tries to push that within the silhouette.” In Los Angeles, the focus was the hip, which she accentuated with a series of leather peplums, creative belting, and nipped-waist overcoats. One of her best collections, for Spring 2026, was devoted to the bust, with almost every model donning a sort of “neo-harness” that the fashion magazine
Numéro
deemed “the must-have accessory of the season.” Vanhée showed the harness with vibrant
indiennes
prints inspired by Provençal folk costumes, suggesting a rooted, anti-porn idea of eroticism. Sex appeal, too, can have terroir.
There may be some practical considerations at play in the bombshellification of the Hermès woman. Peter Malachi, a communications executive at the company, told me, as we rifled through the racks at the Hermès boutique in Beverly Hills, that Vanhée, more than her predecessors, is designing for an American audience. “It’s more body-conscious—you have all these women spending a lot of time doing Pilates and looking amazing,” he said. But Pearmain told me that he sees “a French attitude” in Vanhée’s “bluntness about attraction and shape.” Even if her designs are not her personal diary, as Vanhée put it, they are informed by aspects of her identity. One day, when I asked her about the difference between objectification and liberation, she replied, of the latter, “I think it was showing clothes that could be associated with shame, like the bra or the harness.” She continued, “For me, modesty and sexiness have always had a real tension that also comes from my double background. I think that when one grows up with a Muslim mom and a Christian dad, there’s always this weight about what’s sexy, and I wanted to take that away.”
In June, Vanhée boarded a paddle-wheel boat at a dock on the Thames, en route with a hundred or so V.I.P.s to an Hermès party at the Hurlingham Club, a private polo club a few miles upstream. She was dressed in red again—a scarlet suit and a black lace bustier, accompanied by her trusty La Sportiva sneakers. When we greeted each other, she called me by the wrong name, wincing upon realizing her mistake. I found it endearing to encounter, in a field of facile schmoozers, someone so palpably un-media-trained. A wish for recognition seemed to battle with a gently refractory personality as Vanhée, inhabiting the state function of a fashion designer, welcomed clients and celebrities, including the architect Norman Foster and the actor Josh Hartnett. Waiters circulated with trays of fig-leaf fizzes as the boat pushed off. Forty-five minutes later, we disembarked and walked up a wooded path, shrouded in mist, as some kind of panpipey music emanated from the club grounds.
Ostensibly, the party was being given to celebrate the grand opening, after years of work, of a sprawling new Hermès boutique on London’s New Bond Street. I had been warned that Hermès loves a theme, and that the company’s approach to events could be a little fanatical, but the scene we encountered on the club’s lawns was commitment on a scale I had never seen before. A man sat on a rock, a map spread out over his knees, holding an umbrella. He was a hired performer, as was another man, who was splayed out in a beach chair, tabloid over his face and thermos by his side, like something out of a Martin Parr photograph. A full team of white-suited cricketers batted and bowled on a village green. The hedges were moving, doing pirouettes around a pony-topped Maypole, as though Burning Man had relocated to Albion. Five restaurants had been erected for the occasion, including a tiffin stand and an air-conditioned “potting shed” with chandeliers made of leeks and radishes. I asked a member of the events team to define the evening’s theme. He replied, without further explanation, “It’s a French horse who comes to London and doesn’t know how to act.”
More than a hundred Hermès family members were said to be in attendance. It was fun to try to pick them out, using their perfect tailoring and amusing silk accessories as a sort of Habsburg chin. Pierre-Alexis Dumas, the company’s artistic director, sat nursing a pint in the Horse and Carrot, a wood-panelled English pub, as an m.c. conducted a pub quiz.
“What is the meaning of ‘petrichor’?” the m.c. called out.
People were really getting into it, shouting out guesses (answer: the scent of rain hitting the ground) and generally abandoning the blasé attitude that typically serves as a sort of emotional dress code at fashion-world parties. Bells rang outside, and a team of dancers began wrapping multicolored satin ribbons around the Maypole. Then the sky lit up with a fireworks display in the same colors. Dumas watched, charmed, his arms encircling his wife’s shoulders, and accepted an ice-cream sundae in a silver parfait cup. The evening was beautiful, strange, and so far removed from the prerogatives of retail as to suggest that its entire purpose was not to have one. It was an aristocrat’s folly, positing that real luxury is not so much quiet as super weird.
Vanhée ended the night dancing alongside her bosses to a Fatboy Slim set in the pub. The next day, she visited the sculptor Rachel Whiteread at her studio, a former pickled-walnut factory in Tufnell Park. Vanhée often calls on artists, preferring to draw inspiration from IRL, cross-disciplinary exchange. The women had never met before, but the rapport was easy.
“Was the party fun?” Whiteread, who had declined to attend, asked.
“It was this very Hermès world,” Vanhée said, adding, of the venue, “As a Parisienne, I had to laugh, because apparently it takes, like, forty years to get into that club.”
Vanhée seemed relieved to be in the company of another creative person, and the conversation turned toward the difficulty of maintaining integrity in the ever-more-corporatized fashion and art industries.
“Damien Hirst always says, ‘Back when I was a good artist . . .’ ” Whiteread said, laughing.
“You either fit in or you get killed,” Vanhée replied. “I’m aware of what I’m doing, and I’m still a good designer. My curiosity pushes me to say yes, but I can say no if it’s jeopardizing the sincerity of the work.”
Just as Hermès is at a crossroads in its fashion, Vanhée is facing a critical moment at Hermès. Her growing public presence may express a desire to cement her status at the house before the arrival, this winter, of the highly esteemed, mediagenic British designer Grace Wales Bonner, who is replacing Nichanian, the Hermès veteran, as the creative director of menswear. In a sign of confidence in Vanhée, Hermès recently announced that she will present the company’s first-ever couture collection, in January. Couture is a departure from the house’s origins in industrial-age design, but it is also an extension of what Hermès has always done, in pursuing painstaking construction. Money, after all, buys time. Vanhée told me that she sees couture as an opportunity to dilate on her ideas in an era when time itself feels “increasingly dizzying and increasingly abstract.” She explained, “We can’t stand waiting anymore. We always want everything to be highly optimized and very fast. Couture is the opposite of this.”
Before one conversation with Vanhée, I’d come across a review by
The Cut’s
Cathy Horyn, the doyenne of American fashion criticism. In the past, Horyn had been supportive of Vanhée, calling her “the best women’s designer to work at Hermès” since Martin Margiela and “among the very best working in fashion today.” This review, however, dissented from the widespread view that the L.A. show had been a triumph, suggesting that Vanhée, after more than a decade at Hermès, was mailing it in. Horyn wrote, “I don’t understand Nadège Vanhée’s clothes for Hermès anymore—why they’re trapped in such a narrow and predictable vision of an élite woman in a tasteful leather suit, jodhpurs, and boots, and a horse-inspired harness top with a black skirt. Is that what she really believes in?”
Thinking of Vanhée and Whiteread’s discussion about the limits of creativity, I asked Vanhée about Horyn’s critique. She seemed particularly irked by Horyn’s contention that certain competitors—Dario Vitale, who made raucous, eighties-inspired looks during a brief tenure at Versace; Matthieu Blazy, who is injecting playfulness into Chanel—were doing a better job of expressing the spirit of the day.
“I think she’s probably asking, ‘What is the aesthetic of the twenty-first century?’ And me, too, I’d like to know,” Vanhée said. But some designers “show up with a certain platform, almost like a d.j. reboot,” she added, and remix “a little bit of this, a little bit of that” from various eras and aesthetics. “It’s a bit Grandmaster Flash,
quoi
.” She trailed off for a minute, as if not wanting to offend, then picked back up. “Hermès genetically isn’t looking for that. It’s looking for authenticity.
Vous comprenez le sujet
?” Despite her designs’ frank sensuality, all the harnesses and black leather, her real kink is Hermès’s craftsmanship. “My new obsession is to preserve this savoir-faire that is in the process of disappearing,” she said. She went on, “If the idea is just to do something divisive, that’s easy. That’s never interested me. If it interested me, I would never have done fashion. I would have done art.” ♦

epub_21.title: Tom Sachs Channels Chanel
epub_21.text:
Tom Sachs Channels Chanel
Showcase
Tom Sachs Channels Chanel
At his downtown studio, the perennially provocative artist makes a lo-fi version of the brand’s flagship Parisian store.
By Rachel Syme
September 07, 2026
In the winter of 1994, Barneys, the former high-end Manhattan department store known for its daring storefront displays, unveiled its Christmas windows: three hundred and nine original works by both well-established and emerging artists which the store planned to auction off to support local schools. What began as a gesture of holiday charity, however, soon devolved into chaos, after a three-by-two-by-two-foot sculpture, “Hello Kitty Nativity Scene,” drew the ire of Catholic groups. Fashioned out of colored duct tape by a then little-known twenty-eight-year-old sculptor named Tom Sachs, it was a punky act of pop-culture bricolage that starred Madonna as the Virgin Mary, three Bart Simpsons as the wise men, and the titular white cat as the baby Jesus. After weeks of public protest, Barneys removed the work and apologized in a full-page ad in the
Times
. In the kind of career-making scandal that many young artists dream of, Sachs, who was born in Manhattan, grew up in Connecticut, and studied art at Bennington College, became the city’s newest enfant terrible.
On a recent sweltering morning, Sachs, now sixty, stood outside his sprawling SoHo studio, on Centre Street—where he has been making art for the past forty years—thinking, yet again, about a window display. For his latest work, “31 Rue Cambon,” an immersive installation that opens to the public on September 11th, during New York Fashion Week, Sachs converted part of his studio into an uncanny simulacrum of the luxury fashion house Chanel’s flagship boutique, in Paris. Viewers will enter directly from the street, where Sachs and his team of around twenty people were in the process of re-creating the iconic Chanel storefront, with cream-colored awnings made of cardboard and wrought-iron gates emblazoned with the brand’s interlocking “C”s. Inside, viewers will find a mirrored entrance hall and a showroom stocked with handbags, shoes, sparkly baubles, and Chanel’s signature two-piece suits—all painstakingly handcrafted out of everyday materials such as cardboard, paper, plywood, and broken glass. Sachs, who has the garrulous, jittery mien of a hyperactive teen-ager, explained that he intended to conceal the exterior till the last possible minute. “We’re keeping butcher paper up on the windows until we open,” he said. “I think shock and awe is best.”
This is not the first time Sachs has repurposed Chanel’s enduring iconography in order to shock: in 1998, he made a giant, fully functional guillotine out of stolen police barriers and covered it in Chanel logos—in part, he has said, to make a statement about “cultural fascism.” (The piece now resides in the permanent collection of Paris’s Centre Pompidou.) Over the years, Sachs, whose work is also found in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum, the Museum of Modern Art, and the Guggenheim, has positioned himself as a cultural provocateur who re-creates loaded objects and spaces—he’s made a toilet plunger out of Hermès wrapping, a McDonald’s meal from Tiffany packaging, and a model of a Nazi death camp stamped with Prada insignia—in what he has called a dual exercise in “brand critique and brand affection.” But “31 Rue Cambon” may be his most comprehensive engagement with consumerism yet, and it comes at a moment when Chanel frenzy is at a newfound high, thanks to the brand’s creative director, Matthieu Blazy. (The French label reported a revenue increase of about sixteen per cent in the first half of 2026.) “This store, for me, is
real
, even though you cannot buy anything in it,” he said. “Maybe, in a way, that inaccessibility makes it feel more real. For me, the lust for consuming things is replaced by making them.” As a maximalist
Gesamtkunstwerk
, it echoes another of Sachs’s major works, “Space Program,” which débuted at the Gagosian gallery, in 2007. For that, he built a spacesuit, a
NASA
command center, and a to-scale lunar module out of plywood, plumbing, and found materials. Most recently, he showed a collection of his furniture design at the Upper East Side gallery Salon 94.
On Centre Street, Sachs pointed toward a chandelier in the entrance hall, reminiscent of one in Coco Chanel’s Paris apartment; he and his team built it out of cast-iron woks, Citi Bike reflectors, and lead fishing sinkers. He pushed through a mirrored panel to reveal the main boutique, where, around the room’s perimeter, a dozen or so flat Chanel “suits,” all painted on slabs of three-quarter-inch plywood, were hung up like dream clothes for a life-size paper doll. Coco Chanel began creating suits for women in the nineteen-twenties, but it was a design of hers from 1954—a tweed skirt with a boxy, collarless matching jacket—that became one of her most recognizable silhouettes. Since then, Chanel suits have been worn by style icons from Marlene Dietrich to Michelle Obama. The current version of the ensemble retails for more than ten thousand dollars. A Sachs suit sculpture, by contrast, requires “maybe seven dollars’ worth” of materials. The value, he told me, is in the labor: each one took more than ten days to produce, as he and his team mimicked individual textiles by using experimental techniques. To make a famous ivory-navy-and-red bouclé suit worn by Coco herself, for example, the team used combs from Walmart to crosshatch the paint’s surface and added dollops of paint to imitate bouclé’s popcorn texture. The hand-painted gold buttons, decorated with ornate laurel wreaths, are tiny works of art in themselves, shaped out of sculpted polymer.
Thirty-one suits in total will be on view, mimicking those worn by celebrities such as Naomi Campbell, Elizabeth Taylor, and Olivia Rodrigo, whom Sachs calls “the muses.” A rickrack trim on one suit was made by a staffer piping a wriggle of paint out of a syringe and then smooshing it with wax paper; the look of rough tweed on another was evoked by mixing paint with pumice gel. The accessories featured similar contrasts: a Gripoix brooch of diamantés and Lego elements (the “jewelry” will be presented in a sleek set of glass-fronted drawers and a wall-mounted cabinet), and, nearby, a cardboard facsimile of classic Chanel pumps with stacked wooden heels. Sachs ran his hands over a powder-blue suit, modelled on one worn by Princess Diana. “Sometimes I come into the studio and, like, start crying,” he said. “Because we’re having so much fun. The things that we’ve come up with are so fucked up!”
In recent years, however, Sachs has faced criticism that his studio was not so fun; in 2023, several former staffers accused him of fomenting a toxic and cultlike workplace. Sachs denied specific allegations of harassment, but he did face consequences. Nike, with which he’s put out limited-edition sneakers since 2012, dropped him, though it renewed the relationship a year later, and Sachs had to issue a public apology and undergo sensitivity-and-awareness training. When I asked him about the allegations, he balked a bit. “I’m not sure how much more I can possibly add to what I’ve already said,” he said. “I will say I’m proud of the work that we’re doing here. I could not have done a show of this complexity without an incredibly dedicated team who shares the vision of this.”
Indeed, his team, which works out of a carpentry shop in the basement and a painting studio upstairs, did seem dedicated; I observed a cadre of young artisans gluing hundreds of seed-size rhinestones onto plastic bezels to evoke the look—if not the price—of lavish jewelry. “For me, this show is not about Chanel,” Sachs said. (In fact, he hasn’t spoken to anyone at the brand about the project.) “It’s about honoring and obsessing.” ♦

epub_23.title: The Scourge of A.1.
epub_23.text:
The Scourge of A.1.
Shouts & Murmurs
The Scourge of A.1.
By Ian Frazier
September 07, 2026
Rather than devote this space to humor, as I sometimes do, this week I want to speak about a very serious subject: A.1. Wherever we turn nowadays, we hear about the supposedly frightening phenomenon of A.1. We’re told that A.1. is going to take our jobs, revolutionize our economy, drain our bank accounts, maybe change how our brains work, start wars, and even lead to the end of the world. All of these are real concerns. But let me add some perspective and demythologize the subject a bit. Yes, right now, A.1. may seem overwhelming and scary, but let’s everybody step back, take a deep breath, and remember—
it’s just a steak sauce!
For A.1. to cause such fear is understandable, because many of us are not comfortable with condiments. We see A.1. as belonging to the world of advanced, high-level condiments, and we run for cover. In my case, I struggled with condiments all the way through school. On the condiments SAT, I did so poorly that it almost kept me out of college. My aptitude for condiments is very low—nothing I can do about it—and I know millions are like me in that. But just because we’re not very good at condiments, that’s no reason to fear them.
Also, there is another threatening and somewhat embarrassing aspect to A.1., especially for young men. They are told that when they become sexually active, always use a condiment. They hear this over and over: Use a condiment! Use a condiment! They have that fixed in their minds, and they want to follow this sound advice from parents and teachers and public-health officials, and that’s all good. But nobody ever says
which
condiment. And there are a lot of condiments out there! What with all the uncertainty that surrounds intimacy when you’re young and inexperienced, not knowing the right condiment can be an anxiety-producing issue. When the experts say, “Use a condiment,” do they mean, “Use Louisiana Extra-Hot Iberian Hot Sauce?” Well, here’s a news flash: they don’t! (I learned that the hard way.) Each person must settle on the right condiment by trial and error, through an often painful process, and that’s a problem we tend not to talk about.
Now, I’m going to tell you a fact about A.1. that, once you hear it, you’ll never forget it. A.1. is basically
Worcestershire sauce
. Sure, some tweaks to the formula have been added, but in essence A.1. and Worcestershire sauce are one and the same. A.1. was invented because nobody knew how to pronounce “Wor-shest-er-sher-ster sauce.” A guy takes his family or some friends or clients out for a nice dinner, everybody orders big steaks, and then the guy tells the waiter, “Oh, and bring us a bottle of Wor-shers-ter-shuer-shest sauce,” and he looks and sounds like an idiot, and the evening is ruined. “A.1.,” on the other hand, is easy to say. Plus, everybody is now so terrified of A.1., it makes the waitstaff hop to.
How did such a hard-to-pronounce name as Wor-shest-et-cetera make it into the language in the first place? It turns out that the name goes back thousands of years and refers to a place in England. In the time of the Roman Empire, much of England was under occupation. The English had hundreds of different druidical religions, but only one sauce. In order to confuse the Romans, the local people gave their most strategic places names that were almost impossible to pronounce. One of these places was called, in Saxon, “Wor-shesht-yer-sher-ter-shest-sher,” which meant “The Place of Our Only Sauce, and We Have Just the One.” The Roman Army, which had recently come from Italy, naturally spoke Introductory Latin, then known as Italian. Try saying that name in Italian! It’s no snap for the Italians even today, after centuries of practice.
Recently, you may have noticed that your electricity bill has gone up. This is because A.1.-production centers bigger than any the world has ever seen are using billions of kilowatts to pump out the familiar steak sauce night and day. A study has shown that by early next year we will have enough A.1. not only to garnish all the beef cattle, milk cows, buffalo, beefalo, oxen, and musk oxen on the planet but enough to drown them in an A.1. tsunami seventy-five metres deep. What are the manufacturers’ plans for all this A.1.? Here is where the dangerous part comes in. Many experts say that all this A.1. has some connection to computers, and to something called “coding.” Following this theory, the code may be an ingenious and hard-to-crack cipher in which, perhaps, the letter “A” is represented by the numeral “1.” Talk about hiding in plain sight! But, for the moment, the rest of the code has yet to be solved. ♦

epub_25.title: New Shoes
epub_25.text:
New Shoes
Fiction
New Shoes
By Hisham Matar
September 06, 2026
All of a sudden, with no reason or warning, my brother began to hear from friends he had introduced me to or others we still had in common, those few I had somehow retained over the twelve years since leaving home, that I had been seen in Cairo, walking down a street or sitting alone at a café. This even though I had not lived in that city since, at the age of eighteen, I had waved my brother goodbye at the airport, with my small bag and my hopes and worries, seeing a fugitive and tender doubt plant itself deep in his eyes.
He wasn’t convinced that we had made the right decision. Our parents had done all they could, but in the end managed to save enough for only one plane ticket to Europe. Instead of the pair of us leaving together, it was going to be him alone. Then it was me. Then it was him again. I forget all the reasons for and against, but it eventually settled on me, the younger brother.
Read an interview with the author for the story behind the story.
A year later, I set off, travelling via a circuitous route that saw me attempt lives in some half a dozen cities across Italy and France, constantly sending messages from new phone numbers. Reassuring messages. And money. They are still there in my head, those obsolete numbers and the addresses where I lived, locations where, I suspect, a part of me remains. Perhaps I am occasionally remembered by the people I dealt with in those places. For isn’t it the case that at times, for no particular reason, we suddenly recall the face of a person with whom we had only a passing encounter? It is not obvious why I remember the things that I remember, or, for that matter, forget the things that I forget.
I continued north till I reached London. All in all, the journey, from bidding my brother farewell in Cairo International Airport to landing here, took four years. I arrived tired, and a little changed. I certainly wasn’t as optimistic, or as fearful. London has been home for the past eight years. Home—what a strange word to use about a city that isn’t your own. And yet, some days a terror rises within me that I may never leave it.
“Four years,” my brother said on my first day, and has said a couple of times since, always in a reassuring and happy tone. “The length of a university degree. You have finally graduated, my boy.”
I hate London. I hate and love it all at once. I haven’t told my brother this, out of fear that he would realize we only hate and love the places we believe we will never leave. I know how he thinks. Nor have I told him that I have always accepted that people like me are unwanted here. Needed, perhaps, but not wanted. It is plain to see. Nor have I told him that I learned to be O.K. with this, that in London, as in life, it is impossible to go on without a degree of indifference. You have to not give a shit.
All this to say that I am fine. I have learned to be away and I am doing well. Discovered a talent for business. I now manage not one but three shops, what here they call newsagents.
“Don’t get yourself into trouble,” my mother said when I first went into this line of work. “Stay well clear of politics. Politics brings only ruin.”
This highly amused my brother. I could hear him laughing in the background.
Podcast: The Writer’s Voice
Listen to Hisham Matar read “New Shoes.”
“Mum,” I said, “Newsagents have nothing to do with news. We sell groceries and household goods. You know, milk, eggs, and plungers.”
“And magazines and newspapers,” my brother added. She clearly had me on speaker.
The shops are within a square mile. I spend my days going between them. I employ nine people. The locals know me by now. They greet me when they see me walking. Some call me by my first name. I know many of their names, too, and the names of their children, and even their dogs. You learn things in this job, things that may or may not be important: what people like to drink, what newspapers they read, how parents manage their children’s sweet tooth, how they sometimes weaken and buy themselves tobacco and ask you not to mention it to their spouses, how the lonely pensioners purchase a lottery ticket every week but really only want to chat.
The money I send home every month is more than the amount I keep. During the time I have been away, the exchange rate has climbed sharply and in only one direction. When I first left home, one pound sterling got you eleven Egyptian pounds. Now it’s seventy. If, God forbid, both my father and my brother lost the ability to work, my family would want for nothing.
My brother has been clever, investing nearly half of the money I send. He bought a flat in one of the new developments in the suburbs, “off-plan,” as they call it, before the block was built, which allowed us to pay for it in easy installments. By the time it was finished, it had doubled in value. He rented it to a young family who have been paying on time each month. He is keeping an eye out for similar opportunities, speaks of compiling a “portfolio” of such properties, “so that you can finally return home, and retire in comfortable luxury.”
He, more than anyone else, knew how difficult it was for me to leave, and he, more than anyone else, could sense how frightened I was as he drove me to the airport, how it seemed to me then that time had cracked open, that the past had collapsed, and I could do nothing but go forward, whether I wanted to or not. I remember the grief of it, together with the sharp and manic urge to remake myself entirely. Such passions are with me still, chains tethering me to this fate. And I know that he saw it in my eyes as we said goodbye. He knew how much encouragement I required, and kept on saying that I shouldn’t take it so hard, that before I knew it I would be back home and life would be better, “much, much better.” I didn’t believe him and I needed to believe him. I was angry at him and grateful to him. The opposing emotions battled with each other as I walked away, thinking, He doesn’t fool me. I know he, too, is in pain. But he endured it with a tender deflection, like a man closing his eyes before stepping off a precipice. Even though, of course, it was I, his younger by two years, his best friend, as he liked to call me, who was going into the unknown.
Only after my last visit, some seven months ago now, did my brother start to claim that I had been seen in Cairo. There was something cruel and bizarre about it. I couldn’t understand why he would tell me such a thing. And, every time, it impressed itself upon me in ways I couldn’t fully explain, as though I had been afflicted by a strange fervor. It rendered me consoled and outraged. Whatever the feeling, I had become a passive subject, vulnerable to assault.
The other day, he said that I had been spotted sitting alone in a café in Zamalek, that old and illustrious neighborhood he and I admired as young teen-agers. I remembered us walking through it with romantic dreaminess, looking up at its late-nineteenth-century buildings, picturing ourselves someday living there.
In these dozen years abroad, I have endured some terrible times, and yet I’ve found some comfort in the fact that everyone I truly cared about lived far away, across the sea, and therefore could not possibly know how bad things were. When you live in a foreign land, you can, for example, sleep in parks in summer and in train stations in winter free of the danger of anyone you know ever finding out. What kept me going then was imagining myself one day returning home and buying an apartment in Zamalek, where, at long last, I would be able to set up my own respectable and independent life in the city of my birth, where even with complete strangers I feel as though I share some familial bond.
But in these last few years, since the success God bestowed on me, I haven’t thought of Zamalek much at all. In fact, I can see now, I had managed to almost forget about it altogether, until the first time my brother called to say, with a mischievous smile in his voice, “Apparently, you were seen crossing Brazil Street, in Zamalek.”
We laughed about it.
But then, that night, I couldn’t sleep. I discovered that I had not cured myself of that dream at all but merely suppressed it. I tossed and turned, seeing myself furnishing an apartment on Brazil Street, having tea on the balcony at the hour of twilight, when the Cairo sky and the Nile beneath it appear to momentarily hold their breath.
A week or two later, my brother called again to say that a friend of his swore she had seen me, “prowling through the shelves” of a bookshop downtown.
“And why didn’t you stop to say hello,” my brother had asked her, I imagine with the same smile in his voice.
“Because,” the woman told him, “your brother seemed . . . involved.” She paused before the last word as though to denote that she, too, wasn’t sure what exactly she meant by it. “What I mean,” she went on, “is that he didn’t look as though he was browsing as much as searching for a particular book, one upon which his life depended.”
When my brother called to tell me this, I happened to be standing in front of a bookshelf, with my head tilted to one side in order to read the spines. It was a Sunday afternoon and I had wandered into my local bookshop in the aimless hope of finding something to read. A thriller of some kind, one with blood and wonder, to keep me turning the pages, to make the world recede a little. When I told my brother where I was, hoping that the coincidence would amuse him, but also to confirm that I wasn’t lying, that I was in London, he said, “I see.” He said it languidly, as though he was doubtful.
I could no longer concentrate and walked out of the bookshop empty-handed. Does he really not believe me? Is he truly suspecting that I’m living a double life, that my trips to Cairo are divided between those when I announce my plans to my family and those when I enter the city covertly, perhaps to test what it would be like to live a life there similar to the one I have devised for myself here, a life free of associations, and to do so in tandem? After all, the flight between the two cities is about five hours long, enough time to read a short book. And, if the hesitation I detected in his voice was skepticism, it might also have been an expression of his wish to let me get on with it, in the hope that this would eventually bring me closer, convince me to move back. But, deep within this skepticism or distrust, I sensed a new sadness that had to do with the implied realization that my life abroad had made me in need of convincing, that what was keeping me away now was not only, as he had once called it, “the noble pursuit of one’s fortunes,” but that I had, over these past twelve years, become accustomed to a different life, which had caused the compass of my belonging to ever so gradually shift northward.
I sensed, in my brother’s accounts of these supposed sightings, a tone of wavering disappointment. After his initial amusement, a vague concern lodged itself in his throat, coloring his words. What is even stranger is that I, too, began to sense myself divided, half here and half there. And so, whenever he said that someone had seen me at a particular café or bookshop or walking along one of the streets he and I know so well, I began to feel that I was elsewhere, daydreaming, as though the occasion had birthed in me a violent longing for home and my family. My present self, the self that had left and was getting on with the business of daily life in London, had somehow become divorced from the former and now somewhat hypothetical version of the man I might have become had I remained on my native soil. As the days rolled on, I held on to this superstition that I was cleaving in two. I began to feel lonesome, even more so than before, which made it all the more disturbing that in those alleged accounts of me in Cairo I was either alone or embroiled in some uneasy dispute. My life in London, the life I had cobbled together with the barest of routines, grew thin and unconvincing. It now seldom felt real.
The days passed quietly, with no sense of a precise delineation, as though the division between them had revealed itself to be less definite, and time was not separated into chapters, but appeared as one continuous roll of fabric, monotonously unfolding with few markers. There was peace in this, albeit the peace of falling, together with a numbing evenness, as though I were a fogged landscape, unpunctuated by borders.
My brother, who, for as long as I can remember, was in the habit of calling every second or third day, had gone completely silent. Three whole weeks had passed without my hearing his voice or even receiving a message from him. I would be lying if I said that I didn’t feel a sense of relief at the novelty of it. I continued to get text messages from my mother, of course, focussed on confirming that I was well, healthy, sleeping, eating properly.
Then, one afternoon, when I was sitting on the upper deck of the No. 24 bus going down Charing Cross Road, he called. His voice was off. From the first utterance I thought I detected an agitated or troubled tone. I have long feared the day when he will call with bad news, to tell me that our father or mother has died in their sleep, or slipped and fallen down the stairs, been run over by one of the many careless drivers, or rushed to hospital after a savage stroke that has left them impaired, unable to speak or move or recognize those around them. I kept asking, without giving him a chance to speak, and louder than was necessary—one of the commuters on the bus, a woman sitting three rows ahead, turned around with a disapproving face—“What’s the matter? What’s the matter? Is everything all right? Are you sure? Then why do you sound like this? What are you hiding?” Even as I said these things, I was perplexed by the force of the anxious excitement that had overtaken me.
“Sound like what?” he said. “Nothing. It’s you . . .” he said and stopped. “I just got off the phone with Maged, you see. You remember Maged?”
Of course I remember him. For a time, when we were all at school together, Maged and I were very close. Now he was more my brother’s friend. So why ask such a question? But I kept silent, my eyes on the back of that woman’s head. Her soft brown hair swayed with the motion of the bus.
“He called to congratulate me on your safe return,” my brother said, “asking when he could see you, when the three of us could get together.”
He stopped, as though waiting for me to speak.
“I told him that you are in London,” he continued. “Of course I did. What else was I to say? But he wouldn’t leave it, got upset, asking why I was lying and so on. Kept saying, ‘But I saw him with my own two eyes.’ ”
Here he paused again. Was he waiting for me to confirm or deny it?
“Well,” I said, “that’s clearly nonsense.”
“You were sitting outside a café,” he said. “And he was in a taxi, stuck in traffic. Said that if only he weren’t already late for his appointment, he would have run across the road to greet you, ‘To wrap my arms around him’ was how he put it.”
The woman turned around once more. She saw me frozen, listening, and, this time with a neutral expression, she faced forward again, her hair rearranging itself.
“Maged is fond of you,” my brother said defensively.
I could hear my heart in my ears, and felt it tap on the roof of my mouth.
“There was something else,” my brother went on, “that kept Maged from approaching you.” Here my brother tried to give a little laugh. “I had to ask several times, and when he finally agreed to say it, he kept insisting that I promise not to tell you. He feared you might misunderstand, think he was prying. He’s a decent guy. Wishes you well from his heart.”
For some reason, my mind went back to Venice, where I had worked, that first summer after I left home, as a cleaner in a small three-star hotel. The place was in Giudecca, across the water from the historic center of Venice. I didn’t speak the language. I didn’t speak any language except my own. During my breaks, I would find a spot in the shade and sit by the water, watching the boats go by.
“In the end,” my brother continued, “when he finally told me what he saw, what he begged me not to tell you, I couldn’t see what all the fuss was about. Hardly extreme. You were in the middle of some argument, that’s all, with the man you were sitting with at the café, who was older, as old as our father, Maged said. He was leaning toward you and looked very angry, waving his hands about and, although Maged could not hear, he was convinced that the man was screaming. You were shouting, too, apparently. Maged said he could see the veins bulging in your neck.”
My brother pretended to yawn. I suspected what he was thinking. When I didn’t say anything, he said, “Anyway, I just thought I ought to tell you.”
I held my tongue. Didn’t even give him a brief hum or grunt or any sound to affirm that I was still there.
My brother tried to laugh again. “Strange,” he said, “how the picture corresponds to those times when you were young, the year before you left home, when you and Dad were at loggerheads, arguing over the smallest things, remember?” And then, whether to be kind or else intending to provoke me, he added, “So long ago now.”
The bus was still moving slowly down Charing Cross Road. I tried to return my mind to Venice. Why Venice and why now, I thought, and why that image of the water? Every window of every building the bus crawled past opened a severe yearning in me, as though my life here had become abstract or theoretical. What salvation these rooms, many with blackened windowpanes that looked as if they had not been opened in years, seemed to offer. And yet, the more I looked, the deeper my soul sank. I had to avert my eyes. I kept them pinned to the floor, doing all I could not to remember those arguments. Or not so much the arguments themselves, for whatever they claimed to be about was soon forgotten after I left Cairo. What remained from those disputes, which, had I been allowed to stay home, might have been resolved the way, I suspect, such disagreements between father and teen-age son usually are, is the memory of the acrid vapor they cast over the atmosphere of my early days in Venice, working in silence, where homesickness mingled with bewildered regret. Twelve years later, there I was on the 24 bus detecting that same bitter taste in my mouth.
I got off at the next stop, and walked along the crowded pavement. Isn’t it curious, I suddenly thought, how nearly every piece of clothing I own I had bought in the days before one of my annual visits home, wanting to dress myself up for my family. I realized, very much for the first time, that I have always felt responsible for my absence, guilty for it, and, to console them, in good times and in bad, I brought gifts and turned up looking like a winner. Twelve visits in twelve years. Each lasting no longer than a month. We have, in other words, spent together an accumulated total of about a year since I left the country. One year in twelve. If I’m granted an average life expectancy, I’ll have a total of about four years in my country before I die.
It will now be another four months before I visit again, but I decided to take myself shopping for new shoes at one of the fancy places on Jermyn Street. I was looked after by a man in a suit and tie who, although he was around my age, seemed much younger. He had already mastered that English skill of making you feel accused, obliging you right from the outset to prove yourself worthy. For this reason alone, I decided to try on a battery of models, labelled “Chelsea Boots,” “Oxfords,” “Derbys,” “Loafers,” and so forth. The style I liked most was a lace-up in horse leather. I didn’t even know they made shoes of horse leather. It shone stiffly and was the deep and uneven color of polished antique wood. The shoes were heavy, each one seeming to weigh at least three pounds. I felt steadied by them. They reminded me of when I was twelve and it had rained till the streets of Cairo were flooded. My brother and I had no choice but to walk home from school. The farther we went, the heavier our shoes became, filling up with water. I remembered how much we laughed, how novel and strange and exciting it all was. I kept pacing back and forth across the shop, with the salesman looking bored and detained. I asked him the price.
“Eight hundred pounds,” he said. “As long as you don’t wear them, there is a fourteen-day return.”
“So, if I walk out with them on, that’s it?”
“Indeed,” he said.
I stuffed my old pair in the box and walked to Trafalgar Square. I sat outside the Admiralty pub, lifted my foot up to the sky, and took a photo with Nelson on his column in the background. I sent it to my brother, with the words “New shoes.”
I could see that he had seen it. I watched the screen, expecting him to reply. I looked down at my feet and felt shame and regret. Eight hundred pounds is fifty-six thousand Egyptian pounds, I calculated. That is equivalent to half of my father’s annual salary. All spent on a pair of shoes. And my feet hurt in them. The man in the shop had said that’s because they would need to be broken in. I put the phone in my pocket. The sun was out. It was a nice evening. I decided to walk all the way home. ♦
