Grandmaster Flash’s Remix of Hip-Hop History
In his new book, “Birth of a Culture,” the trailblazing d.j. tells his version of how it all began.
By Vinson Cunningham
September 07, 2026
Check out a dance floor the next time you get a chance. Take note at the point in a song when the real dancers stop messing around. (“That was my part,” one of them might later say, or, like the grownups I used to know, “It got good to me.”) Usually, it has something to do with drums. A snare, or a kick, or a tom, or the rattle of an 808 tickles something in the groin or the hips, and the focus of the dancers sharpens. Their movements become more spiteful than woo-woo, more sculpture than painting, more an argument than an idle thought. Now, the sorcery of the dance floor is that this is never happening to only one dancer. This thing with the beat, the heightened part of the song that makes the room get suddenly serious—somehow it’s as objective as math, observable by everybody in the room. The drum hits just so, and it gets good to a whole crowd, all at once. Somebody cries out “Ay!!!” or “Whooo!!!” to acknowledge what’s going on.
One of the luckiest art-related miracles of the past century or so is that there was a young boy named Joseph Saddler, who’d later go by the name Grandmaster Flash and become the Promethean d.j. whose technique on the turntables would help usher into being the mix of sounds and attitudes that we now call hip-hop. Joseph got so obsessed with this moment of collective frenzy, and frustrated by the fleetingness of the part of the song that made it happen, that he spent his life learning to extend it indefinitely. In his new book, “Birth of a Culture” (Amistad), written with Scoop Jackson, Flash reminisces about spying on parties put on by his parents and older sisters. A favorite song at these parties was Curtis Mayfield’s “Move On Up”:
It’s 1970 and this is when I started paying scientific attention to the drum beat. That song had the world’s longest drum break—it had to be two minutes or more. I would get lost in that drum break, trapped. So when I started listening to other records, I’d notice that when the drum break came in, the backsides of my mom and dad’s friends would move more. Their behinds gyrated with more purpose; their dancing seemed to become more intense and serious. So, in my toddler mind, the best part of the record has to be when the least of the band members were playing in accompaniment with the drummer. They called it “the drum solo”—whether it be the drummer and the bass player, the drummer and the cellist, or the drummer and the trumpet, to any other instrument in connection with the drummer. This was very exciting for me. My thought was that all records had this long drum solo like Curtis Mayfield’s record. As I was listening to other artists, to my disappointment, the drum solo on other records was over as soon as I blinked my eyes.
It’s funny: the great Grandmaster Flash, born in 1958, in the Bronx, calls himself a “toddler” in this anecdote, even though he was twelve at the time. Maybe this is because he views his adolescent self, enjoying a sensual perception whose implications he hadn’t yet begun to puzzle through, as still a baby in the context of the history of the music he’d eventually help invent. From the beginning, he had a scientific cast of mind, and not only about the fervors of dance. Confronted with the mystery of his father’s nighttime habit of listening to records—where’s the music coming from, and what does it have to do with this needle and that black disk?—Flash sneaked, over and over, despite many hard-handed spankings from his dad, into the closet that housed the vinyl.
Joseph, Sr., was physically abusive to his wife, as well as his son, and before long the family split up. Flash and his siblings moved with their mom from Throggs Neck to Fox Street, in the South Bronx. Amid so much chaos, and perhaps—although Flash never makes this connection—because of it, Joseph, Jr., hyper-fixated on electronics. He ripped apart record players and other gadgets, terrorizing the rest of his family with his curiosity and his surgeon’s willingness to attempt to operate on the bodies of household appliances. The tunnel vision that would make him a genius to the wider world first marked him as bad at home.
His mother had the wisdom to send him to a vocational-and-technical school where Flash learned the rudiments of amplified sound. Soon, he could put the gadgets back together, and even produce versions of them. Pining after the power of the disco d.j.s on the radio, he made his own d.j. set. But he still wanted to know: How could he keep the best parts of his favorite songs playing over and over? “The root of everything I was trying to discover was based on science and math,” he wrote.
Flash tricked out his homemade d.j. set, adding a felt bed for his records instead of the standard metal platter. He marked up the surface of his vinyls with crayons so that he could know when exactly the “break” of a song—the drum break that dependably made the partyers go wild—began and ended. He then figured out a blasphemous move: touching the surface of the records with his fingers to drag them in the opposite direction of the turntable’s motion, thus starting the break over. He used two copies of every record—toggling back and forth, catching the beat each go-round with impeccable timing, giving the illusion that the drum break never stopped, that it had always, at least implicitly, been a slice of something infinite, and that now, under his trance, it would never stop, until he gave it a chance to mercifully die. Then he mixed one break with another, sometimes letting them bleed together, sometimes making an abrupt switch that felt like a natural fact. True to his lifelong experimental bent, he called his invention the Quik Mix Theory.
Flash knew of the two other d.j.s who were working in the Bronx at the time, with whom he’d later share credit for the genesis of hip-hop. There was Kool Herc, who was one of the pioneers of the “needle drop” technique for extending breaks, and who had the best speaker setup in town. And there was Afrika Bambaataa, who had the widest and most cosmopolitan collection of records of the three, the most sophisticated sense of the history of Black sound, and a reputation for uniting rival gangs and reorienting them toward peaceful community aims. Neither, though, had the technical mastery of Flash, nor did they have his knack for the mathematics of the dance floor. Flash would glide from break to break, taking parts of the Incredible Bongo Band’s rendition of “Apache”—whose great effect, according to his “science,” “was the way they put the reverb on the snare,” their kick like “thunder and lightning”—and fitting them together with, say, “Heaven and Hell Is on Earth,” by 20th Century Steel Band, knitting a quilt of sometimes quite disparate older music and making of it something thrillingly new. He couldn’t stand to let the tension drop for even a second. If hip-hop seems excessive, this is why: its sound was invented, at least in part, to deliver too much of a good thing.
The early chapters of “Birth of a Culture” are devoted to telling Grandmaster Flash’s origin story, but the rest of the book is an episodic telling of hip-hop’s later history; Flash talks about or interviews rappers such as LL Cool J and Q-Tip in order to establish bonds of continuity between his achievement and theirs. (His first book, “The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash: My Life, My Beats,” from 2008, was a more straightforward memoir.) He is careful not to make his accomplishments, or hip-hop itself, sound like the product of a solitary genius. He always gives credit to Herc and Bambaataa, despite his personal (and, often, sonic) conflicts with the former. And he points out the aspects of life in the tough South Bronx—“no crystal stair,” to borrow a phrase from Langston Hughes—which enabled the rise of hip-hop. A party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, on August 11, 1973, thrown by Herc and his sister, has been mythologized as the unofficial beginning of the genre, but the truth is that throughout the seventies there were dozens of events like this, many of them held outdoors, in parks. Flash would rewire a street light to provide power for his turntables and speakers, and local kids—usually girls—passed out fliers and served as impromptu publicity teams. Shared space and equipment were put to rogue purposes, funkily repurposing municipal goods for the people. The d.j.s practiced in community centers and Police Athletic League locations, or, say, in the basement of a building where somebody’s dad was the superintendent or had otherwise come into possession of a spare key. Parents of friends would give Flash records from their collections, scarcely aware of what transformations their dusty music would undergo. A neighborhood girl named Anna, according to Flash, improvised the word “hip-hop” while drilling her brother who had signed up for the military:
Cookie started teasing their brother in cadence, “Your left, your left, your left, right, left!” And as she was doing that the other girls, including Anna, were saying, “Hip-hop-hip-hop, it don’t stop,” in the same military-type cadence, but with a rhythm like we were at a jam. She said they were doing that because that’s the way the soldiers walked. “One-two-one-two, pivot, turn, one-two-one-two.”
Anna, in Flash’s telling, was a kind of verbal virtuoso, a proto-rapper who rallied her similarly talented girlfriends to provide lines for the largely male m.c.s who rhymed over Flash’s soundscapes. The point of these anecdotes isn’t to direct sole credit to Anna—there are many rival accounts of the origin of the name “hip-hop”—but to illustrate the communal nature of the beginnings of the music and the culture.
This teeming togetherness becomes evident even in Flash’s music. Listen, for instance, to “The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash on the Wheels of Steel,” from 1981, the first record to showcase the Quik Mix Theory. During the recording session, Flash used three turntables instead of the customary two, so urgently did he feel the need to crowd the song with intriguing earfuls. The cut luxuriates in the pure sound of the songs that make up its collage. The cool, feline bass lines from Queen’s “Another One Bites the Dust” and Blondie’s “Rapture” are enlisted to form a spine, jangling against each other with a dissonant elegance. A snippet of the falsetto vocal from “Good Times,” by Chic, materializes and dissolves like a sun shower. “Apache,” that favorite track of the nascent hip-hop cognoscenti, appears with a knowing wink. Each of these references is made to dance via hypnotic repetition, each graffitied by the sleek scratches that Flash made with his fingers on the vinyl.
Flash is always, in different ways, calling himself a cloistered geek in his book. But “The Adventures of Grandmaster Flash” is the work of a confident cosmopolitan, someone who achieves his most important education outside on the streets, after dark. The scenario that comes to mind is of standing on a city corner at the promising beginning of a hot Saturday night, under a blue-black sky, perhaps waiting for a group of friends to show up, listening with a passive intensity to the music pouring out of car windows as they speed by. The rock kids, the funk kids, the disco-ers, the club rats are all fleetingly conjoined by one pair of highly attuned ears loitering on the streets. It’s the ultimate dance music, the flowering of Flash’s initial desire: to keep the liveliest part of the party going forever.
New York City in the seventies and early eighties, the crucial backdrop for hip-hop’s rise, was a Technicolor place of exaggerated ironies. In 1975, banks stopped underwriting the city’s daunting debt, which caused a fiscal crisis. The answer was austerity. Layoffs swept New York, and youth services suffered cutbacks. People left in droves. Landlords in search of insurance payouts set fire—often fatally—to abandoned buildings in the Bronx, dozens at a time at the height of the phenomenon; the now famous conflagrations glowed like bright symbols of urban decay. Drugs ravaged the streets, leaving needles and even more emptiness in their wake.
But the hollowed-out city became an impromptu stage, especially for the Black teen-agers who, in ad-hoc and decentralized fits and starts, bred the culture with which Flash is so clearly still besotted. Privation couldn’t stop the creative urge. Kids were spray-painting impressive murals on the sides of buildings and the bodies of subway cars. Others practiced a new form of highly kinetic, implicitly aggressive dance which would later be called b-boying, or break dancing. One of these early hip-hoppers was Flash’s eventual friend Fred Brathwaite, known on the streets as Fab 5 Freddy. Earlier this year, Freddy released his own memoir, “Everybody’s Fly.” He was a natural sophisticate whose father was close friends with the jazz drummer Max Roach, and he was a lifelong museumgoer who didn’t understand why he and his fellow-graffitiers couldn’t be considered fine artists. He came into the company of Jean-Michel Basquiat and Keith Haring, plus Debbie Harry from Blondie.
Hip-hop wasn’t the only growing vogue—punk was coming of age, and New Wave was becoming more popular. Black or white, uptown or downtown, it was art-obsessed kids who gave New York its brilliant spark back. Freddy straddled all these worlds, observing their points of intersection and grooves of adjacency. In his book, he muses, for instance, about how “dancehall reggae’s toasting, New York City’s mobile d.j. scene, and rap developed almost simultaneously . . . largely inspired by slick, jive-talking Black disc jockeys on the radio.” And he was dazzled by Flash, too, whose heretically physical way with records—touching and scratching the vinyl like a vandal—reminded him of the heedless white kids he’d come to know downtown. “He was breaking all the rules, which was the most punk thing you could do,” Freddy writes of Flash. “Rap and punk: They were both so wrong they were right.”
Lots of people were running around the Bronx with the name Grandmaster back in the day—a d.j. named Grandmaster Flowers was first, according to Flash. Grandmaster Caz, of the Cold Crush Brothers, was another. Nothing too new there. As a kid, I always wondered if that title, this in-group’s slightly humorous mark of high-ranking nobility, was a fly retort to the dorky Grand Wizards of the Ku Klux Klan, the dangerous losers in the pointy hats with so much terror on their minds. The realm of racism and hatred and death, that kingdom whose violence had spurred the Great Migration, which had in turn created the sometimes harrowing urban conditions that gave hip-hop its environment and raison d’être—they had their weird nomenclature, so why not us?
“Birth of a Culture” might have a similar joke embedded in its title, sharing, as it does, a phrasal structure with “The Birth of a Nation,” D. W. Griffith’s racist apologia for the K.K.K., which also happened to be the first-ever multi-reel blockbuster. Like all of hip-hop’s early heroes, Flash is fixated on the genre’s history—righting its wrongs, fighting a headwind of faulty tellings over the years. He knows that the practice of d.j.’ing—the real origin of hip-hop—has long since been overshadowed by the art of rapping. (He helped this along, too, by recruiting talented rappers—guys nicknamed Kidd Creole, Melle Mel, Scorpio, Cowboy, and Rahiem—to form his backing group, the Furious Five.) But, still, he feels he has to get things straight, perhaps because he knows that the power of a people, and of a culture, comes in part from the practice of fruitfully and generously interpreting the facts that gave them their rise.
In one omission, however, Flash praises Bambaataa’s message of love and peace, but conspicuously fails to mention the many credible allegations of child sexual assault that marred Bambaataa’s later life and career. And Flash has gripes with how things went down. One of the most famous songs in the history of hip-hop, “The Message,” was released as a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five record, even though Flash and his Quik Mix Theory appear nowhere in its music. (“I think it would have been a bigger record had our formula as a group been on that record telling that story,” he wrote.) He doesn’t like that Herc claims to have invented the “merry-go-round” technique of multiple d.j.s taking turns on the table, balancing the beat together, without citing Flash. When everyone goes gaga for the practice of sampling, he feels left out in the cold: “It becomes weird and very alarming when you watch something—a concept, an idea, a practice, a love, a theory—that you created evolve in front of your eyes, and you do not get any credit for what that idea has been turned into.”
In 2007, Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five became the first hip-hop act to enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. In 2023, Flash was the subject of a soft-focus interview on the “Today” show, to celebrate the fiftieth anniversary of hip-hop’s invention. He emphasized his happiness at the genre’s development. “Something that is loved by so many people has to change and has to go through its changes and do different things,” he said. “It has to.”
Here’s all the credit he needs: get some friends together, ones who really know how to catch a beat and feel it in their bodies, put on a Grandmaster Flash record, and watch the world spin. ♦

The Art of American Sophistication

The Art of American Sophistication
How striving, self-invention, and charm became a national style.
By Adam Gopnik
September 07, 2026
The prompt, let’s say, is “American sophistication.” What does it make the L.L.M. in our heads, trawling the riverbed of our old reading and viewing, produce? Whom do we think of first? Fred Astaire, I suspect, still comes to mind as the exemplar, even among many of those who know him only from stills or streaming. And, if we have a rudimentary knowledge of who he was and where he came from, we can begin to discern a larger pattern: he was not a New Yorker but a Midwesterner, a boy from Omaha, Nebraska, pushed along by a strenuous stage mother, the son of an Austrian Jewish father. His distinctive manner was eerily captured by
Scott Fitzgerald
, himself a refugee from the Middle West, in his description of Gatsby,
another
escaped Midwesterner, as someone possessing “that resourcefulness of movement that is so peculiarly American . . . He was never quite still; there was always a tapping foot somewhere or the impatient opening and closing of a hand.” Astaire to the life. He could have played the part perfectly.
For that matter,
Cole Porter
, Astaire’s greatest word-giver and another model of sophistication, as we commonly use the word, arrived at Yale from Peru, Indiana. So perhaps American sophistication is something that begins, like a Broadway show, out of town. But is this more a general rule than an American peculiarity? Maurice Chevalier and
Cary Grant
are the first two names that the prompt might supply for France and England. Chevalier was the working-class son of an alcoholic housepainter; Cary, born Archibald Leach, was neglected by his father, a tailor’s presser, and became a travelling acrobat before immigrating to New York. His debonair manner—which came to embody an American ideal of sophistication even more than an English one—was as hard-won as Edmund Hillary’s summit. Much the same can be said of
Noël Coward
, who learned his crisp enunciation through sheer aspirational effort. The one poshly reared product of high-period Hollywood was
Humphrey Bogart
, who grew up in a wealthy Manhattan household among private schools and tennis courts, and whose authentic upper-class sneer first found its natural American use as the expression of a desperate, cornered criminal.
Sophistication, one begins to think, is a thing won against the grain of privilege—a substitute for it, a social sleight of hand. A “classy” entertainer is almost never someone from the upper classes; sophisticated people are mostly smart people passing as rich people. At its sharpest, this inversion conferred titles of nobility on those denied social ease: the only Americans ever credibly, rather than jeeringly, called Duke and Count were Black musicians who spent their exhausted lives on buses and trains, and in segregated diners. At the same time, the Wasp élite regarded the top-hat-and-tails sophistication of the Astaire sort as amusingly forced and fraudulent, their own sophistication being evidenced by slightly frayed trousers, white-bread sandwiches, and suits worn for half a century. (There’s a whole world of Wasp resorts whose positive value is their sheer shabbiness.) Only truly sophisticated taste, in this code, grasps the superiority of deprivation over the more ethnic notions of actual comfort and good food.
Now Ross Posnock, an emeritus professor at Columbia who has previously written thoughtfully on Philip Roth, among many other subjects, offers an encyclopedic study of this one, “
American Sophistication: How the Casual Became Cool
” (Princeton). The book is breathtakingly large in scope and purpose, tracking the ideal from pre-Revolutionary America to the postmodern age. Almost flamboyantly digressive and parenthetical—with long excursions into Henry James’s memoirs and the elegance, or lack of it, among the
Partisan Review
crowd—it will invite plenty of quarrels and cavils. A good thing, since a book of this kind should provide stimulation rather than what Humpty Dumpty would have called a knockdown argument. A big, comprehensive book on, say, the history of cancer or the evolution of astrophysics should give us irreproachable information and sound conclusions. But from a book on a general squishy human subject like sophistication or masculinity or eros we want something else. We don’t need to be persuaded; we want to be provoked.
And we are, so much so that we might come to think that the idea of sophistication, like that of intelligence, is a composite chimera, hardly worth analyzing. Yet we know what we mean when we use it. A Paul Simon song like “Something So Right,” with its jazzy dominant ninth chords, is sophisticated in a way that “Bridge Over Troubled Water” is not. The term seems to imply a mastery of all the resources of a form, displayed in a surprising context without self-conscious artfulness. That’s Astaire: a perfectionist with Mozartean skills as a tap dancer but no pretensions to ballet. Or
Ellington
, a genius of harmony, one of whose greatest surviving works is a dance-hall concert recorded in Fargo. No one would think to call Stravinsky or Mondrian “sophisticated” in this sense, since their reputations already assume it. Sophistication implies a rising from a simpler background. You could do it the obvious way; you chose another.
Posnock’s pages on Astaire and Ellington are among those in which the argument locks most satisfyingly into place while still striking some original notes. He sees Astaire as both “a glorious exception to the rule of American ambivalence about sophistication” and “a distinctive version of that anxiety.” One expression of that anxiety, he shrewdly points out, is Astaire’s almost invariable pairing in the classic R.K.O. films not just with Ginger Rogers but with a fussy, effete opposite number, often Edward Everett Horton, Jr., whose presence marks Astaire’s dancing more securely as masculine.
Posnock is equally good on Ellington’s cultivation of “composure,” an achieved serenity in music and life alike, and on the repressed anger that this presumably cost him. He tellingly quotes the photographer
Gordon Parks
on Ellington’s “socializing of cool”: “Ellington never grinned. He smiled. Ellington never shuffled. He strode. It was ‘Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen,’ never ‘How y’all doin’?’ ” He was extending into Black show business the strict code that he had learned in his Black bourgeois family, in Washington, D.C. Yet, Posnock notes, “his statement of transparent filial piety contains a wink within its sincerity, a reminder of the artifice involved in possessing a manner”—a truth that he could well have confided to Astaire.
Posnock is also strong on what someone must have named the Grant-Leach dichotomy, and he generally lands on the right people and the right points. He has a flair for aphorism: “Sophistication insists that being and appearing coincide. We do not express sophistication; we appear sophisticated.” (True, certainly, of Astaire and Ellington.)
A persistent difficulty, though, is that Posnock seems to use “sophistication” to describe two very different categories of people, without ever quite distinguishing between them. There is the term as we use it of Astaire or Ellington. That’s Sophistication One: effortless elegance and apparent ease. But he also uses it in another way, Sophistication Two, for people who are broadly erudite across a surprising range of subjects, such as the
New Yorker
critic Edmund Wilson, whom he greatly admires—but whom one can’t imagine in a top hat, or even in a well-cut suit, or as an ornament at a dinner party.
The members of the first clan are hardly intellectual at all; indeed, the follies of intellect are part of what they mock or, in Grant’s case, have to escape to become worthy of Katharine Hepburn (e.g., “Bringing Up Baby”). The members of the second clan, meanwhile, can’t be relied on to dance or to wear clothes well—just look at the images of Wilson on the beach at Truro, holding forth in a dress shirt. A very few figures cross or combine the two types, most notably
Leonard Bernstein
, to whom Posnock devotes some good pages. Bernstein was a know-it-all who was also a showoff, to put it bluntly, with both qualities neatly packaged as high style. If we need an ideal type of the American sophisticate, Bernstein is it.
And what, as Edward Everett Horton might have sighed sibilantly in one of those R.K.O. movies, of the distaff side? The book is a bit thin on sophisticated ladies. Several friends of mine, when prompted, gave Jackie O. as their first choice; she appears here only briefly, as an adjunct to J.F.K. Hepburn gets a single reference against Grant’s multiple ones. Sadly scanted are the still underrated writers
Dawn Powell
and Anita Loos, whose genius for putting extremely canny judgments in the mouth of her seeming simpleton Lorelei Lee is exactly what we mean by a sophisticated joke. The novelist and journalist Mary McCarthy, by contrast, is discussed at length, though her inclusion even in the second sense seems unconvincing. What gives her work its bite is not so much assured knowingness as a persistently disingenuous sense of surprise. Florence, sex on trains, the Vietnam War, Lillian Hellman’s dishonesty—McCarthy registers a kind of wide-eyed disbelief at everything she encounters.
The book does eventually reveal an arc and find a climax. Posnock firmly identifies the nineteen-fifties as the high-water mark of American sophistication. From there, he rises to a kind of grand unified theory of the subject, complete with a family tree: “Younger New York sophisticates coming of age in the 1950s and 1960s, among them
Mike Nichols
, Jean Stein,
Sontag
, Jason Epstein,
Baldwin
,
Avedon
,
George Plimpton
, and
Stephen Sondheim
, affirmed urbanity as if a birthright (and in some cases, it in fact was) and their inevitable subject matter.” He continues, “Inspiring both generations were the Olympian models of national sophistication who had been reigning since the 1920s and 1930s: Astaire, Ellington, Grant, and Katharine Hepburn”—a “critical mass of sophistication as enacted ideal.”
He rightly insists that
the satirical duo of Nichols
and
Elaine May
were the most rewarding and complex comedians of their time, or ours, because they built their act around a failed sophistication, in their improvised characters, that presupposed an achieved sophistication in their audience scarcely imaginable a decade earlier. They harvested the comic fruit of the great revolution in liberal education, which marked the period when, as Auden wrote, soldiers who had stood up to the Nazi assault were now “shot to pieces by the shorter / Poems of Donne.” The great Nichols-and-May lines—“I can never believe that Bartók died on Central Park West,” or, on Albert Schweitzer, that he was “a lot of laughs” though “I personally have never dated him”—still ring as portraits of arrivistes eager to show that they know what everyone around them is expected to know. (The two met, it turns out, at the University of Chicago during its great heyday, though neither graduated, and May didn’t even enroll.)
Curiously, Posnock is cautious, even grudging, toward the apotheosis of this moment and this style in the brief Presidency of
J.F.K.
, whose apparent display of sophistication he treats skeptically, as a kind of façade drawn up for the masses, a goatee painted on his face by Jackie. But, compared with his predecessors and successors, J.F.K. really does seem to incarnate both types of American sophistication: he knew how to dress and how to make a dry joke, and he was genuinely erudite, at least given the field. He didn’t entirely write the books he bylined, but his enthusiasm for David Cecil’s “
The Young Melbourne
” was very real.
In a work so dense with references, mistakes will sprout like crabgrass; write a big book on André Le Nôtre’s formal gardens and the earthworm experts will gather to deride your confusion. The more you know the ground, the more crabgrass you see. So
The New Yorker
, in developing its distinct sophisticated voice, wasn’t really trying to be “urbane”; its decisive turn came when the anti-urbane E. B. White and James Thurber became the magazine’s voice, insisting that nothing could be more chic than to reminisce about Columbus, Ohio, or escape to Maine. The magazine’s urbanity lay in the anti-urbanism of its singular voices. Its most characteristic contributor, John Updike, left New York as quickly as he could for the fleshpots of Ipswich, Massachusetts, and made that and its people his subject for half a century. (Posnock also makes perhaps unduly heavy weather of the opening scene of the 2022 movie “Tár,” treating a scripted exchange—in which a character bearing this writer’s name and impersonated by this writer interviews a fictional musician—as though it were a spontaneous metropolitan conversation.)
A larger idea survives these local confusions and is neatly summed up by Posnock’s subtitle: casualness added to elegance is the particularly American contribution to the kind. Ellington and Astaire are surely instant winners by this definition. Like any general truth about a vast country and culture over a long period of time, it is bound to be a half-truth, but, then, all sociological truths are half-truths, and this one seems hardy enough to make its half as close to whole as we can hope to get.
But is a more illuminating idea missing from his account of American sophistication, one that perhaps most neatly distinguishes it from older European kinds? Since the Renaissance, the European ideal has rested on the pursuit, or, rather, the nonpursuit, of sprezzatura, unhurried grace, an ideal Posnock recognizes and celebrates. Certainly, the greatest image of sophistication ever conjured is Raphael’s 1514 portrait, now in the Louvre, of Baldassare Castiglione, who gave the ideal its name. The work is a miracle of resourcefulness: a “Venetian” portrait, painterly, almost monotone, and shimmering, by an Urbinate trained in sharp-edged drawing. Its point, if a painting can be said to have a point, is that the perfect gentleman doesn’t make a fuss, just as he doesn’t overdress. It is a pasquinade against posing.
Yet Castiglione’s sprezzatura, though humane, is not in itself charming. American sophistication has its sprezzatura—Astaire made an art of it—but characteristically turns effortlessness outward, into charm, something ingratiating and democratic-seeming. Charm is what turns the arriviste’s effort into a social gift. As the Cambridge critic Adrian Poole and others have observed, Henry James uses “charm” over and over, almost obsessively, the way Shakespeare uses “sweet” as his highest term of praise. It belongs to James’s own inescapable Americanness, and to his effort to delineate an American style. No English or French author would have used it in quite the same way. Proust uses “
charme
” often enough, but usually to mark the limits of an illusion. We are charmed by the charming Odette as a snake is charmed, held swaying in wonder, only to be disillusioned afterward.
American “charm,” as James incarnates it in characters from Daisy Miller, in her own novella, to Isabel Archer, in “
The Portrait of a Lady
,” is a kind of weaponized naïveté: innocence about the rules joined to impatience with following them, which wins the hearts of those who know the rules and would secretly rather not see them followed. What James means by “charm” is naïveté married to aesthetic ambition. Behind American sophistication lies the charm of American ambition: not where we find ourselves effortlessly but where we’ve put ourselves purposefully. Daisy wants to see the Colosseum by moonlight; it’s a foolish, and ultimately fatal, ambition, but in its way a fine one. Astaire’s dance steps are always directional, carrying him somewhere and toward something—the girl, the boat, the park bench.
And that alloy of innocence and impatience connects Astaire with Grant, whose tone, though we call it “sophisticated,” is less hauteur than genial affability punctuated by exasperation. The balance is intelligence against impatience, warmth against energy: the physical restlessness of Gatsby and Astaire, or Whistler’s refusal of finish, the most American of painters in his very expatriation, who said that “completeness is a reason for ceasing to exist.” The late Calvin Tomkins’s “
Living Well Is the Best Revenge
,” a biography of Gerald and Sara Murphy, describes how an overeager American couple became, through a kind of wonderful unself-conscious bluff, the cynosure of European modernity. The Murphys went to the South of France off-season, both a terribly ingenuous choice and a shrewdly worldly one that everyone copied. That mix of wide-eyed naïveté and pragmatic nous does seem typically American. Even Ellington’s willed composure is the composure of the afterglow, to use a term he liked—the calm that follows exertion, rather than the grace that pretends exertion never happened.
Posnock ends, dourly but necessarily, on the inevitable evil figure: Donald Trump as the opposite of any kind of sophistication. Instead, this “graceless” figure reminds us that true sophistication can help immunize us against “the depths of the subterranean.” Yet America was once, and at moments still is, a place of passionate pilgrims and new arrivals; as the old advertising slogan put it, We try harder.
When my wife and I first arrived in New York, we went, as often as we could afford, to the Bemelmans Bar, then a dark, cool, largely unvisited place at the Carlyle Hotel, with its beautiful, half-lit, uncleaned murals of children in an imaginary Central Park. (I went after my first seminar report and was so unprepared for the effects of a Black Russian on a grad student that I passed out and had to be lifted from the carpet by the Italian waiters.) It was our nearest approach to sophistication. Later, it became an object of amusement to our genuinely sophisticated friends, one of whom sent a photo of Ludwig Bemelmans with the slightly supercilious text “See you at the bar!” There was something naïve about our twentysomething readiness to try on so roomy an overcoat of sophistication, but, looking back, I suppose that this could have been . . . part of our charm. If there was doubtless something pathetic in the pursuit—we could have been down at CBGB, being punks—all culture begins in imitation, with the hope of growing into what one pretends to be.
Nowadays, the Bemelmans Bar overflows with tourists fresh off the bus and twentysomethings who have pre-screened it on Instagram, and has lost its old, beautiful emptiness, but doubtless the same pull that drew us draws them. Perhaps sophistication is not a way of feeling superior to the world but a wish that the world would itself
become
superior. Sophistication seems a shared longing more than a set style; it’s the desire to see the world shine brighter than it does while still knowing that all the light that shines from it is the light we bring to it. In a darkening time, maybe it isn’t so shabby an aspiration. The luminous Bemelmans himself began his life in New York as a busboy, was then promoted to waiter, and only afterward emerged as an artist: one more ambitious American arriviste, like Astaire, like Porter, like Gatsby, like the rest of us. ♦

Briefly Noted
Books
Briefly Noted
“The Breakup,” “All Them Dogs,” “Sex and Dissent,” and “We Want to Believe.”
September 07, 2026
The Breakup
, by Kurt Andersen (Random House)
. This comic novel is set in a hysterical vision of the year 2045, in which what was once the United States has been split apart by a civil war between liberals and a
MAGA
-like rebel group. The country is now divided into the so-called Free American Republic and what remains of the U.S. In this tense, uneasy landscape, a separated couple, Natalie and Asher, reunite to take their child, Logan, on a trip to tour colleges in both territories. Asher and Natalie’s disunion serves as almost a microcosm of the country: he a rabidly engaged liberal and she a head-in-the-sand moderate. The book is enlivened by Andersen’s gift for satire, which plays up the comic potential of ideological extremes.
All Them Dogs
, by Djamel White (Riverhead)
. “I was Wardy. Tony bleeding Ward. Lethal weapon forged in 1997,” the protagonist of this bold début novel proclaims. The statement is mainly a reminder to himself, as he returns home to Dublin after five long years on the run. Tony had to flee after killing a member of a rival gang; now he has joined the ranks of another outfit, notionally in search of money and protection, but ultimately out of a longing to have “someone else do the thinking.” As Tony strains to navigate brewing street wars, the most intimidating battles he faces are still internal—between expectation and desire, between who he is and who he might want to be.
What We’re Reading
Discover notable new fiction, nonfiction, and poetry.
Sex and Dissent
, by Meaghan Beatley (Penguin)
. This vividly reported book centers on recent feminist movements in Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Spain. Beatley, a journalist, profiles women protesting abortion restrictions, sexual assault, and femicide—an act that, she writes, lies “atop layers of normalized and socially sanctioned abuse.” While documenting acts of resistance, she examines the way that these feminists’ cultural contexts inflect their organizing. As she points out, many were influenced by struggles against military dictatorships of the twentieth century; some are the children of disappeared dissidents. “What sets Latin America apart is not violence itself but the clarity with which women understand its roots,” she writes.
We Want to Believe
, by Adam Kirsch (Columbia Global Reports)
. In recent decades, technological advances have vastly expanded our knowledge of the universe and led to the discovery of thousands of exoplanets. This has coincided with a widespread belief that humans will inevitably confirm that extraterrestrials exist. But, Kirsch argues in this concise treatise, the fact that our search has so far yielded nothing decreases the probability that we’ll ever find intelligent life beyond Earth. Why, then, has public opinion moved in the opposite direction from the science? Kirsch contends that the rise of serious discussion about extraterrestrials has paralleled the decline of the “traditional religious vocabularies” that once helped people grapple with the deepest questions of existence. In the end, he writes, “all our thinking about aliens and how to find them is best understood as humanity’s evolving self-portrait.”

Willem de Kooning’s Excavations of Intimacy
The Art World
Willem de Kooning’s Excavations of Intimacy
The first major show of the artist’s drawings articulates his pain and anger and the frightful era he lived in.
By Hilton Als
September 07, 2026
Drawings, like dreams, can often feel open-ended, prompting a multiplicity of thoughts. As painting’s poor cousins, they usually command a lesser fee in the art market, and their position somewhat to the left of capital may account—at least in part—for the fantastic, unfixed energy you often find in them: an artist draws not in the service of a career but in search of a self. Drawings, for me, are a kind of calligraphy of the soul, and, as you take in “Willem de Kooning Drawing” (at the Art Institute of Chicago through September 20th), it’s the enormous spirit behind many of the works—a searching spirit—that holds your attention, as do the artist’s questions about line, volume, voice, what the eye sees, and what the hand is capable of.
De Kooning drew throughout his long creative life. (He died in 1997, at the age of ninety-two.) When he allowed the younger artist Robert Rauschenberg to erase one of his drawings for the piece “Erased de Kooning Drawing” (1953), he knew that part of the poetry of the work would be the idea of him watching himself disappear. It would have been a nice touch to include “Erased de Kooning Drawing”—a bridge between modernist and postmodernist thinking—in this first major show of de Kooning’s works on paper, but, even without seeing it, you can keep it in mind as you study de Kooning’s own ghostly markings.
De Kooning, who grew up with almost nothing and then had everything, struggled with both deprivation and abundance. His story? It’s such an American one, especially if you think of having grown up elsewhere as definitively American. Born in Rotterdam in 1904, he was the child of Cornelia and Leendert de Kooning. His father, closed off and remote, tried to make a living bottling beer. His mother, hemmed in by poverty and the limitations of gender, had a dramatic personality and thought nothing of expressing her rage. Her anger was the great event of her life—and of her son’s. De Kooning’s affable but aloof personality was formed in part in reaction to Cornelia’s volubility; as a young man, he became known for his ability to defuse fights in bars and for his interest in theatrical women. His parents separated when he was two, and he shuttled back and forth between them through his childhood and adolescence. Still, his destitution and his spiritual orphanhood did nothing to eclipse the pleasure that he found, from an early age, in drawing.
There was no explaining de Kooning’s aptitude for art. Though he didn’t get far in his formal education—he left school at the age of twelve, and that was that—his teachers noticed his talent, and so did Cornelia’s second husband, Jacobus Lassooy, a barkeep. Because drawing was a marketable skill, Lassooy took the boy to various places to see if he could get work. He was accepted as an apprentice at a design firm that specialized in interior decoration. De Kooning’s renderings there were strong enough that, after some time, his boss encouraged him to apply to the Academie van Beeldende Kunsten en Technische Wetenschappen, a technical art school in Rotterdam.
In the school’s drawing program, de Kooning copied classical works, mostly from Greece. He was also trained in commercial art. The experience forever bonded him to artisans. As Mark Stevens and Annalyn Swan point out in their definitive 2004 biography, “De Kooning: An American Master,” the young de Kooning’s development was unlike that “of many later artists, who grew up when becoming an artist was considered more a matter of temperament than of know-how. De Kooning began by learning the hows, rather than the whys. His hand led his mind.” Rotterdam was a port town, and its red-light district, full of music and women—and conveniently situated near the Academie—was one of the jazziest in Holland. That scene, the energy of it, nourished de Kooning: the accidents of life, the meetings and partings in an environment dominated by sound, fed his imagination, as did his dreams of freedom, and of becoming an artist.
After finishing his fourth year at the Academie, de Kooning went to work as a commercial artist for Cohn Donnay and Company, a large department store. His supervisor, Bernard Romein, encouraged the restless youth to stay in school and helped open his mind to the world of art. The De Stijl movement, Mondrian, Bauhaus: Romein turned de Kooning onto all of this. But Holland was a backwater when it came to modern art. In 1924, de Kooning spent time in Belgium—to prepare himself, he said, for going to America—and while there he drew a series of cartoons. We see a bunch of them at the beginning of “Willem de Kooning Drawing”: light, all-on-the-surface illustrations. The best one, untitled and executed in Conté crayon and pencil (ca. 1924), shows a girl, perhaps in her early teens, holding a dark balloon, while a boy beside her grips a lighter-colored one, on a shorter stick—a not insignificant psychological detail. There are two younger boys to the girl’s left, but the girl is the emotional center of this piece. Stevens and Swan, among others, identify this drawing as an early example of de Kooning’s fascination with the female figure and power, but, at the show, I was less interested in the cartoons than in the part they played in his move to America.
The work that excited de Kooning in those years was the illustration he saw in American magazines. He wanted to be an illustrator, and in 1926, when he was twenty-two, without saying goodbye to his family he stowed away on a freighter and travelled to Hoboken, New Jersey. By 1927, he was in Manhattan, living in the kind of here-but-where limbo that characterizes the immigrant experience. At first, de Kooning found work painting signs and designing window displays. In 1935, he was hired by the Federal Art Project of the Works Progress Administration to create murals, and although the gig lasted barely two years, it was pivotal in helping him give up his commercial mind-set and concentrate on the difficult task of finding his own voice as a visual artist. At the W.P.A., de Kooning could work on a larger scale, but what story would he tell to fill this new expansiveness?
New York opened the world of modern art to de Kooning. Admired for his seriousness and for his eagerness to learn, as well as for his movie-star face and sturdy body, de Kooning was a looker in a city full of lookers. He went from a paucity of love to a series of sometimes overlapping, complicated relationships. He was also porous, open to being claimed by older artists, as he had been by his mentors in Holland. The New York that he settled in was teeming with new, experimental talent, including Stuart Davis and Arshile Gorky, who had fled Armenia during the genocide and with whom de Kooning shared a close and uneasy friendship—but what other kind is there between mentor and protégé? De Kooning relied on the experience of more seasoned artists to tell him who to become. Gorky was using European traditions—Roberto Matta’s Surrealism, Picasso’s neoclassicism, Cézanne’s explorations—to make work that captured New York’s sexiness, skittishness, and force. The mind-and-eye-expanding “Water of the Flowery Mill” (1944), like a number of his other paintings, builds on a series of lines that coalesce in an expanse of colors that shadow and seemingly swim away from one another. Gorky’s art not only presaged the Abstract Expressionism of which de Kooning would become a towering figure; it also pointed the way to color-field painting.
It’s moving to spend time at “Willem de Kooning Drawing” looking for Gorky; it’s like searching for any unknowable father. Gorky and Davis are evoked, rather than imitated, in “Three Studies of Men” (1938). The drawing shows one man sitting, one standing, and one almost fading into the background. The standing man waves an admonishing finger at the passive, seated one; he is perhaps an older man looking at a younger friend or a student. The drawing has the feeling of a dream—that dream in which you unwittingly let your mentor down. I believe that Gorky also shows up in the great “Self-Portrait with Imaginary Brother” (ca. 1938), which isn’t at the Art Institute, though you can find it in the show’s catalogue. In the drawing, two male figures are rendered in pencil. They stand together, their hands almost touching; one holds a ball, the other a pencil. The symbolism would be comical if they didn’t look out at the viewer with such tenderness, a tenderness that inhabits the drawing itself, which is faint, as though you were seeing it through mist or memory. At the Academie, de Kooning had learned to “smudge”—to rub the fine lines of a pencil drawing with his fingers—a way of visually marrying technique with what I see as the accident of feeling, a controlled mistake. By smudging himself and another male figure, perhaps inspired by Gorky, de Kooning brought his emotional life, his desire, to the page, just as Rauschenberg would do, fifteen years later, when he smudged de Kooning.
Again and again, I returned to works in which men were de Kooning’s focus, because I wanted to see the division in de Kooning’s art between the romantic and the sexual. I don’t think he was able to bring the two together, at least not with ease, given the romance of his drawings of men and the ferocity and the staggering sexuality he conveyed in his “Women” series, which he began in 1950. In an unpublished 1971 interview with the critic Harold Rosenberg, de Kooning said, “I was painting those male figures . . . but I found out that that didn’t get me anywhere.”
Men had loved and helped de Kooning from the time he was a boy, but because of this he could go only so far with them as subjects. What was missing in most of his early work was not just the drama of resistance that his mother had supplied but the drama of psychological exile, coupled with actual exile. You may try not to be like your parents, but still you create situations in which you are their child, over and over again. De Kooning was forever Cornelia’s scorned and abused boy. Mother and son meet up again in the painting “Excavation” (1950), though the work isn’t a portrait of Cornelia; it’s a portrait of where de Kooning’s anguish about his mother led him, a canvas that articulates his pain, the intimacy of anger, and the frightful, destructive epoch he was living in. (The show’s curators, Kevin Salatino, Mel Becker Solomon, and Charlotte Healy, have included a number of major canvases and sculptures, which help to anchor the more than a hundred and fifty drawings.)
De Kooning parked his “nice” side in his pencil portraits of men. The artist who made “Excavation” was someone else: inconsolable, wounded, wry, unforgiving. “Excavation” is one of the ugliest and most gorgeous modern paintings I have seen, a monster that swallows you whole. The main colors here are black and white, with flashes of red and blue. The artist said that “Excavation” was inspired by the neorealist Italian film “Bitter Rice” (1949), a depiction of workers in northern Italy which is dominated by the bodies of women. The painting shows a world of bodies, too, but they are fractured, and seemingly feed on other bodies and on birds and on paint itself. The drama here is rendered in sharp and round lines that stop and start, leading to other lines and to fragments of figuration: gaping mouths, elongated necks. All of these—the abstracted figures, the colliding lines—look as though they’re trying to escape the painting. It’s an emotionally claustrophobic and, in a way, hopeless work, but at the same time one that is thrilled by its own newness, the newness of its language.
“Excavation” screams as excruciatingly as Picasso’s “Weeping Woman” (1937) does, but in a different register. It was completed five years after the Second World War ended, in the intense early period of the Cold War. De Kooning needed that time to become more himself, so that the work could be more itself, too. There are no fully executed figures in it, no Cubist unity to pull the broken bodies together again. The painting exists as a whole because of the way de Kooning works and reworks the surface. It brings to mind newsreel images of Holocaust victims—prying camera eyes gazing at mountains of bodies, limbs tossed here and there, the dead shovelled on top of the dead. Abstraction was the mode of the fractured postwar world. But de Kooning, unlike his near-contemporary Jackson Pollock, believed that “even abstract shapes must have a likeness.”
De Kooning was still poor in 1950, but his reputation among critics and painters was growing. Part of his poetic and dramatic genius was in bringing together pieces of the world that American art hadn’t seen—or been willing to look at—before. He could do this because he was learning to face the complications of his adopted country, just as he faced the complications of his relationship to women. Psychoanalysis was a hip thing to talk about and sometimes experience in de Kooning’s bohemian circles, but the artist, without necessarily being aware of it, showed us, in his “Women” series, what it actually looked like, and thus felt like, to uncover one’s primal feelings. No doubt buoyed by the success of “Excavation”—which was included in the Venice Biennale and, the following year, in an exhibition of abstract painting and sculpture at
MoMA
—de Kooning wanted to delve deeper into this new psychic freedom, to find more of what he knew or could face imagining. His ethereal drawing of his wife, the wily and captivating Elaine de Kooning—whom he married in 1943 and never divorced, although they were separated for decades—is as romantic as de Kooning gets, which is to say that Elaine, in that drawing, might as well have been one of his men. But in the works that followed de Kooning’s elegant, sure-handed lines were disturbed once again.
In the “Women” series, the real and the mythic, memory and reality, wrestle for pride of place in de Kooning’s consciousness. He may be strong, but when he pushes these women they push back, and in that heated exchange the viewer is likely to get burned. In the fascinating charcoal drawing “Monumental Woman” (1953), a woman exists in a series of swirls; we see her belly, her breasts, but she seems to be asking if we’re seeing enough of her. On the left side of the drawing are a series of markings that may be hair—or perhaps they’re de Kooning trying to get the woman, and by extension himself, to shut up. Neither he nor the woman wins, and neither will be silent—about the soul’s relationship to desire, at least, which can only be misunderstood or misinterpreted. “Two Women” (1951-52) is less robust than “Monumental Woman,” and it affords us the opportunity to see the fineness of de Kooning’s hand in what at first appears to be a quieter sphere. The two women—but there seem to be three—are at the center of the field, with air around them. The main figure has a tiny head, while the others are a series of smudged pencil markings. The drawing is an abstraction of flesh, floating in a kind of amusement-park world: de Kooning’s New York. To spend any time with this magnificent piece is to see the body at work, a wall of stretched and stretching limbs, a modern version of the Three Graces, who stand there not to be admired but to be claimed by the only thing they understand: distance.
“Two Women” and other pencil drawings from the same period show us de Kooning in relation less to visual art than to theatre and dance: especially George Balanchine’s “plotless” ballets, such as “The Four Temperaments” (1946) and the ever-astonishing “Agon” (1957). The Russian-born Balanchine—another émigré artist who survived a brutal, forlorn childhood with his poetry intact—dressed his dancers in black and white leotards, the colors of New York cool. Like Balanchine, de Kooning made images for the mind about the body as it was expressed in the streets of the city. Sometimes, when I watch Balanchine’s choreography, I can’t help imagining “Monumental Woman” and other drawings from the “Women” series flashing behind the dancers as they embody de Kooning’s symphony of flesh. ♦

What Carla Lalli Cooked After Her Divorce
On and Off the Menu
What Carla Lalli Cooked After Her Divorce
With “Food Is a Feeling,” the cookbook author joins a lineage of writers who have explored the appetites of the newly unmarried.
By Hannah Goldfield
September 07, 2026
In 2012, the poet Sharon Olds published a collection, which would later win the Pulitzer Prize, about the dissolution of her thirty-two-year marriage. She called it “Stag’s Leap,” after her ex-husband’s favorite wine label. In one poem, “Attempted Banquet,” she describes a summer meal they’d hosted not long before they split—“lugging of shellfish in coolers, boiling / and bouillabaissing”—and her realization, later, that behind his “joyless labor / in the heat” and the salmon that “​​undulated out the kitchen door in its / half-slip of thin cucumber scales” lay the fact that he’d been planning to leave her. Too few guests attended, she writes,
and the wasted food was like some kind of
carnage. We lived on it a week, as we’d been
living, without my seeing it,
on the broken habit of what was not lasting
love.
In Olds’s poem, food is both poignant metaphor and quotidian backdrop, evidence that life happens even as it’s falling apart. It plays an analogous role in Nora Ephron’s 1983 novel “Heartburn,” a seminal divorce text which appears to fictionalize the dramatic end of her marriage to the journalist Carl Bernstein. Ephron’s narrator and alter ego, Rachel Samstat, writes cookbooks and hosts a TV show. Even as she divulges the humiliating circumstances that lead to the breakup—she discovers that her husband is cheating on her while she is seven months pregnant—she expounds matter-of-factly and almost cheerfully on food, weaving more than a dozen recipes into the narrative. Some encapsulate wistful memories (bread pudding eaten on a romantic trip to New Orleans); others Rachel’s efforts to comfort herself: “Nothing like getting into bed with a bowl of hot mashed potatoes already loaded with butter, and methodically adding a thin cold slice of butter to every forkful.” She includes instructions for the Key-lime pie she throws in her husband’s face the night she realizes that the relationship is unsalvageable, and for the vinaigrette she teaches him to make on the surprisingly tender night before she moves out.
In the literature of divorce, food is often marked by its absence—by the rupture of routine, the disappearance of appetite, and the sudden weight loss that is almost inevitably framed as a morbid silver lining. “Maybe it’s God’s way of gearing you up to go back into the dating world,” the actress and writer Isabel Gillies suggests in her 2009 memoir “Happens Every Day.” Gillies’s book, a tale of Waspy spousal desertion, was, perhaps, ahead of its time; it didn’t capture the Zeitgeist in the way that Belle Burden’s “Strangers” did this year. (Which is a shame—Gillies’s book is vivid, funny, and self-aware where Burden’s skews grim and self-serious.) Burden, too, grew thinner after her husband left. “I can see how you’re suffering,” she remembers an acquaintance telling her.
Yet the newly single woman—it’s almost always a woman writing a divorce book—is also prone to culinary epiphany. In many stories, the end of a marriage prompts the rapturous rediscovery of tastes, habits, carnal desires. Gillies recounts being miserable at brunch with her children and soon-to-be ex-husband until she takes a bite of a dish that seems to demand, she writes, “a culinary leap of faith”: pancakes made with asparagus, ham, and Gruyère, topped with fried eggs and served with maple syrup. “It was sublime,” she writes. “I called out, ‘Sweet lord, these are incredible!’ . . . At that very moment, my life was being saved. I thought if I could get such a kick out of these pancakes, I hadn’t died.”
Elizabeth Gilbert’s “Eat, Pray, Love,” the defining divorce memoir of the early two-thousands, is animated by a similar evangelism. If Gilbert’s soliloquy on Neapolitan pizza is insufferably cute—“I love my pizza so much, in fact, that I have come to believe in my delirium that my pizza might actually love me, in return”—a passage about needing larger pants is genuinely moving. “I came to Italy pinched and thin,” Gilbert writes. “I did not know yet what I deserved. I still maybe don’t fully know what I deserve. But I do know that I have collected myself of late—through the enjoyment of harmless pleasures—into somebody much more intact. The easiest, most fundamentally human way to say it is that
I have put on weight
. I exist more now than I did four months ago.”
This month, Carla Lalli, a former
Bon Appétit
editor and a best-selling cookbook author, will publish “Food Is a Feeling,” a cookbook-as-divorce-memoir. Though it resembles her other two books, “Where Cooking Begins” (2019) and “That Sounds So Good” (2021)—bibles of technique and inspiration for the busy yet ambitious home cook—Lalli announces, in the introduction, that she’s trying something different. Throughout her career, she’d been advised to maintain a consistent and upbeat writing voice, but she’d recently gone through a metamorphosis, prompted by the end of her twenty-four-year marriage. “With due respect to my former self and to anyone who has cooked my dishes before,” she writes, “it didn’t feel right that my recipe voice should stay the same, because I am not the same.”
Recipe development can be a self-effacing task, obliging the writer to anticipate the appetites and routines of her imagined reader. Lalli’s new recipes, interwoven with essays, are proudly idiosyncratic, tracing the contours of a “tumultuous, pensive, painful, joyful, transformative, celebratory, solitary, and exciting time in my life.” The book begins with a dish that Lalli improvised for dinner with her sister on the night that she moved into a sublet apartment: “Greens, Garlic, and Mom Rice,” with the rice cooked in butter, as their mother prefers. She shares the “Separation Pork Chops” she served after she and her ex-husband broke the news to their children, and the heart-shaped chicken cutlets she made for herself and her younger son after their household cleaved in two. Lalli’s ex hated tomatoes, especially raw ones with their “gooey guts,” she tells us, before pointedly providing a trio of recipes that accentuate their “amniotic” juices and “messy, pulpy” flesh.
In her solitude, Lalli was “flooded with memories” of cooking and being cooked for, and felt inspired to eat whatever she felt like, whether that was popcorn for dinner or a spontaneous glass of sake (against the advice of her therapist). She told me recently that she bucks against the idea that “eating your feelings” is negative, because cultivating a reader’s emotional connection with food is part of her job. “As food writers, we talk about how great it’s going to be when you make this meal for other people, and how lovely of a time you’re going to have—I love these feelings,” Lalli said. Why, she wondered, have we remained attached to the image of “someone creeping down to the freezer at two in the morning to eat Dove bars in secret”?
Rather than feel ashamed of her private bedtime snack, Lalli canonizes it in an arch recipe for “Night Cereal”— a chic Brooklyn mom’s alternative to Liz Lemon’s “night cheese.” It’s made with ice-cold rice milk, a “heaping cup” of crunchy cereal, frozen blueberries straight from the bag, “a few whispers” of maple syrup, and a pinch of flaky sea salt. “The extreme coldness of the milk makes it hard to eat the cereal quickly, stretching the experience—layers of flavors and textures, the spoon, the bowl, the crunches, and the slurps,” Lalli explains. “Night cereal had the power to turn my mood around.” “When I finished,” she adds, seeming to relish the innuendo, “I felt content, taken care of.”
To sell the book, Lalli had to convince her editor and publisher that “the conversation had changed around divorce,” she told me. They worried about portraying food as something other than “the fun bits”; her aim to convey “that food exists in hard times, and as a form of coping” seemed to freak them out. The book’s tone can be frank and disarmingly raw, occasionally veering toward the woo-woo: “Breathe so your belly rises. Commune with animals,” Lalli intones in a list of mantras for anyone feeling out of sorts. “The thing about spring is that it always comes back, you just have to wait,” she recounts saying in a toast at a vernal-equinox party, which, she notes, moved one or two people to tears.
I didn’t cry reading “Food Is a Feeling,” though I felt validated, and a little relieved, by Lalli’s account of grieving a version of herself. After a close friend died earlier this year, I experienced some of what she describes in the book: a powerful, if painful clarity of want and need; a heightened, nearly euphoric bodily awareness. At first, I’d given myself a hard time about my sudden yen for my children’s chicken fingers and French fries, and my impulse to order a second margarita; through Lalli’s lens, these simply seemed like the things that I required. Luckily for the rest of us, what Lalli required was typically inventive and satisfying: caramelized Japanese sweet potatoes with labne, black vinegar, and chili crisp, to help her build muscle while strength training; a “personal pot of beans and greens,” seasoned emphatically with anchovies, fennel and coriander seeds, turmeric, and Aleppo pepper.
A few years ago, I adopted one of Lalli’s kitchen maxims, “always be downsizing,” or A.B.D.—she recommends continually moving the contents of your refrigerator and pantry to size-appropriate containers as you make your way through them, to keep the shelves uncrowded. As I read and cooked from “Food Is a Feeling,” the slogan started to seem, too, like a metaphor for life. “Every time you finish what you need to do with an ingredient and relocate it,” Lalli wrote last year in her newsletter, “You create space for yourself.” ♦

epub_32.text:
The Prolific Storytelling of This Is Lorelei
Pop Music
The Prolific Storytelling of This Is Lorelei
Nate Amos writes songs that both embrace and lampoon dusty singer-songwriter tropes.
By Amanda Petrusich
September 07, 2026
In the summer of 2024, Nate Amos released a record called “Box for Buddy, Box for Star” under the sobriquet This Is Lorelei. (The name is a reference to an episode of “Star Trek: The Animated Series.”) The ten-song album felt like a kind of début, though Amos had already established himself as half of the art-pop duo Water from Your Eyes—his project with the musician Rachel Brown—and uploaded hundreds of scrappy, idiosyncratic folk songs to Bandcamp, starting in 2014, when he was a twenty-two-year-old college student living in Chicago. “Box for Buddy” is suffused with heartache—the narrators of these tracks are choking on the backwash of poisonous relationships—but it’s also a playful, visionary album that both embraces and lampoons dusty singer-songwriter tropes. It seesaws between woeful love songs that are set to acoustic guitar and toy piano (“Where’s Your Love Now”) and woeful love songs that are laced with Auto-Tune and keening synthesizer (“Dancing in the Club”).
With Brown, Amos makes twinkly, off-kilter experimental songs that sometimes sound as though they’re being piped out of a cursed music box. “Box for Buddy” earned him comparisons to Neutral Milk Hotel and the Postal Service, artists beloved for their urgency and their tenderness. A “super deluxe” version of the album, released earlier this year, features covers by a murderers’ row of indie musicians, including Waxahatchee (“Where’s Your Love Now”), MJ Lenderman (“Dancing in the Club”), Snail Mail (“Two Legs”), and Power Snatch (“Perfect Hand”), Hayley Williams’s duo with the producer Daniel James. Last December, during a solo piano show in Los Angeles, Cameron Winter, the front man of the band Geese, performed a soaring and intensely plangent version of “Where’s Your Love Now,” a song about looking back with a mix of bitterness and clarity: “I said, where’s your love now? / Long after your song is over / You left me to drink, I thought I’d die in my sleep / But I’m healthier now.” Amos’s current popularity nods, seductively, to an earlier era, in which artists were discovered not via algorithmic meddling but by the endorsement of their peers and old-fashioned word of mouth.
“It’s been very trippy, getting to know all those covers,” Amos told me this summer, over lunch at a Himalayan restaurant in Ridgewood, Queens. “It almost feels like a proud-parent moment. The song survived adolescence, and now it’s its own functional thing.” This month, Amos will release “The Singer in My Band,” his second full-fledged album as This Is Lorelei, and his most elemental and concise work yet. “I love a forty-five-minute album,” he said. “But, honestly, that’s a lot of prolonged attention to ask of people, with things being the way they are. So I figured I would shave ten minutes off that and be, like, Come on, lock into my thirty-four minutes. You can do this!”
Amos wrote, engineered, performed, and produced the record himself, excepting some banjo playing by his father, Bob, and occasional backing vocals by both his sister, Sarah, and his fiancée, the bassist Al Nardo. It’s the first release where Amos’s Americana bona fides—he grew up in a family of bluegrass musicians, mostly in Winchester, Virginia, a center for Appalachian music—feel evident. “I didn’t really attempt to play guitar until fifth grade,” Amos said. “By then, I had seven years of just sitting at bluegrass jam sessions and observing. The thing with bluegrass is that everything is a rhythm instrument—with the exception of the fiddle, sometimes—so it’s as if everyone is operating a giant musical drum set, and if one person isn’t holding their own then the whole thing completely collapses.”
“The Singer in My Band” sounds tighter and more expensive than Amos’s previous LPs. His voice, which is grainy and earnest, is often doubled in the mix, though when he leaps into a higher register, as he does on the single “Oh No Now My,” it sounds airy, almost celestial. These are hooky, likable songs about rambling around, encountering oddball characters, receiving their wisdom and warnings, and then keeping it moving—part Robert Frank, part Robert Altman, with a minor but hallucinatory dose of Hunter S. Thompson. Many have the gentle, foggy quality of a Polaroid: dim, half remembered, fleeting. “I always think about this Mitch Hedberg joke, that photos of Bigfoot aren’t blurry, they’re actually in focus—he’s just a blurry monster,” Amos said. He has come to think of the album’s structure in literary terms, comparing it to Ray Bradbury’s “The Martian Chronicles”: “It’s a larger narrative, but it’s told in short-story form.” His writing is unusually rife with proper nouns—Buddy, Sarah, Evie, Genevieve, Billy, Joey, Miss B. When I asked him if the work feels explicitly autobiographical, he paused. “I mean, there isn’t anything on this album that I haven’t experienced in some capacity,” he said. “But my approach toward writing is not so much trying to tell a specific story or communicate a particular thing but to create a kind of playground for the listener’s subconscious to build their own story.” It struck me as a generous impulse—confessional songwriting is often framed as a kind of bloodletting for the writer. “The way I’m thinking about it is, I’m forcing the listener to do their end of the work,” he said.
As a kid, Amos listened to a lot of the Beatles and Stevie Ray Vaughan, though for the past two and a half months, he said, “I haven’t really listened to anything other than ZZ Top. I’m beginning to be slightly worried.” Amos has also been publicly ebullient about his devotion to Blink-182’s “All the Small Things,” a goofy pop-punk hit from 1999. “That’s a God-tier pop song,” he said. “I got really fixated on that song in a way that, honestly, in hindsight, was not normal. I wasn’t even listening to the original recording. I was just finding every cover of that song I could possibly find and putting it on a giant playlist.” He admired the track for its agility, its economy, and its ability to transcend genre (the lyrics, essentially a series of grunts, are incidental to its melodic pleasures). “A sign of a really tight pop song is that it translates to all these different formats really well,” Amos said. The same, of course, is true for Amos’s work—distilled to its essence, and free of affectation, it remains enormously poignant.
After lunch, we took an Uber to the Cage, a baseball complex in Middle Village, a quiet, mostly residential part of Queens. In 2005, the Cage was opened by Ross (the Boss) Friedman, a founding member of the pugnacious and seminal punk band the Dictators, stalwarts of the early CBGB scene. (In 1978, both the Dictators and Bruce Springsteen were recording at the Record Plant, a beloved studio on West Forty-fourth Street; per punk lore, Springsteen shouts the “One, two, three, four!” count at the top of the Dictators’ “Faster and Louder.”) Friedman, who also played lead guitar in the metal band Manowar, passed away in March, and the Cage is now operated by his son Jesse. There’s something sort of ineffably rock and roll about the place—maybe it’s the hundreds of fist-shaped craters punched into the ceiling, evidence of fly balls careening toward Heaven and meeting plaster. As we selected our equipment, I asked Jesse if he had any advice before we went in. He gave me the kind of withering look you can receive only in the outer boroughs of New York City. “Don’t die,” he said.
Amos and I set our machine to a moderate lob and started swinging. Amos is a good batter: steady, confident, strong. He got off some dingers. The Cage felt like a useful spot to work out any resentments lingering in your psyche, all the old grievances dissipating with the clang of aluminum on cowhide. Afterward, standing on the sidewalk, we agreed that it seemed as though we’d accomplished something important. “It’s like a step up from bowling or mini-golf. How do we make mini-golf more extreme, so it’s dangerous?” Amos joked. “I think we did really good,” he concluded, lighting a cigarette. “We didn’t die.” ♦
