Seeing It All Hang Out at the Fringe
The Theatre
Seeing It All Hang Out at the Fringe
Twenty-odd shows from Edinburgh’s annual avant-garde rumspringa.
By Emily Nussbaum
September 03, 2026
The strangest, most beautiful thing I saw at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe felt less like theatre than like mass hypnosis. In the silky, largely wordless “Dracula: Lucy’s Dream,” by the French-Norwegian troupe Plexus Polaire, Bram Stoker’s orange-haired Victorian waif Lucy, her body jellyfished into a loose nightgown, gets stalked and bitten by Dracula night after night as she darts among drifting monoliths. But the viewer is quickly disoriented, thrown by the presence of at least three Lucys onstage, not to mention a murder of Draculas, some of them hinge-limbed, human-size puppets eerily indistinguishable from the actors manipulating them. Each morning, after Lucy’s panicked helpers struggle to shake her awake, the cycle begins again, punctuated by lurid tableaux: three Lucys cradle three babies, then bite their tiny necks; a tri-headed Lucy kicks and hisses at her nurses. When the show ended, the audience burst into rattled applause, as if we’d been woken from our own dream, still unable to tell the reverie from the real thing.
That kind of bracing communal experience is exactly why people attend the Fringe, an event that launched, in 1947, as a thumb in the eye of a mainstream arts festival in the city. This was my first time attending, and though I know that the Fringe has changed a lot—it’s at once an avant-garde rumspringa and a bid for “Fleabag” fame—it was still a delirious spectacle, a choose-your-own-adventure of more than four thousand shows, featuring combo platters of standup, improv, clowning, drag, musical theatre, drama, circus performance, and burlesque. (Then, there’s the occasional shock show in which a performer, say, drinks his own urine.) In four and a half days, I saw twenty-one shows—twenty-two, if you count ten minutes of standup in a pitch-black dungeon. But even the duds were worth it. By Sunday, I felt not unlike Lucy: drained but craving just a little more.
Of dozens of venues, the most unusual was a sauna erected behind Summerhall, where I slipped into a bathing suit, then reclined with six fellow-guests on tiered wooden benches that surrounded radiant rocks. As the heat softened us into linguine, we absorbed audio excerpts of “The Waves,” Virginia Woolf’s incantatory “play-poem,” recorded by actors. Meanwhile, two sauna masters shovelled ice infused with fragrant oil onto the rocks and performed an Aufguss, a German ritual in which towels are twirled to spread scented air. During intermissions, we dipped into a frigid pool. I’m not sure how much the towel dance added, but the sensory overload hit me like a love drug, intensifying “The Waves,” with its braided soliloquies, and heightening the feeling that our individual minds were lapping like waves within a broader consciousness. That rush of insights went unscribbled, since notebooks don’t make sense in a sauna. But I left joyful and shocked, dizzy to my heels.
As it happened, both “Dracula” and “The Waves” also turned up in a very different context: Garry Starr’s bawdy, disarming “Classic Penguins,” a one-man show that is coming to New York this month, at the intimate Studio Seaview. In Edinburgh, at the enormous Pleasance Grand, the audience filed in to find Starr—the alter ego of the Australian performer Damien Warren-Smith—seated and facing the back wall, naked but for a top hat, a huge ruffled collar, a gentleman’s tailcoat, and penguin flippers. He swivelled to face us, smoking a pipe, from which he calmly inhaled, “Masterpiece Theatre” style. Then he stuck the pipe into his asshole and, somehow, expelled smoke both from there and from his mouth. “The Aristocrats”!
The intro functioned as a jovial dare: all bets were off, for his body and for ours. A fit, middle-aged man with a twinkling, louche charisma, Starr swiftly laid out the show’s intent, which was to celebrate each of the Penguin Classics paperbacks, thereby elevating the glory of “literaturaaah.” What followed was a sort of highbrow “Jackass,” an exhilaratingly silly cavalcade of slapstick, dad jokes, and audience participation, as Starr thumped each book on a desk, its cover displayed on a screen, and then performed a goofball gag, the style of which ranged all over the map. For “Dracula,” Starr slurped down “blood”; then, with his abdomen grotesquely distended, he swapped out the book for Sartre’s “Nausea,” then pulled on a white bonnet for “The Handmaid’s Tale.” His “Wuthering Heights” featured aerial gymnastics and an air cannon. These stunts may sound crude, but—hear me out!—the group experience felt liberatory and oddly innocent, a joyful dropping of taboos that erased any easy line between smart and dumb. A lot of the show’s effectiveness had to do with viewers eager to play along. At one point, some enthusiastic geezers embraced our nude m.c., and I teared up at the moment’s intimacy; it felt like a masterly trust game, although I guess that’s true of all well-made theatre, naked or not.
Clowning—the extreme sport of comedy—is deep in the DNA of the Fringe. Still, several of the best things I saw were small, earnest acts, such as the lovely “Jitters,” a scripted two-hander, by Ellen Robertson, about a wedding-day showdown between a wannabe trophy wife (a very funny Charly Clive, all evo-psych self-justification) and her soon-to-be stepdaughter (Robertson, wryly acidic). It was a clash between millennial feminisms that could easily have curdled into polemic but instead felt fresh and surprising. My other favorite was “Lions,” a more madcap but equally heartfelt show about fathers, starring Scott R. Sheppard and Alice Yorke, the artistic directors of the gifted Philadelphia troupe Lightning Rod Special. “Our dads are dead! Thanks for coming,” they announced, as they stood before a table full of paternal detritus: a basketball, a record player. What began as an anarchic vaudeville act performed in dandyish masculinity drag (ascots, wacky mustaches) evolved, in smart, layered stages, into a bittersweet eulogy, as the performers used the props to reënact—and investigate—their fathers’ lives, down to their deepest disappointments, all while dramatizing the disorienting limbo of a family making end-of-life decisions.
I’d hoped to spot the next “Operation Mincemeat,” but instead the first musical I caught was a vapid, if impressively belted, princess tale, “Bliss,” a glittery bummer that resembled “Six,” minus the wit, or “KPop Demon Hunters,” only two notches hollower. Significantly better was “Evita Too,” a more gonzo girl-power celebration that was definitely not for kids. To be fair, Louise Mothersole and Rebecca Biscuit, the brassy duo behind Sh!t Theatre, could have booked a black box and still hooked viewers merely by reciting the surreal résumé of Isabel Perón, Juan Perón’s third wife. Instead, the pair wove incendiary themes of sex, fascism, and feminism into a clever meditation on the relationship between shaggy shows like this one and West End blockbusters such as the O.G. “Evita.” Like Garry Starr, they used every tool at hand, jumping merrily from nude roller-skating to investigative documentary, in a production that culminated with the alarming sight of a jumbo-sized Evita puppet corpse whose face bore a suspicious resemblance to Andrew Lloyd Webber.
Less developed, but still appealing, was “The Real Kyle McCarren,” a soulful homage to the dead friend and former bandmate of the show’s co-creator and star, Andy Roninson. Staged concert style, the musical had a cerebral mournfulness reminiscent of “Tick, Tick . . . Boom!,” with a killer cast and strongly crafted indie-rock numbers that found new angles on grief, many from the perspective of a man too awkward for a group hug. If the show faded toward the end—hobbled, perhaps, by an unwillingness to take big liberties with a true story—it had a throb of authentic, unforced emotionality.
On my final afternoon, I squeezed in another gutsy little musical, a drag-queen fantasia about climate change called “Acid’s Reign.” It ran late, so I race-walked across town to the King’s Theatre, excited to see Ivo van Hove’s five-hour minimalist deconstruction of Tony Kushner’s “Angels in America,” in Dutch, with subtitles, as part of the Edinburgh International Festival. Sadly, the production was a downer, draining Kushner’s masterpiece of color and humor and inserting, in their place, gloomy projections of cityscapes and, unaccountably, David Bowie songs. Maybe the idea was to strip away pageantry and get to a raw core, but now that Prior, the H.I.V.-positive gay man abandoned by his boyfriend, no longer wore drag, key jokes—“Ready for my closeup, Mr. DeMille!”—were incomprehensible. Bold edits, such as eliding the wild, mesmerizing “I— I— I— I” of the Angel and cutting the special effects that herald her arrival, left me cold—and it felt oddly untransgressive for Prior to be mystically aroused not by a terrifying female seraph but by a blond male hunk in nurse’s scrubs. Maybe because I’d rewatched the cult-classic Canadian TV show “Slings & Arrows,” which depicts a Shakespearean theatre festival, I was uncomfortably reminded of the show’s preeningly experimental director Darren Nichols siphoning the passion from “Romeo and Juliet” in favor of an arid landscape of signs and signifiers.
That let-down made me feel grateful for the many shows I’d seen at the Fringe that had sashayed down the bright path “Angels” had burned, in the nineties, by treating gay life as a default, drag as an art form, and queer humor and rage as paired, crucial qualities. Among these was a gloriously weird, mock-nihilistic act called “Creepy Boys: Slugs,” in which a queer Canadian clown duo struggle to stage a dazzling extravaganza empty of meaning, only to find that various
somethings
—guns, the climate, gender anxiety, sexual desire—keep penetrating the razzle-dazzle. The show climaxed in a Bonnie and Clyde-ish stickup, a demand for arts funding at the point of a gun. That’s probably not an ideal solution, but “Creepy Boys” did leave me longing for a way for performers to take bigger, more ridiculous swings back in New York, where recent chatter has been about the difficulty of sustaining anything risky for long, let alone for about twenty dollars a pop. We have Coachella and Sundance; we have Burning Man, an immersive carnival that is far out of reach for most people. Shouldn’t there be a true, supersized Fringe in the U.S., a safe space that lets a hundred clowns bloom? ♦

The Blockbuster Audacity of “Hope”
The Current Cinema
The Blockbuster Audacity of “Hope”
In Na Hong-jin’s monster movie, violent small-town comedy and big-budget Hollywood imperialism collide.
By Justin Chang
September 04, 2026
At the start of the giddily entertaining monster movie “Hope,” the director and screenwriter Na Hong-jin serves up a load of bull. No, really. We’re on the South Korean side of the Demilitarized Zone, and a large male bovine has been found slashed to death near an open field. Flies buzz over the rotting carcass, which is riven by claw marks so unnaturally deep that no one can determine whomauledit. A bear? Unlikely. Maybe, one man suggests, it was that tiger from the north—the one that, flouting the rules of peninsular diplomacy, often steals across the border in search of food. This is a joke, but a telling one; the characters in this movie are used to living on high alert. The small town that they inhabit may be called Hope Harbor, but it exists in an everyday purgatory of barbed-wire fences, undetonated land mines, and signs urging residents to “
report spies
” and “
protect the nation against infiltration
.” Who could have guessed that their worst enemy would hail not from across the border but from the skies?
The people of Hope Harbor don’t know it yet, but an alien invasion is under way—and Na, a horror-thriller maximalist of uncommon patience, takes his time breaking the news. Subscribing to Spielberg’s law, definitively proved in “Jaws” (1975), that the predators we don’t see are the ones that scare us the most, the director spends the first of this movie’s two and a half hours methodically setting the scene—which, in this case, means laying waste to the scenery. Rattled by the mystery of the bull, Bum-seok (Hwang Jung-min), the bumbling, trigger-happy police chief of Hope Harbor, drives back into town and is confronted with a disaster zone. “A freaking huge monster,” in the words of an irascible eyewitness, has torn through the village, gutting shops and homes and leaving bodies strewn amid the rubble. The cinematographer, Hong Kyung-pyo (“Burning,” “Parasite”), slows the camera to an ominous crawl as Bum-seok draws his weapon and tiptoes through the debris: broken beams, caved-in ceilings, bloodstained tiles, and piles upon piles of precious, ordinary, soon to be forgotten stuff. Admirers of Na’s previous films, none more bewitchingly bonkers than “The Wailing” (2016), will recognize the cluttered crime-scene handiwork of his longtime production designer, Lee Hwok-young. Buildings, like bodies, have innards, too.
There’s a dread-soaked wit to the movie’s drawn-out approach, especially in this first hour. We may think that we’re seeing the aftermath of a creature’s rampage, but we are, in fact, being introduced to the creature itself: we are what we destroy, Na seems to be saying. From this particular trail of devastation, we can deduce that the perpetrator is colossal, fast, and possessed of a strange mix of clumsiness and stealth. As Bum-seok zeroes in on his target, Na lures us into a crafty game of predator peekaboo; we can track the monster’s proximity through the explosions that it triggers in the vicinity and the lethal projectiles that it lobs from afar. Na is so good at this brand of menace by misdirection that, by the time you finally lay eyes on the monster, you might wish you hadn’t. For one thing, the creature, whom the end credits call Va’migere (and who is played, via performance-capture technology, by Cameron Britton), is properly fearsome to behold: an unjolly green giant that chases after Bum-seok on all fours, shrieks like an emphysemic banshee, and generally brings to mind the love child of the Incredible Hulk and “The Exorcist” ’s Regan MacNeil. But it is also, deflatingly, a computer-generated creepy-crawly, and unlike some other movie monsters—say, the amphibious kidnapper from “The Host” (2006) or the sharp-eared stalkers from “A Quiet Place” (2018)—Va’migere has a humanoid face and form, rendered with an almost hyperreal incongruity. It might have wandered, or crashed, into the movie from a decade-old zombie-apocalypse video game.
Na’s solution to this problem is speed: the faster he can keep his aliens moving—Va’migere, alas, is not alone—the less likely we are to scrutinize the malevolent jumble of pixels they are. The film’s first chase is a tour de force of kinetic delirium: Sung-ae (Hoyeon), a brave junior cop, drives Bum-seok through the streets of Hope Harbor, with Va’migere sprinting furiously after them. Hong, favoring a backward-facing view of the mayhem, shoots in lengthy takes that swerve and snake with rough-and-tumble precision; the energies of car and camera seem to fuse into one. Compare this with a similarly arresting later sequence, set deep within a magnificently mossy forest, where a band of hunters, led by Sung-ki (Zo In-sung, full of rascally charisma), do battle with Va’migere’s alien friends. If the street chase transplanted “Bullitt” to the D.M.Z., this earthier showdown, which puts Sung-ki and his fellow-fighters on horseback, has the verdant majesty of a woodland Western.
Here and elsewhere, Na stretches out the action to an almost luxuriant degree, and he makes a virtue of attenuation: a run-and-gun stunt that seems repetitive the third time is somehow smashing on the eighth. It helps that the aliens are almost as hard to kill as Wile E. Coyote, and, indeed, should you emerge from “Coyote vs. Acme” with your craving for comic violence unsated, you might consider going straight into “Hope,” which is something of a live-action cartoon writ large. (There’s a touch of the Tasmanian Devil to the way Va’migere crashes through walls, leaving behind vaguely Va’migere-shaped holes.) Yet Na also insists on treating his aliens as objects of contemplation and pathos—reflections of our own misshapen humanity. In one slow-motion scene, we peer into Va’migere’s wraithlike visage and see not just rage or monstrosity but an all too relatable terror. We are what we destroy.
All four of Na’s features were shown at the Cannes Film Festival, but “Hope” was his first to appear in the main competition. Predictably, its selection triggered the kind of reflexive critical grumbling that often ensues when a gory genre movie, be it “Oldboy,” “Drive,” or “The Substance,” is elevated to the highest of world-cinema pedestals. For some of us, though, Na’s upgrade seemed overdue. His films, all of which have been critically and commercially successful, have long blurred the lines between the aspirations of the art house and the pleasures of the grind house. I still can’t shake the grisly final moments of “The Chaser” (2009), a blisteringly cynical police procedural that takes a hammer to the mere notion of competence or integrity in law enforcement. Na’s films are propelled by brutal individual acts, but they also swarm with systemic rot. His finest movie, “The Yellow Sea” (2011), strands a debt-ridden Korean Chinese immigrant in the midst of a mob war, forcing him to run and run—and kill and kill—in order to survive. It’s bleak as hell; it’s also exhilarating.
“Hope,” which is Na’s first film in a decade, represents both a step up in ambition and a step down in finesse. The movie has a goofy, galumphing beauty; it’s a bigger, dumber, shinier object than its predecessors, yet it also manifests the crudely violent small-town comedy that is one of Na’s signatures. The people of Hope Harbor speak almost exclusively in barked expletives and insults, and nearly all of them are packing serious heat; Bum-seok’s irritation at the sheer glut of unregistered weapons becomes a sly running gag. One colorful customer spouts a fabulously ripe monologue about how the aliens nearly caught him mid-defecation—a close encounter of the turd kind. More disquietingly, several of Na’s characters seem at least as fond of the art of disembowelment as their alien overlords are: witness an overeager coroner merrily firing up a chainsaw as she tackles her first alien autopsy, or a village doofus (Eum Moon-suk) whose unfortunate taste for taxidermy may have set this entire tragedy in motion.
Whom, exactly, are we supposed to root for here? Bum-seok, Sung-ae, and Sung-ki do find a shambolic Hawksian unity, after a fashion; Sung-ae, in particular, has only to step out of a car with a military-grade rifle to elicit spontaneous applause. But Na’s most interesting countermove is to seed the enemy ranks with Hollywood actors, including Michael Fassbender, Alicia Vikander, and Taylor Russell—not that you’re likely to recognize them under their gobs of shape-shifting C.G.I. Belatedly, Fassbender and Vikander, sweetly cast as a sort of alien couple, are given the most soulful lines in the entire picture, though whether soul is called for is unclear; a script that boasts a five-minute soliloquy about diarrhea is suddenly rife with mythical earnestness and impenetrable last-minute world-building. Is Na, in merging unforgettable spectacle and unutterable dialogue, laying claim to the mantle of “Avatar”-era James Cameron? Does he yearn to put the “Na” in Na’vi? Perhaps this saga of planetary conquest is also a sly commentary on Hollywood imperialism, in which even the most far-flung of small-town tales must be overwhelmed by big-name stars in visual-effects drag. Na has clearly succumbed to the blockbuster mentality: as he confirmed at Cannes, a sequel is already written. Could the next movie begin to make sense of its predecessor’s hilarious and confounding final minutes? Hope springs eternal. ♦

Ode to Being Born with Teeth and Sharpening Them Every Day
Poems
Ode to Being Born with Teeth and Sharpening Them Every Day
By Barbara Hamby
September 06, 2026
If you like surprises, being born has to be the best,
one minute swimming in nothing, and the next
popping out into a hot late July day in New Orleans
like a gumbo of sweat and bad news,
because the war is over and your father has come home,
but others are lining up, ready to take his place
in the murderer’s row, rat-a-tat-tat and all that, the blood
that spills like ketchup from a broken bottle in lands
so far away they seem like a dream or a book written
by a mystic with time on his hands, and that’s all
you had then, acres of time, your teeth biting off
each day like a piece of rough bread and chewing it—
learning to eat, speak, walk, everything you needed
to take on the days ahead, and going to school,
you had to sharpen your teeth for that, like the time
in the third grade when some mean girls
were tormenting a boy who wore his pajamas under
his pants, probably because it was cold at home,
and when I said, “Leave him alone,” they ganged up
and sang, “Barbara and Scott sitting in a tree,
K-I-S-S-I-N-G,” which was so ludicrous that I turned
and walked away, and the engine of their malice
sputtered, crashing on the wooden floor of the classroom,
though how did I know to turn my back on them,
which is a question I ask myself every day, as in how
do I get from one to four, the hours when nothing
is syncing in my brain, and I feel as stupid as molasses,
but I still have my teeth, which are an asset
until the power grid in my brain box starts sending signals
to the thinking terminals, and I am myself again
instead of a wretched baby without teeth, crying
for my mama who has been dead for fifteen years,
but still lives in my heart, and why didn’t I ask her every
question I could when she was still walking
around reading Revelation, because I knew she could die
at any moment, and so she did—
Pop!
went something
in her brain, and she was off to her next adventure,
as good a death as anyone could wish for,
though it left a hole in my little world, which has closed
inch by nano-inch but without her archipelago
of selves: the laughing policeman, the Bible-thumping
sun worshipper, maker of box cakes, diviner of mistakes,
right-wing lover of those with broken wings, despiser
of lies, queen of the dream wreck, O Mama,
thank you for my body, with its gears and switches,
its cannisters of blood and ooze, its “On” switch
for love and hate, its black bile and dance moves,
its slide to the left when the jackboots approach,
its party hats and hard candy when the lights go out
and the hurricane is swirling in the gulf,
when the monsters rip off their masks to snarl and tweet,
O giver of all gifts, thank you for my teeth.

Letters from Our Readers
The Mail
Letters from Our Readers
Readers respond to Becca Rothfeld’s review of Rachel Cusk’s latest novel, Alexandra Schwartz’s piece about death doulas, and Zach Helfand’s Talk story about the Old News Newsstand.
September 07, 2026
Character Studies
Having read one Rachel Cusk novel, and intensely disliking its flat narrative voice, I was grateful for Becca Rothfeld’s review of Cusk’s latest book, “Life of M” (Books, August 24th & 31st). Rothfeld’s analysis clarified my understanding of my own reaction. In books such as “Anna Karenina,” we encounter particular lives, lived in textured and convincing times and places. Though Tolstoy begins the novel by telling us that all happy families are alike, he ironically insists on tracing the obstacles his characters face. Nothing about them is abstract or general; as a result, we are with them. This is what fiction has offered us and can still offer us.
Julie Diamond
New York City
As someone who was once mesmerized by Cusk’s “Outline” trilogy, I read Rothfeld’s critique with interest and, eventually, embarrassment. Were the novels really so intent on narrowly subjectivizing the world? Were some of the lines really that cheesy? Rothfeld is right that Cusk’s project of dismantling personhood can leave us with a void that is actually personhood radicalized, and thus anything but insightful or liberating. But I wonder if she has missed what made the trilogy so meaningful to many of us: the novels’ sharp depiction of the existential drift and dread that overwhelm the self when the structures that constituted it collapse.
To me, the “Outline” trilogy remains an original meditation on the old adage that we don’t know what we’ve got until it’s gone. We want to believe that the structures of a life and a self are like muscles: after being torn, they grow stronger. Cusk suggests something harsher and truer. Our selves can shatter without the relief of annihilation, leaving fragments that remain recognizably ours but can no longer make a whole. And, when the self fragments, we become hungrier for meaning. We subjectivize the world and grasp at pseudo-philosophical pronouncements because they might contain what we now lack. The trilogy’s conversations enact this dialectic of disappointment and discovery. We tire of the grandiosity and then suddenly encounter an insight that cuts more deeply because it has been sharpened by the rubble.
All this is more moving when staged within the novels than when taken up as an external, reflexive attempt to dismantle plot and character. Rothfeld is right to ask whether anything is left after the demolition, and righter still to suggest that Cusk’s project has run its course. But the riveting middle of that journey was worth the disappointment of watching it peter out.
Edward Hahn
Columbia Heights, Minn.
Last Gifts
I enjoyed Alexandra Schwartz’s report about death doulas and the evolution of hospice care (“End of Story,” August 17th). A detail many readers may have missed was the suggestion by the doula Virginia Chang that her client Eleanor Lennard donate her brain to science, and Lennard’s enthusiastic response. As a neuropathologist with a long career in clinical and research practice looking directly at the postmortem human brain, I can attest that donations like this are extremely valuable. Clinical biomarkers and neuroimaging do not hold all the answers; many disorders—such as Alzheimer’s and some types of strokes—still require postmortem analysis for diagnostic confirmation. Such donations offer many other public-health benefits. (It’s also worth noting that these donations cannot be made simply by having “organ donor” on one’s I.D. but must go through either a brain bank or the National Institutes of Health.)
R. D. Folkerth, M.D.
High Falls, N.Y.
Fit to Print
Although I otherwise appreciated Zach Helfand’s dispatch from the Old News Newsstand, which sells outdated copies of newspapers, there was one word in the piece that stood out to me as old news (The Talk of the Town, August 10th). Describing the owner’s appearance, Helfand writes that he wore a “button-down, unbuttoned, over a wifebeater.”
As an editor, I have at times found it hard to keep up with the number of progressive-leaning changes that institutions such as the A.P. have introduced to English-language stylebooks in recent years, but if I’d seen “wifebeater” nixed, I would’ve calmly agreed. Sure, the term is evocative for American readers, but it deeply offends some—by implying that people who wear them are prone to domestic violence—and makes no sense whatsoever to people from other countries. I once had to explain the term to a Pakistani colleague in a newsroom. Coming from a place where domestic violence is an endemic issue, she was aghast, and rightly insisted that we go with “sleeveless undershirt.”
The
New Yorker
might consider the same.
Ellery Roberts Biddle
Philadelphia, Pa.
If Aaron Reiss, the proprietor of the Old News Newsstand, really wants to specialize in the sale of stale news, he cannot responsibly omit the Los Angeles
Times
from his inventory. For a nominal sum, the paper each day serves up authoritative accounts of sports events that occurred as much as a day earlier, give or take. Perhaps that delay is the result of an idiosyncratic printing schedule. Some subscribers, of course, are unbothered that the L.A.
Times
delivers news more in the style of Pheidippides than Hermes. For that demographic, form is everything, and the paper acquits its pledge that every dog must have its daily.
Mark Steinberg
Los Angeles, Calif.
